topic_rules: DATA CAVEAT FIRST: ep01 got 43 views, but only about 20 came from impressions (862 x 1.97% = ~17 Suggested, 34 x 8.82% = 3 Browse, 0 Search). The other ~23 came from links, the channel page or direct visits. About 19 of the views were on phones. Trust the direction of every finding below, not its decimals. The Browse CTR of 8.82% rests on 3 clicks and may be the owner's own circle, so it does not prove the thumbnail works.

T1. Pick a concrete subject you can picture from 3 words: one named place, object or event (a specific lake, bay, island, flood, wreck or town). Ep01's subject was an abstract pattern spread across 7 landmasses ('continents point south'), and neither a thumbnail nor a phone screen can show that at a glance.

T2. The core payoff must be something you SEE change or appear, rendered photoreal by our engine: drain the water to show the floor (DEM seafloor), remove the ice, compare a coastline before and after, lay a true-size overlay, or fly into a place nobody can visit. An argument is not a payoff. Ep01's payoff (a Gondwana breakup explains the tips) was a chain of reasoning. Its one praised moment, the antipode overlay at 2:40-3:05, was a spatial reveal. Choose a topic whose story naturally contains 5-7 such reveals.

T3. The topic needs one clear, true answer that fits in a single sentence, with no hedging. Ep01's answer was 'They're not [a coincidence]. Not entirely.' A hedged truth leaves only weak packaging or clickbait. Reject topics whose honest answer is 'partly' or 'scientists still debate it'. Use a myth-busting frame only when the myth is widely believed and the correction is crisp; otherwise frame the video as a true story or a reveal.

T4. Give the film a human story spine with stakes: one event or protagonist, a timeline with a turning point, and real consequences (lives, money, a mistake, a survival). Use at most 3 named people in the whole film. Ep01 was the history of an idea (Bacon, Forster, Humboldt/Guyot, Green, Wegener, a magazine writer, a geologist) with no single protagonist, and the idea-history chapter is exactly where phone viewers left (they averaged 2:11, and chapter 1 ran to 2:15).

T5. The topic must show demand on both surfaces a new channel depends on (98% of ep01 viewers were non-subscribers, and 93% of impressions came from Suggested). (a) Search: the core phrase has real volume, roughly 50K or more estimated monthly searches, or a strongly rising keyword. Ep01 got 9 search impressions and 0 clicks. (b) Suggested 'host' videos: at least 3 existing videos on the same place or premise with 500K+ views, and at least one of them under 3 months old and still gaining (300+ views/hour, like the drain / without-ice / forbidden-island outliers). Our Suggested impressions come from sitting next to those hosts. Ep01 had no active host cluster, so YouTube tested it beside videos whose viewers did not want it (1.97% CTR).

T6. The angle must not be saturated. Reject the topic if 2 or more recent, well-made long-form videos with over 1M views already tell the same story from the same angle (check with the ytsearch probe). Aim for a proven premise applied to an untold place or angle.

T7. Give it a US anchor. The US was 28% of views but 43% of watch time, so US viewers watched about 1.9x longer than everyone else (43/28 vs 57/72). Prefer a US place, US stakes or a subject Americans know, and use US-familiar scale comparisons (miles, feet, football fields, Texas). It must still make sense to a global audience.

T8. Keep the geography phone-sized: the subject must work at regional zoom and fill at least a third of the frame. Avoid topics whose point needs the whole globe, or many small features on screen at once. Ep01 needed Greenland, Florida, Baja, Kamchatka and India on one globe, and each was a few millimetres wide on a phone.

T9. Pick a topic that gives viewers something to comment on: a personal stake or an opinion (have you been there, would you go, who was to blame, what would you have done). Ep01 got 0 comments and 0 shares.
packaging_rules: P1. Design for the Suggested feed on a phone first, because 93% of ep01's impressions were Suggested, at 1.97% CTR. Before upload, mock the package in DARK MODE at two sizes: the full-width phone card (about 390x220 pt) and the compact list/sidebar card (about 168x94 px). Place it beside the 5 strongest host-video thumbnails. If ours is not the most readable and brightest card in that strip, redo it.

P2. Title: 35-50 characters (ep01 had 55; the niche outlier median is 51; past about 45 characters, compact cards start to cut it off). Put the proper noun in the first 3 words, include one concrete noun the viewer can picture, and use no hedge words ('Not Just', 'Sort Of', 'Maybe', 'Kind Of'). Ep01, 'Why the Continents Point South (Not Just a Coincidence)', spent its bracket on a hedge instead of a cancelled obvious answer.

P3. Use the exact place or event words that the host videos and searchers use, so YouTube's content matching can place us next to them and Search can surface us. Then add our twist. Name the subject in the first spoken sentence and in the first line of the description too, because the transcript also feeds the matching.

P4. The curiosity gap must be a specific withheld thing the viewer already wants to know (what is at the bottom, why nobody may land there, what happened to the people). It must not be an abstract question the viewer did not have before seeing the card; ep01's 'POINTING AT WHAT?' needed the viewer to care about a pattern first. A statement that withholds one detail beats a vague why/what question.

P5. Thumbnail composition: one focal subject filling at least 50% of the frame. Use 0-3 words of text, each line at least 20% of the thumbnail's height, white on a black box with one accent-colour word. Use at most ONE graphic device (one arrow OR one ring). At least 40% of the area should be bright or saturated, never a navy-dominated background, which blends into dark-mode YouTube. Ep01's thumbnail had about 5 competing elements (3 orange continents, 3 arrows, a ring, a '?' and 3 words of text) on a dark navy map.

P6. The thumbnail image creates the gap by showing the BEFORE or PARTIAL state of the hero reveal: a half-drained basin, a shape under the water, a forbidden shore with one marker. The text adds emotion or stakes and never repeats the title.

P7. Frame 1 of the video is the thumbnail image in motion (keep this from ep01). The video delivers part of the thumbnail's promise on screen within 30 s and all of it by the end. That confirms the click and protects watch time and satisfaction.

P8. Targets: Suggested CTR of 5% or more (2.5x ep01) and overall CTR of 5% or more. Measure watch time per impression (CTR x average view duration): ep01 got about 5.2 s (2.27% x 231 s). The ep02 target is 15 s or more, about 3x.

P9. Upload 3 thumbnails to Test & Compare, but do not read the result before roughly 10K impressions. At ep01's 925 impressions, a 2% versus 3% difference is noise. Choose the default thumbnail with the mock-feed test in P1, not by gut.
hook_rules: H1. 0:00-0:03: frame 1 is the thumbnail in motion. The first spoken line names the subject and the stakes in 12 words or fewer. No logo, no title card, no intro sting.

H2. The first 10 s must work with the sound off. Home-feed inline playback on phones starts muted with captions, and viewers who arrive by autoplay from Suggested never chose the video. Use motion plus ONE big label, and upload accurate captions.
H3. By 0:15, state the single central question in the same words as the title or thumbnail, to confirm the click.

H4. By 0:30, show the first hero shot: the best photoreal spatial reveal in the film, including a partial view of the thumbnail payoff. Ep01's best shot, the antipode overlay, came at 2:40, after the average phone viewer had already left at 2:11.
H5. By 0:45-0:60, start the actual story at a specific person, place and moment. Open in the middle of the action if possible, then rewind.

H6. No menu or table of contents. Never use 'along the way', 'by the end you'll know' or a list of upcoming topics (ep01 did this at 0:37-0:54 with 'dig to China, an 1875 theory, future collisions'). Allow at most ONE forward promise, and it must be the story's own question.
H7. No historical asides, quotes, Latin, static portraits or 'history of the idea' dates in the first 2 minutes. Ep01's Bacon Latin quote over a static portrait (1:00-1:25) is the example to avoid.

H8. Density cap for 0:00-1:00: no more than 2 named people, 1 date and 1 number, with sentences of 15 words or fewer. Ep01's first chapter as aired (0:00-2:15) packed roughly 5 named people or sources, 5 dates or eras, 2 statistics and a 3-item menu, and phone viewers averaged 2:11.
H9. No hedging in the hook (ep01 said 'They're not. Not entirely.'). Commit to the true, clear claim.
H10. Something moves every second, and the camera is close (regional view). Never open on a slow whole-globe drift.

H11. Retention targets: 70% or more still watching at 0:30, 60% or more at 1:00, and mobile average view duration of 30% or more (ep01: 14.1%). The 0:30 and 1:00 figures are niche rules of thumb, not from our own data.
pacing_rules: C1. Cut cadence: ep01 averaged 10.75 s between hard cuts (93 cuts in 1,011 s). Ep02 target: a hard cut or a new visual event every 3-5 s, an average shot length of 5 s or less, and never more than 6 s without a new element. Ep01's QC flagged 25 near-static stretches longer than 3.5 s.
C2. Camera moves: point-to-point flights take 1.5-3 s with easing. Use slow drifts only underneath an overlay that is changing. 'Slow globe moves' were one of ep01's named phone problems.

C3. Text size for phones: in portrait, the 1920 px frame shrinks to about 390 pt (x0.2). Set labels at 64 px or larger at 1080p (about 13 pt on the phone) and key words at 90-120 px. Lines, arrows, borders and arcs that matter must be 8-10 px or thicker. Show at most 3 labels at once, and keep text out of the bottom 20% (captions) and the top 8%.
C4. Subject size: whatever the narration names must fill at least a third of the frame's width at that moment. Whole-globe shots last 3 s or less and take no more than 10% of the runtime.

C5. Idea budget: at most 2 new ideas per minute, at most 1 new named person per chapter (3 in the whole film), at most 1 spoken number per minute, and at most 5 big on-screen numbers in the whole film (owner rule: only a few big vivid numbers). Each number appears as a counter at least a quarter of the frame tall. Every idea is shown on screen, not only said.
C6. Narration: 150-160 words per minute and sentences of 15 words or fewer. Quotes stay under 10 words and appear only when the picture shows the action, never over a portrait.

C7. Re-hook every 60-90 s with a reveal, a change of location, an in-world gag or a new open question. Each chapter tops the one before it in stakes or spectacle. Ep01 peaked at 2:40, then slid into a history of ideas.

C8. Chapters: 5-6 chapters of 2-3 minutes each (ep01 had 9, averaging 1:44, the shortest 63 s). Chapter 1 is the hook and lasts 1:30 or less. Chapter titles tease in the story's own words: never the answer, never 'Intro' or 'Conclusion'. Each chapter = one sub-question + one hero shot + one mini-reveal + a last line that opens the next question.

C9. Payoff placement: the full answer to the thumbnail question lands at 85-90% of the runtime. Ep01 answered its core question at 9:13-10:43 (59-69% of the runtime), then ran about 4:50 of extra sections (the joke, what doesn't drip, future supercontinents).

C10. No call to action inside the story: no subscribe, like, 'Juice Check' or comment prompt before the final line. Ep01's 4:57-5:07 subscribe break interrupted the flow just before its strongest reveal. A recurring branded beat is allowed only if it is a story beat, not an ask.

C11. Humour: in-world visual gags of 3-6 s every 2-3 minutes, using characters on the real terrain and keeping the story moving. Funny lines in the script (like ep01's 'left the planet on the dashboard in July') stay, but each one gets a visual.
visual_rules: V1. One visual language for the whole film: a photoreal real-Earth base (the Blue Marble/VIIRS globe, DEM terrain and seafloor, NASA GIBS satellite patches), with one colour grade, one font, one accent-colour system and one label style from first frame to last.

V2. The CC0 low-poly characters appear only inside the photoreal scenes. They stand on the real terrain with matched lighting, shadows and believable scale, like figures on a relief model, never in a separate stylised set. Ep01's stylised corridor scene (7:35-7:50) clashed with the globe look. If a beat needs a set we cannot build photoreal, cut it or stage it on the terrain.
V3. Public-domain archival photos: 4 s or less each, always moving (Ken Burns), with the same frame treatment, and no more than 1 per minute. Never cover an aside with a static portrait.

V4. Build the film around the thing viewers loved: spatial overlays on the real 3D Earth that make an invisible relationship visible. The antipode overlay at 2:40-3:05 was called 'remarkably vivid and professional'. Plan 5-7 such hero shots: the first by 0:30, then one per chapter (about every 2 minutes), with the payoff as the last. The engine's natural hero shots are draining the water (DEM seafloor), true-size overlays, before/after coastlines, cut-aways and flights into places nobody can visit.

V5. Frame for the phone: use regional camera altitudes and keep the subject at least a third of the frame. Dim and desaturate the surroundings and colour the subject with a single accent (ep01's subject-highlight approach was right). Avoid dense maps with many borders, rivers and labels on screen at once.
V6. Give each moment one focal point. Do not stack a drift, a morph, labels and arcs at the same time; one thing moves meaningfully while the rest supports it.
V7. Keep the thumbnail, frame 1 and the payoff shot continuous: the same subject, the same accent colour and the same camera angle family, so the film visibly keeps the thumbnail's promise.
ending_rules: E1. The payoff is the last story beat. The final line answers the thumbnail question in one sentence over the final hero shot. No recap, no stacked closers and no speculative coda after the answer; ep01 put a recap and the future-supercontinent section after its answer.

E2. Within 0-3 s after the final line, give a one-sentence spoken hand-off to ONE specific next video on a related theme. Phrase it as a new question; if ep02 is a water or drain story, the channel's Lake Peigneur film is the natural pick. The aim is to keep the viewer watching our channel.

E3. The end-screen elements (YouTube's 5-20 s window) sit over a last shot that is still moving, never an empty or black frame. The whole end screen lasts 15 s or less, and the video cuts about 1 s after the hand-off line. Ep01's end cards came too early, over an empty frame.
E4. End-screen layout: the one specific next video, plus the subscribe element. The 'best for viewer' slot is secondary.

E5. At most one short subscribe line, folded into the hand-off and never before the payoff; leaving it out entirely is fine. The comment prompt lives in the pinned comment and in at most one closing sentence. Tie it to the story with an opinion or 'what would you do' question, not a generic ask (ep01: 0 comments).
result.target_length: 12:30-14:00, aiming for 13:00 (about 1,950-2,100 words at ~155 wpm), with a hard ceiling of 15:00 and the payoff at about 11:15-11:45. The reasoning: (1) Length was not what drove phone viewers away. They left at an average of 2:11, inside chapter 1, which points at the opening and its density, not the 15:34 runtime. Meanwhile desktop (7:53, 50.7%) and TV (8:24, 54.1%) viewers, the biggest share of US watch time, stayed for half of a 15-minute film. Going very short (around 10 minutes) would therefore give up watch time from the viewers who already liked the film. (2) Ep01 still carried dead weight: 77 s had to be cut in post, and about 4:50 came after the core answer. Its strong material was roughly 10-11 minutes. A 13-minute film with the answer at 85-90% of the runtime removes that tail. (3) The numbers: a 42% average view duration on 13:00 is 5:28 (ep01: 3:51), and 30% on phones is 3:54 (ep01: 2:11). At 5% CTR that gives about 16 s of watch time per impression, roughly 3x ep01's 5.2 s. (4) In the outlier pull, the spectacle formats won at 11-12 minutes (Antarctica without ice 11:21, all ice melted 11:58) and the story or forbidden-place formats at about 20-22 minutes (Iwo Jima 20:02, the Contour Atlas drains). 13 minutes sits between the two, inside the 10-18 minute rule. A story-heavy topic may run to 15 minutes only if each extra minute carries its own hero shot. (5) Staying above 8 minutes keeps mid-roll ads possible once the channel is monetized. (6) Production does not limit length: Colab renders about a minute of film per minute. The real limit is having 5-7 hero shots at roughly one every 2 minutes.
result.topic_vs_execution:
VERDICT: ep01's reach problem (CTR and Search) was mainly a TOPIC problem. Its phone-retention problem was mainly an EXECUTION problem, made worse by the topic. Topic is the bigger lever, because CTR decides how many impressions YouTube will ever test: ep01 got 925 in 35 hours, then stalled.

TOPIC PROBLEMS:
(1) Search demand was close to zero: 9 search impressions, 0 clicks. Nothing in execution could fix that.
(2) Most of the 1.97% Suggested CTR. The premise is an abstract pattern across 7 landmasses with a hedged true answer ('not entirely a coincidence'), and no active cluster of host videos existed. YouTube placed it next to videos whose viewers did not want it, and no thumbnail can sell an abstract, hedged premise to a viewer who is mid-video on something else.
(3) The structure was a history of an idea (a chain of thinkers from 1620 to the 1970s) rather than one event with a protagonist and stakes. That structure came from the topic, and it is where phone viewers left.
(4) The whole-globe scale made phone legibility hard by nature: many small features had to be on screen at once.
(5) No personal stake for viewers: 0 comments, 0 shares.

EXECUTION PROBLEMS (all fixable regardless of topic):
- A menu hook at 0:37-0:54.
- A Bacon static-portrait aside at 1:00-1:25.
- The best shot buried at 2:40, after the average phone viewer had left (2:11).
- A 'Juice Check / Subscribe' break mid-story at 4:57-5:07.
- A clashing stylised corridor scene at 7:35-7:50.
- About 10.75 s between cuts, 25 near-static stretches, small labels, dense maps and slow globe moves.
- The payoff at 59-69% of the runtime, followed by about 5 minutes of extra sections.
- End cards that came early, over an empty frame.
- A busy, dark thumbnail with about 5 competing elements, and a title bracket spent on a hedge.

NOT THE PROBLEM:
- The narration quality, the photoreal look and the 3D-overlay craft. A 50.7% average view duration on computers and 54.1% on TV for a 15:34 film shows the core craft holds attention on a big screen. The US (43% of watch time from 28% of views) was the audience that stayed.

MIXED:
- Phone retention of 14.1%: roughly half execution (opening, density, text size, cut pace) and half topic (abstract, global scale, no story spine).

SAMPLE-SIZE CAVEAT:
- About 20 algorithm-driven clicks and about 19 phone views. The directions are consistent with YouTube's own retention critique, but the exact percentages are noisy.

SOURCES:
- All Studio numbers and critique timestamps come from the context file.
- For ep01's actual title, thumbnail, chapter times, cut cadence and opening script, I also read ep01's own release package: /home/user/juicytea-media/longform/ep01-continental-drip/release/metadata.md, /home/user/juicytea-media/longform/ep01-continental-drip/release/thumb_B_pointing_at_what.jpg, /home/user/juicytea-media/longform/ep01-continental-drip/README.md (QC: 93 cuts, 10.75 s apart, 25 static stretches) and /home/user/juicytea-media/longform/ep01-continental-drip/research/script_locked.json.
- No vidIQ tools were called.

candidates.working_title: The Dutch Actually Drained a Sea. They Found 400 Ships at the Bottom.
candidates.premise: Everyone else on YouTube pretends to drain a lake. The Netherlands really did it: they dammed and pumped dry most of the Zuiderzee, a sea of about 5,000 km2, and farmers ploughing the new seabed kept hitting shipwrecks, more than 400 of them, plus wartime bombers with their crews. The payoff is that a city of over 200,000 people (Almere) now stands on what was open sea when their grandparents were born, and the sea has tried to take it back.
candidates.archetype: The drain-reveal premise, done for real. Evidence: 'We Drained the Chesapeake Bay' 170K in 1 week and 'We Drained the Great Lakes' 165K, both on Contour Atlas with 1.4K subs; 'What Antarctica Looks Like Without Ice' 1.8M on 2.9K subs. Proven demand for the Dutch-vs-sea subject: 'How the Netherlands Built a Country Below Sea Level that Shouldn't Exist' (NextGen Manufacturing) 2.96M in 3 months, 'How People Live in Netherlands...' (Impossible Travel) 2.84M in 2 months, OBF 2.73M, Practical Engineering 3.45M. Every one of those takes the engineering or how-people-live-there angle. None asks what was lying on the seabed.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: a fresh polder field, 5 m below sea level and tens of km from any coast. A plough hits black oak. It is the hull of an 18th-century merchant ship, and there are hundreds more. (Use a documented find, e.g. the 2018 Groningen University excavation of an early-18th-century merchant ship in the Noordoostpolder.) MYSTERY/PROTAGONIST: how did a sea become farmland? The engineer Cornelis Lely planned it in 1891 and nobody would pay. BEATS: (1) The January 1916 storm flood drowns Marken and the shores, and the government finally says yes (Zuiderzee Act of 1918). (2) On 28 May 1932 the last gap in the 32 km Afsluitdijk is closed, which is great crowd footage in the CC0 Anefo archive. (3) The pumps start, the seabed appears and the shipwrecks surface: archaeologists race the ploughs, and about 430 wrecks are recorded, among the largest 'dry' ship graveyards in the world. (4) Schokland, an island village evacuated by royal order in 1859, is now an island stranded in a sea of grass. Urk, a fishing island, wakes up landlocked (funny animated beat). (5) The sky war: Allied and German aircraft that fell into the lake during WWII are still being dug out with their crews (the Lancaster ED603 recovery). TWIST: on 17 April 1945 retreating German troops blow two holes in the Wieringermeer dike and the sea takes the whole polder back in 48 hours. The Dutch drain it again within months. PAYOFF: Almere, a modern city of over 200,000 on the 1960s seabed, and the last polder, the Markerwaard, never drained, so its ships are still down there. Final line: in one lifetime a sea became a city.
candidates.hero_image: Top-down shot of a ship's ribcage, a 300-year-old wooden skeleton, lying in a bright green Dutch field with a tiny red tractor beside it. A blue water line floats high above it to show where the sea surface used to be.
candidates.mobile_fit: One huge, simple shape (ship skeleton) on one flat colour (green field) with one line (old sea level). It reads at thumbnail size, and the irony of a ship in a farm field lands in under 3 seconds. Inside the film, the before/after map morph of sea turning into land is a single bold change that works at phone size.
candidates.engine_fit: Excellent. The AHN national lidar DEM (open, 0.5 to 5 m) shows the polders below sea level at real scale. Rijkswaterstaat IJsselmeer/Markermeer bathymetry plus historical Zuiderzee charts give the 'drain' animation, and coastline morphs (1900 vs today) are natural for our engine. Public domain/CC0: the Nationaal Archief/Anefo photo collection (CC0) covers the Afsluitdijk closure, the polder works and the 1945 dike breach, with Rijksmuseum CC0 maps. Low-poly farmers, fishermen and a tractor are covered by our CC0 packs.
candidates.probes: Queries: 'the dutch drained a sea flevoland shipwrecks' found 0 matching long-form videos at 100K+, and the only relevant hit was 'Salvaging Lancaster ED-603' at 62K. 'netherlands drained the zuiderzee' found 0 matching at 100K+; the top results are generic engineering (Practical Engineering 3.45M/1y, NextGen Manufacturing 2.96M/3mo, Geography Geek 921K/5y). 'how the netherlands stole land from the sea' returned NextGen 2.96M/3mo, Impossible Travel 2.84M/2mo and OBF 2.73M/5y, all engineering or lifestyle angles. 'schokland island in a field' maxed at 14K (Dutch TV). 'what they found when the dutch drained the sea' found 0 matching long-form. A web search turned up no Nat Geo 'Drain the Oceans' episode on the Zuiderzee or Flevoland. Verdict: there is massive demand around the Netherlands, and the seabed angle is unclaimed.
candidates.risks: The Netherlands reads as 'engineering' rather than 'mystery', so the packaging has to sell the ships and the bombers, not the dams. The story spans 1916 to 1968 and needs a tight spine (the sea as the antagonist, Lely as the dreamer) so it does not become a timeline. Wreck counts vary by source (about 400 to 430 recorded, some estimates above 500), so use 'more than 400'. The WWII aircraft count needs a reliable number before it goes on screen. The US share may be lower than for a US topic, though Dutch-engineering videos clearly pull global and US views. The generic 'We Drained X. Here's What Was Hidden at the Bottom.' title is now cloned weekly; I saw 12+ copies in 7 days, and the latest ones get 74 to 1,400 views. Our title must say it really happened.

candidates.working_title: The Roman Party City That Sank Into a Supervolcano (And It's Rising Again)
candidates.premise: Baiae was ancient Rome's Las Vegas, where Caesar, Cicero, Nero and Hadrian partied. It slowly sank under the sea, so its villas, streets and statues now lie 4 to 10 m underwater. The reason is that it sits inside the breathing caldera of Campi Flegrei. The twist is that the same ground is now rising again: Pozzuoli has risen about 1.4 m since 2005, and 2025 brought the strongest earthquakes there in 40 years.
candidates.archetype: Hidden-under-the-Mediterranean plus volcano news. Evidence: 'We Finally Know What's Hidden Under The Mediterranean Sea' 719K; 'Zanclean Flood' 219K on 8.8K subs (382x); Nat Geo 'Lost Worlds of the Mediterranean' 6.7M and 'Secret Sunken Cities' compilation 1.37M. Campi Flegrei news demand: NOVA 'The Next Pompeii' 1.0M, Stefan Burns 'Italy's Strongest Earthquake in 10 Years Struck Directly Under a Supervolcano' 335K in 7 months, Down The Rabbit Hole 404K. Ancient Rome is one of the strongest US-audience subjects on YouTube.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: AD 59, a moonlit night on the Bay of Baiae. Emperor Nero sends his mother Agrippina home on a boat built to collapse. The lead-weighted canopy crashes down, the boat fails to sink cleanly, and she swims to shore (Tacitus, Annals 14). The scene of the crime is now under 5 m of water. MYSTERY: why is Rome's most glamorous resort at the bottom of the sea, and why do the marble columns in nearby Pozzuoli have holes bored by sea creatures 7 m above the ground? BEATS: (1) Baiae at its peak: hot springs, oyster farms, villas, and Caligula riding across a roughly 3-mile bridge of boats in Alexander the Great's breastplate (Suetonius). It is a natural comedy scene. (2) Clue: the hot springs mean they are living on a volcano, and the whole bay is a 12 to 15 km caldera. (3) Over centuries the ground sinks (bradyseism) and the sea swallows the Nymphaeum of Emperor Claudius, statues and all; divers found them in 1969. (4) 1538: the ground rises, then Monte Nuovo, a new mountain, is born in about a week. (5) 1830: Charles Lyell puts the Pozzuoli columns on the frontispiece of 'Principles of Geology', the proof that land goes down AND up. (6) 1982 to 84: Pozzuoli rises about 1.8 m and about 40,000 people are evacuated. TWIST: since 2005 the ground has been rising again, about 1.4 m so far, with M4.4 to 4.6 quakes in 2024 and 2025. The breathing that drowned Baiae is lifting it back up. PAYOFF: drain the bay to show the whole Roman city reassembled, then pull back to show it sits inside the mouth of a supervolcano that 500,000 people call home. End on what scientists actually say: unrest, not a countdown.
candidates.hero_image: The bay drained dry, with white Roman statues and mosaic floors standing on the exposed seabed, and the wide, steaming rim of the caldera filling the background like a giant crater.
candidates.mobile_fit: Statues standing on a dry seabed is one strange image a stranger gets instantly, and the crater rim behind adds 'volcano' without any text. The film's key moves are big and simple (water drops away, then the ground rises and falls like breathing), with no dense labels.
candidates.engine_fit: Strong. TINITALY 10 m DEM (open) plus EMODnet bathymetry let us render the caldera and the drained bay. InSAR uplift can be shown as a slowly inflating dome. Public domain: Sir William Hamilton's 'Campi Phlegraei' (1776) plates by Pietro Fabris, Lyell's 1830 frontispiece of the Serapeum columns, 18th/19th-century engravings and Grand Tour paintings. Low-poly Romans give us a comedic collapsing-boat scene and Caligula's bridge, all inside the photoreal terrain style.
candidates.probes: Queries: 'baiae sunken roman city' found 0 matching long-form videos at 100K+; best were a 69K Italian doc (8y), 60 Minutes clips at 45K and diver vlogs at 20 to 35K. 'the roman las vegas that sank' maxed at 24.7K (Darius Arya). candidates.working_title: What Hawaii Looks Like Without the Ocean
candidates.premise: Drain the Pacific around Hawaii 1,000 m at a time and paradise turns into the tallest mountain on Earth (Mauna Kea, about 10,000 m from base to peak), fields of house-sized landslide debris, and a chain of dead, sinking islands that runs all the way to Midway. The twist: Midway, where the US turned WWII in 1942, is a drowned old Hawaiian island. The carriers from that battle lie 5 km down on its flank, and every Hawaiian island is on the same conveyor belt.
candidates.archetype: Direct sibling of the biggest outlier in our pull: 'What Antarctica Looks Like Without Ice' 1.8M on 2.9K subs (773x). The same uploader (Unseen Works) just posted 'What the Pacific Ocean Looks Like Drained?' (115K in 4 days), and a Korean channel's 'What Would We See If We Drained the Pacific Ocean?' has 1.12M in 2 months, so the drained-Pacific spectacle is pulling right now. Hawaii itself has huge US demand: RealLifeLore 'Why You Can't Travel Between Hawaii's Islands by Boat' 7.07M, 'How the US Conquered Hawaii' 4.73M, Map Pack 949K. The Midway carriers pull too: House of History 3.18M, Nautilus Akagi survey 613K.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: 1 April 1946, Laupahoehoe on the Big Island. Children arriving at school watch the ocean suddenly drain away and expose the reef. Students and teachers run down to look, then the sea comes back as a wall of water (24 killed at Laupahoehoe). 'For a few minutes the sea drained away. We are going to finish the job.' MYSTERY: what is Hawaii, really, under the blue? BEATS (a drain ladder, one reveal per level): -120 m shows the Ice Age shorelines; Maui, Molokai, Lanai and Kahoolawe were one island (Maui Nui). -1,000 m shows the Nuuanu slide: half of an Oahu volcano collapsed into the sea, with debris blocks the size of cities. -4,000 to -5,500 m: the Big Island stands up as one colossal mountain taller than Everest, and its weight bends the ocean floor into a moat. Then follow the chain northwest as the islands get older, smaller and lower (Kauai, Nihoa, French Frigate Shoals) until Midway, a ring of reef on a dead volcano. On its flank at about 5,000 m lie Kaga, Akagi and USS Yorktown (found 1998 and 2019). TWIST: the battle that turned the Pacific war was fought over the corpse of an old Hawaiian island, and every island you know is headed the same way. Beyond Midway the Emperor Seamounts bend north at the famous 47-million-year kink. PAYOFF: swing back southeast. Below the Big Island, Kama'ehuakanaloa (formerly Loihi), the next Hawaiian island, is already growing underwater. Refill the ocean: 'Everything you have seen of Hawaii is the very tip.' Optional coda: Polynesian navigators found these tips by the stars, which ties to the rising keyword 'ancient polynesian star navigation methods'.
candidates.hero_image: The Big Island shown as one gigantic dark mountain rising from a dry abyss, with a small white Everest silhouette next to it for scale and a thin ring at the top marking where the beaches used to be.
candidates.mobile_fit: One giant silhouette next to a familiar one (Everest) is the clearest possible comparison on a phone. The drain ladder is a single repeating move (water level drops, one new thing appears), so each scene carries one idea, which fixes the 'dense globe' problem from ep01.
candidates.engine_fit: Ideal. The SOEST Hawaii multibeam synthesis and GMRT give high-resolution bathymetry (the landslide debris fields are visible in the data), and the island DEMs are excellent. 'Lower the water plane' is exactly what our terrain engine does. Public domain: NOAA/USGS 1946 tsunami photos, US Navy Midway battle photos, USGS Kilauea imagery. CC0 low-poly characters cover the Laupahoehoe children and a Polynesian canoe crew.

'mauna kea taller than everest documentary' found 0 long-form at 100K+; Bright Side 'What Hawaii Looks Like Without Water' 9K (105-min slop), a Korean 'If You Drain the Hawaiian Ocean...' 2.3K (8 days old). candidates.risks: The fastest-moving competitor: Unseen Works and the Korean channel are working through drained oceans and could do Hawaii next, so speed matters. The film is geology-heavy and the human stories (1946 children, Midway, the voyagers) are spread out, so the drain-ladder structure has to carry the momentum. Laupahoehoe death splits vary between sources, so use '24'.

candidates.working_title: We Drained the Deadliest Water in the Pacific (Ironbottom Sound)
candidates.premise: Off Guadalcanal lies a stretch of sea so full of sunken warships that sailors renamed it Ironbottom Sound. More than a hundred ships and hundreds of aircraft went down in the 1942 to 43 campaign. Drain it and you can walk from wreck to wreck through the night battles that decided the Pacific war. In 2025 Bob Ballard's Nautilus finally mapped the floor and filmed 13 wrecks, four of them for the first time, including the severed bow of USS New Orleans.
candidates.archetype: A drain reveal plus a deep-wreck reveal with a fresh news hook. Evidence: drain-format outliers on tiny channels (Chesapeake 170K/1 week and Great Lakes 165K on 1.4K subs). The same battles pull huge numbers: Yarnhub 'Guadalcanal's Friday 13th' 4.2M, House of History Guadalcanal naval campaign 599K and 400K. Deep-wreck premise: Caladan Oceanic 'The Deepest Wreck Ever Located' 6.9M. 'Why Can't You Visit Iwo Jima?' 4.4M on 3.5K subs shows Pacific-war geography pulling small channels in the US.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: the night of 8 to 9 August 1942 off Savo Island. Allied cruisers on picket, exhausted crews asleep. Japanese cruisers slip past unseen, flares go up, and in about half an hour four heavy cruisers (Quincy, Vincennes, Astoria, HMAS Canberra) are sinking. It is one of the worst defeats in US Navy history. MYSTERY: what lies on the floor of that water today? Drain it. BEATS: (1) The basin empties, 600 to 900 m deep between Guadalcanal, Savo and the Florida Islands, and the first wrecks appear. (2) The Tokyo Express: Japanese destroyers running supplies every night. (3) Friday the 13th of November 1942: a point-blank brawl in the dark in which Admirals Callaghan and Scott are both killed. As the damaged USS Juneau limps away it is torpedoed, and the five Sullivan brothers are lost (the case behind the US 'sole survivor' policy). (4) Two nights later, the battleship duel: USS Washington, guided by radar, sinks Kirishima. (5) Tassafaronga: USS New Orleans has its bow blown off and survives without it. TWIST: the bow lay alone in the dark for 83 years until Nautilus found it in 2025 while mapping more than 1,000 km2 of seafloor. The sea floor holds both navies side by side. PAYOFF: refill the Sound. Today Solomon Islanders fish above a steel floor. End on the bow.
candidates.hero_image: A deep dry basin under a tropical sky with warship hulks scattered across its floor, one cruiser bow standing alone in the foreground, and the green peak of Guadalcanal behind.
candidates.mobile_fit: Ship silhouettes on a dry floor are big, high-contrast shapes, and the scale of 'a seabed made of warships' reads instantly. The battle beats can be staged as simple top-down tracer arcs at night (bright lines on black), which read well on phones.
candidates.engine_fit: Good. GEBCO/GMRT bathymetry of the Sound plus SRTM for the islands gives the drain shots, and night-battle arcs are our great-circle-arc tool on a regional map. US Navy and National Archives photos (public domain) cover the whole campaign, which is an excellent archive. The main cost: we need simple procedural warship hull models, since there are no CC0 warships in our packs. Low-poly sailors work for a few human beats.
candidates.probes: Queries: 'ironbottom sound wrecks' found 0 matching long-form videos at 100K+; top relevant: Yarnhub 'Guadalcanal's Friday 13th' 4.2M/3y, the 1993 Nat Geo 'Lost Fleet of Guadalcanal' re-upload 607K/8y, Casual Navigation 'What Devastation Created Iron Bottom Sound?' 90K (6:47), Skynea History wreck episodes at 7 to 84K. 'ironbottom sound drained guadalcanal' found 0 matching; Nat Geo DTO 'Pacific War Wrecks' (2.47M) covers Lexington and Indianapolis, not the Sound. 'guadalcanal graveyard of warships drained' found 0 matching long-form. A web search confirmed the 2025 Nautilus/NOAA/Navy survey (13 wrecks, 4 new, New Orleans bow, Teruzuki). Verdict: the battles are popular, but no one has done the drained-Sound reveal.
candidates.risks: It overlaps with Scapa Flow as a 'naval graveyard' premise, so pick one. Animated-battle channels (Yarnhub, House of History, The Operations Room) own the tactical retelling, so we must stay on the reveal, not the tactics. Warship modelling is a production cost. Juneau sank outside the Sound proper, so frame the Sullivans as part of the same battle, not 'on the bottom here'. Totals are fuzzy ('more than 111 vessels' covers the whole campaign), so say 'dozens of warships' unless sourced. Tone: these are war graves.

candidates.working_title: There Are Ships Buried Under San Francisco's Skyscrapers
candidates.premise: In 1849 so many crews abandoned their ships to chase gold that hundreds of vessels were left rotting in San Francisco's cove. The city turned them into hotels, a jail and warehouses, then buried them as it filled in the cove, and the shoreline moved blocks inland. Construction crews still dig them up under the Financial District (the Niantic in 1872, 1907 and 1978; the General Harrison in 2001). Drain the Bay too, and you find a shockingly shallow bay, a 100 m deep canyon at the Golden Gate, and the wreck that killed 128 in the fog of 1901.
candidates.archetype: US-region 'is hiding something' plus the hidden-under reveal. Evidence from our pull: 'California Is Hiding...' 311K, 'What's Hiding In The Deep South...' 302K on 14K subs, 'What's Really Going On in the Midwest?' 313K on 2.7K subs, 'Why Appalachia Is Sitting On...' 473K on 6.1K subs. San Francisco Bay drain demand: Nat Geo 'Drain Alcatraz' 8.44M. Drowned-town demand: Mark Rober 'Uncovering America's Underwater City' 30.7M. The buried-ship angle itself: IT'S HISTORY 'Why San Francisco was built on Hundreds of Shipwrecks' 163K in 6 months.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: 2001, a foundation pit near the Embarcadero. An excavator bucket comes up with ship timbers: the General Harrison, a Gold Rush ship buried for 150 years under downtown. MYSTERY: why is there a ship under a skyscraper, and how many more are there? BEATS: (1) 1849: gold news hits; ships pour in and crews desert for the hills, leaving a forest of masts (500 to 1,000 ships at the peak) in Yerba Buena Cove. (2) A city with no buildings uses ships as buildings: the Niantic becomes a hotel and warehouse, the Euphemia becomes the city's first jail, others become saloons and storeships (comedy beats). (3) Land is worth more than ships, so the city shovels its sand hills into the cove, waterlots are sold, and ships get boxed in by new streets. (4) The fires of 1851 burn ships to the waterline and the fill goes over them; Montgomery Street, once the beach, is now blocks from the water. (5) Rediscoveries: Niantic in 1872, 1907 and 1978, General Harrison in 2001; estimates of 40 to 70 ships still down there. (6) Drain the Bay: most of it is only a few metres deep, the Golden Gate is a 100 m canyon, and on its floor lies the SS City of Rio de Janeiro (1901, fog, 128 dead, located by NOAA in 2014). Ice Age coda: the Bay was a valley and the coast lay out by the Farallones. TWIST: the 1849 shoreline still shapes the city. Filled ground shakes and liquefies in earthquakes, and in 1989 the worst damage followed the edges of old fill (the Marina was built partly on 1906 rubble). A map from 1849 predicts which streets shake hardest. PAYOFF: overlay the 1849 waterline on the modern skyline, then descend in a cutaway from a glass tower into fill, then to a ship's ribs.
candidates.hero_image: Cutaway of a downtown glass skyscraper whose foundations rest on a buried wooden sailing ship, with the masts poking up through layers of sand and rubble.
candidates.mobile_fit: A skyscraper on top of a sailing ship is a single, absurd, high-contrast image anyone gets in a glance. Most of the film is one city, one bay and one line (the 1849 shoreline) moving, which suits a small screen.
candidates.engine_fit: Excellent public-domain archive and data. USGS high-resolution San Francisco Bay bathymetry (public domain) and SRTM/USGS 3DEP lidar for the city give the drain and 'remove the city' shots. Library of Congress 1850 to 51 daguerreotype panoramas of the masted cove, 1850s maps of waterlots and buried hulks (the 1857 coast survey), and NOAA wreck imagery are all public domain. A cutaway is a natural motion-graphic. CC0 low-poly Forty-Niners and sailors make good comedy scenes.
candidates.probes: Queries: 'ships buried under san francisco' found 1 matching long-form video at 100K+ (IT'S HISTORY 163K/6mo; same channel 'San Francisco's Lost Docks' 186K/2y), then Voyager 51K/8mo and Alex the Historian 15.5K. 'what is hidden under san francisco' maxed at 135K (Chinatown), and the rest is Tartaria slop at 30 to 40K. 'what if san francisco bay was drained' returned Nat Geo 'Drain Alcatraz' 8.44M/3y (Alcatraz only), a USGS flyover at 158K and Bright Side 'We Drained SF Bay' at 1.2K. 'gold rush ships abandoned san francisco bay' found 0 matching long-form at 100K+. Verdict: the subject is proven and only lightly claimed, and the combination of buried ships, drained bay and the old shoreline is unclaimed.
candidates.risks: One mid-sized channel (IT'S HISTORY) already made the buried-ships piece, so we must win on the drain-plus-quake twist and on visuals. Estimates of the number of buried ships vary widely (40 to 70 still underground; 500 to 1,000 abandoned at the peak), so quote ranges. The liquefaction twist must be stated carefully (filled ground amplifies shaking, per USGS) without fear-mongering. The 'Rome' ship sometimes cited online is unverified, so leave it out. A city topic carries a risk of political comment; stay historical.

candidates.working_title: The Day Germany Sank Its Own Navy: What's Still at the Bottom of Scapa Flow
candidates.premise: On 21 June 1919, a boatload of Orkney schoolchildren on a field trip watched the interned German battle fleet start rolling over. Some cheered, thinking it was a show put on for them. In about five hours 52 warships sank themselves. Then a scrap dealer with no salvage experience bought the sunken navy and raised it, some ships upside-down. Twenty years later a U-boat crept into the 'impregnable' harbor and sank HMS Royal Oak. Drain the Flow and two world wars lie side by side.
candidates.archetype: Drain reveal plus a story twist. Evidence for the format: Chesapeake 170K in 1 week and Great Lakes 165K on 1.4K subs (Contour Atlas). Evidence for the hooks: 'Why Steel from Before 1945 is Weirdly Expensive' (Half as Interesting) 1.47M and 'The Bizarre Market for Old Battleship Steel' (Today I Found Out) 932K show the wreck-steel angle pulls. Historigraph 'Surrender of the German High Seas Fleet' 413K, House of History U-47 279K, Dark Seas 'When the German Navy Sank Its Own Fleet' 202K.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: midsummer 1919. About 160 to 400 Stromness schoolchildren (sources vary) are aboard the tender Flying Kestrel touring the interned German fleet. The giant ships begin to list and roll over; some children cry, some cheer, and the boat races home to parents on the pier. MYSTERY: why would a navy sink itself, and what is down there now? BEATS: (1) After the armistice, 74 German warships sit interned in Orkney for months with skeleton crews, rats and boredom. (2) Admiral Ludwig von Reuter, believing peace talks are failing, waits until the British squadron sails out on exercise and signals 'Paragraph eleven. Confirm.' Sea cocks open everywhere. (3) British guards open fire on the boats and 9 German sailors die, often called the last deaths of WWI. (4) Drain the Flow: a navy lying upside-down in shallow water. (5) Ernest Cox, a scrap dealer, buys the wrecks and spends about eight years raising 32 of them, pumping air into capsized hulls; his men work inside upside-down battleships. TWIST 1: in October 1939, Guenther Prien slips U-47 through a gap at Kirk Sound and sinks HMS Royal Oak, killing 835, more than 100 of them boys. Churchill orders the barriers, built partly by Italian prisoners of war, who also turned a Nissen hut into the Italian Chapel. TWIST 2 (myth-bust): the claim that Scapa steel flew on Voyager. The real reason pre-1945 steel is prized (atomic-age contamination) is true; the space-probe legend is shakier. PAYOFF: the seven big wrecks still down there (3 battleships, 4 cruisers), and Royal Oak, a war grave still seeping oil. Refill the Flow.
candidates.hero_image: A huge grey battleship lying upside-down on a drained seabed, its red hull pointing at the sky, with tiny workers standing on top of it. (This was the real 1920s salvage scene, and period photos exist.)
candidates.mobile_fit: An upside-down battleship is one unmistakable, slightly absurd silhouette, and the scale of tiny people on a giant hull reads at thumbnail size. The cold open with the children is a simple, emotional, animatable scene.
candidates.engine_fit: Good. UKHO/EMODnet bathymetry plus OS Terrain 50 for Orkney gives a compact, shallow basin that is perfect for a drain shot. Period photos of the 1919 scuttling and the 1920s Cox and Danks salvage are mostly old enough to be public domain (check each one with Orkney Library and the IWM). Royal Navy and German low-poly sailors, a field-trip boat and Italian POWs are good character beats.
candidates.probes: Queries: 'scapa flow scuttling german fleet' found 2 matching long-form videos at 100K+, both 7 years old (Historigraph 413K, Dreyer1916 animation 301K), plus The History Guy 147K. 'the germans sank their own fleet' returned Dark Seas 202K/3y and Timeline 50K. 'what is at the bottom of scapa flow' returned U-47 stories (Big Old Boats 347K, House of History 279K, History Guy 195K), and no drained-Flow treatment. 'low background steel scapa flow battleships' returned Half as Interesting 1.47M and TIFO 932K on pre-1945 steel; none build the Scapa story around it.
candidates.risks: A web search shows Nat Geo 'Drain the Oceans' season 1 (North Sea episode) already covered the scuttling, and its WWI episode, possibly 'Ultimate Battleships' at 2.15M, is on YouTube, so this is not untouched. It is British and German, and WWI interests the US less than WWII. It overlaps with Ironbottom Sound as a 'naval graveyard', so choose one. The Voyager steel claim is disputed and must be checked before using it even as a myth-bust. The number of children varies by source, so say 'a boatload'.

candidates.working_title: Britain Was Attached to France, Until a Waterfall Cut It Off
candidates.premise: About 450,000 years ago a chalk ridge joined Dover to Calais and held back a giant ice-dammed lake where the southern North Sea is now. The lake overflowed in waterfalls that drilled 100 m deep plunge pools into the rock, until the ridge broke and Britain was cut off. Sonar maps of the Channel floor proved it in 2007 and 2017. Drain the Channel and you see the scars, plus a thousand years of human wrecks on top of them: the White Ship that sank the heir to England, the Armada, D-Day.
candidates.archetype: Megaflood / drowned-land premise. Evidence: 'Zanclean Flood: The Refilling of the Mediterranean' 219K on 8.8K subs (382x); 'The Moment the Atlantic Filled a Desert' (Deep Science) 4.73M in 2 months; Tomas Pueyo's megaflood video 2.16M. Doggerland outliers from our pull: 213K on 1.1K subs (526x) and 279K on 1.6K subs, and History Time's Doggerland 3.96M. 'The Lost Continent That Connected Philippines & Indonesia' 272K on 2.2K subs (1,047x) shows lost land bridges pull small channels.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: an Ice Age landscape, a white chalk ridge from Dover to Calais, and behind it a vast lake with ice to the north. The water starts spilling over the lip as a row of waterfalls. MYSTERY/PROTAGONISTS: geologists Sanjeev Gupta and Jenny Collier (Imperial College) look at sonar maps of the Channel floor and see a line of giant holes, too big and too round to be anything ordinary. BEATS: (1) 2007: the maps show a giant flood-carved valley on the Channel floor. 2017: the holes are confirmed as plunge pools, around 100 m deep and kilometres wide, under a vanished line of waterfalls (Fosse Dangeard). (2) A first breach about 450,000 years ago and a second catastrophic flood about 160,000 years ago carve the Channel valley. (3) Drain the Channel today and the river canyon and the plunge pools appear. HUMAN LAYERS ON THE SAME FLOOR: 1120, the White Ship hits a rock off Barfleur and the only legitimate son of King Henry I drowns, setting off the 19-year civil war known as the Anarchy. 1588, the Armada scattered by fireships. 1703, the Great Storm wrecks a squadron of warships on the Goodwin Sands in one night. 1944, D-Day: Mulberry harbour caissons and swamped DD tanks still on the bottom. TWIST: water broke Britain away from Europe twice. When engineers finally re-joined them with the Channel Tunnel, one of the British boring machines was steered into the rock and left buried under the seabed, in the same chalk the waterfalls cut. PAYOFF: refill the Channel; a ferry crosses above the drowned waterfall line.
candidates.hero_image: A colossal curtain of waterfalls pouring over the white cliffs between England and France, with a tiny map inset of Britain still attached to the continent.
candidates.mobile_fit: White cliffs plus a huge waterfall is one bold image with an instantly understood claim ('Britain was attached to France'). The flood sequence is a single dramatic motion, and each human story is one wreck on one seabed spot, so there is one idea per shot.
candidates.engine_fit: Strong. EMODnet/UKHO bathymetry is high-resolution enough to show the Lobourg Channel and the plunge pools, and our paleo-geography tool covers the Ice Age lake and the breach morph. Public domain: the White Ship scene in a 14th-century manuscript, Armada paintings, US Army and Royal Navy D-Day photos, Channel Tunnel construction photos (check the rights). Low-poly medieval sailors make a strong White Ship beat; the crew was reportedly drunk, which gives a funny-tragic scene.
candidates.probes: Queries: 'what if the english channel was drained' found 0 matching long-form videos at 100K+ (results were Nat Geo DTO generics and Channel Tunnel engineering). 'megaflood that made britain an island' found 1 match: an Imperial College lecture at 342K, 14 years old; History Time Doggerland 3.96M/6y is adjacent. 'britain was connected to france waterfall dover' found 0 matching long-form. 'white ship disaster 1120' maxed at 245K (The History Guy, 4y). 'drain the oceans english channel d-day' returned Nat Geo DTO 'Secrets of D-Day' at 744K, which covers only the D-Day wrecks.
candidates.risks: This is a composite: the 450,000-year geology and the human history are linked by place, not by one protagonist, so the Gupta/Collier detective thread has to hold it together. Nat Geo DTO already did the D-Day wrecks, and Doggerland is well covered, so keep D-Day to one beat. The megaflood ages come from models (about 450K and 160K years) and must be stated as estimates. Interest is UK/Europe-weighted, with D-Day as the main US hook. Goodwin Sands casualty figures vary, so verify them. A copycat 'We Drained the English Channel' could appear any week given the current clone wave.

candidates.working_title: Why Namibia Sealed Off a Desert for 100 Years (The Diamonds Were Just Lying There)
candidates.premise: In 1908 a railway worker shovelling sand off the tracks near Luderitz picked up a diamond, and it turned out the stones were lying loose on the surface. Germany's colonial government fenced off about 26,000 km2 of coast as the Sperrgebiet, the 'Forbidden Zone'. A rich town grew up in the dunes and was then buried by sand. In 2008 miners pushed back the sea to dig the seabed and found a 500-year-old Portuguese treasure ship with about 2,000 gold coins inside the forbidden zone.
candidates.archetype: Two proven premises in one: (1) 'Why can't you visit X', as in 'Why Can't You Visit Iwo Jima?' (Where They Stood, 3.5K subs, 4.4M views, 1 month old) and 'Every Forbidden Island You're Not Allowed to Visit' (Earthyphus, 1.5K subs, 878K). (2) 'Drained / what was hidden', as in 'We Drained the Chesapeake Bay...' (Contour Atlas, 1.4K subs, 170K in 1 week) and BRIGHT SIDE's 'Shipwreck Full of Gold Found in Desert After 500 Years' (1.1M) and 'Namibia's Diamond Miners Find Shipwreck With Treasure' (490K). Treasure, forbidden land and a ghost town together have wide appeal in the US and everywhere else.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: April 1908, wind-blown sand on the Luderitz-Aus railway. Zacharias Lewala, a worker who had seen diamonds at Kimberley, notices a glint and hands the stone to his supervisor August Stauch. PROTAGONISTS: Lewala, who found it, and Stauch, who got rich from it. ESCALATION 1: the stones are picked up by hand, a rush starts, and in September 1908 the government declares the Sperrgebiet (trespassers arrested), a strip of coast about the size of Vermont. ESCALATION 2: Kolmanskop, a German town in the dunes with its water shipped in, gets an ice factory, a bowling alley and a hospital said to have the southern hemisphere's first X-ray machine, reportedly also used to catch workers who swallowed diamonds. By the mid-1910s this coast supplied about 20% of the world's diamonds. ESCALATION 3: richer gravels turn up further south, the town is empty by the mid-1950s, and dunes move into the living rooms. Mining then moves onto the beach and into the sea: bulldozers build sand walls and pump the Atlantic out to mine the seabed. TWIST: April 2008, behind one of those walls, a worker finds copper ingots. They come from the Bom Jesus, a Portuguese ship lost in 1533, carrying about 2,000 gold coins, about 17 tons of copper and elephant ivory, all hidden for 475 years inside the zone nobody could enter. PAYOFF: a zone closed off out of greed protected one of the most untouched deserts on Earth (now Tsau //Khaeb National Park, still mostly off limits), and history barely recorded the name of the man who started it.
candidates.hero_image: A single hand on dark sand holding a few glittering diamonds, in front of a weathered red-and-white sign reading 'SPERRGEBIET - FORBIDDEN'. Alternative: a doorway into a ghost house with a sand dune flowing through it.
candidates.mobile_fit: One object (glitter on sand), one sign and one strong colour contrast read instantly at thumbnail size. Each scene carries one idea: a man with a shovel, a fence going up around a desert, a house filling with sand, the sea being pushed back, gold coins in the mud. There are no dense labels; the forbidden zone is a single red overlay on the coast.
candidates.engine_fit: Excellent. The opening globe move goes to the Namib coast. GIBS satellite patches and SRTM plus GEBCO data give the dunes and the offshore shelf in 3D. The signature shot is the engine's 'drain the water' move used for real: animated sand walls push the Atlantic back and the seabed appears, with the Bom Jesus scatter field revealed. Animated sand covering Kolmanskop suits Canvas2D or three.js. CC0 low-poly workers and a ship model work here, as do public-domain colonial-era photos of Kolmanskop and Luderitz (pre-1926 German photos on Wikimedia). The cast is small and the time jumps are clear (1908, 1910s, 1950s, 2008).

candidates.working_title: The Coldest Place on Earth Lost Power. Nobody Could Come.
candidates.premise: On the night of 12 April 1982, just as the eight-month polar night began, a fire destroyed the power plant at the Soviet Vostok Station high on the East Antarctic ice. One man died and twenty were left with no heat as the temperature headed toward -80 C, with no aircraft able to reach them until spring. They improvised and survived, and the next winter the same station recorded -89.2 C (-128.6 F), the coldest temperature ever measured on Earth's surface, while under their floor, about 4 km down, lay a liquid lake sealed under the ice.
candidates.archetype: Remote research station with real people (named in this lens), combined with huge demand for 'coldest place' content (Ruhi Cenet's Oymyakon 120M; Outlier Atlas 'Living at the South Pole' 1.0M in 3 weeks) and the engine-native Antarctica spectacle ('What Antarctica Looks Like Without Ice', Unseen Works, 2.9K subs, 1.8M in 3 weeks, 773x). It is a survival story with a deadline, the same shape as 'The 119-Day Survival Story That NOBODY Believed' (1.5M).
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: about 4 a.m., 12 April 1982, 3,500 m up on the ice dome. Fire in the annex of the diesel plant; in roughly 15 minutes the generators are gone. Mechanic Alexei Karpenko dies. STAKES: 20 men, no power, no heat, no light, buildings cooling fast, the nearest coastal base about 1,400 km away, and no plane able to land until the southern spring because fuel and hydraulics freeze. ESCALATION: fire extinguishers only hiss in the cold; a shift in the wind saves the fuel depot; a stored kerosene stove warms the mess hall; they build drip stoves from gas cylinders burning diesel and live in soot. An old 2 kW drilling-rig generator powers the radio, a coded radiogram goes to Moscow, and they dig a bigger old generator out of the snow and repair it. They decline outside help, keep the weather observations going, and later a second fire breaks out at the drilling rig. RELIEF: the first aircraft of the season, January 1983, roughly nine months later. TWIST 1: the next winter, 21 July 1983, Vostok's thermometer reads -89.2 C. TWIST 2: a cut-away through about 4 km of ice shows Lake Vostok, a huge body of liquid water directly beneath them. PAYOFF: end on the single lit window of the hut in an endless white.
candidates.hero_image: One tiny hut with a single orange window in an endless blue-white ice plain under stars, with a huge '-89C' (or '-128F' for the US) in the corner. Alternative: a cut-away showing the hut on top, 4 km of ice and the dark lake at the bottom.
candidates.mobile_fit: The image is very simple: a small warm dot against a vast cold field, one big number, and maximum colour contrast (orange on blue). The story stays in one location with one clock (8 months) and one dial (temperature). The cut-away is a single vertical slice, not a dense map.

No archival photos are needed: Soviet photos are a copyright risk, so animation carries the whole film, which suits the engine. One consistent visual language throughout (photoreal ice plus stylised warm interiors only if built in the same render style).

candidates.working_title: Why You Can't Visit the Islands Off San Francisco
candidates.premise: 27 miles past the Golden Gate is a jagged chain of islands nobody is allowed to land on. During the Gold Rush men fought a deadly gun battle there over seabird eggs, the government later dumped about 47,500 barrels of radioactive waste nearby, and an atomic-test aircraft carrier was sunk off them. In 2015 a robot found the carrier sitting upright and intact. The real reason the islands are closed turns out to be what saved them.
candidates.archetype: 'Why can't you visit X' with a US location: Iwo Jima 4.4M on 3.5K subs; IT'S HISTORY 'Why New York's Plum Island is Totally Forbidden' 1.2M and 'Why Pollepel Island is Totally Forbidden' 942K; SideNote 'Why this Tiny Island in New York City is Inaccessible' 4.9M. Plus the drain-the-sea reveal format (Contour Atlas 170K/1 week on 1.4K subs; NatGeo 'Drain the Oceans' NYC 4.9M). The US is the most valuable market and a San Francisco landmark gives instant recognition.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: June 1863, dawn. Armed men in boats row toward a rock in the Pacific; shots are fired and two men die. The prize is eggs. ESCALATION 1: Gold Rush San Francisco has exploded in size and has almost no chickens. Big speckled common murre eggs sell at premium prices, rival 'egg companies' gather them by the hundreds of thousands, and the Egg War follows. ESCALATION 2: lighthouse keepers and their families live on the rock (lighthouse from 1855) among sharks, storms and millions of birds. ESCALATION 3: from 1946 to 1970 at least 47,500 barrels of radioactive waste are dumped in a 540-square-mile area starting just south of the islands, and in January 1951 the carrier USS Independence, a target ship in the 1946 Bikini atomic tests, is towed out and scuttled. TWIST 1: in 2015 NOAA's survey finds the carrier upright and 'amazingly intact' at about 2,600 ft, with readings showing normal background radiation. TWIST 2 / PAYOFF: the islands are closed not because of radiation or great white sharks but to protect birds. A wildlife refuge brought the murres back from near-collapse, and today only a few biologists live there. The forbidden status is what saved the place.
candidates.hero_image: A jagged black island under a red 'NO LANDING' band, with the Golden Gate Bridge small on the horizon behind it. Alternative: the drained seabed with a full-size aircraft carrier sitting upright on it, with the Farallones in the background.
candidates.mobile_fit: Two instantly recognisable shapes, the Golden Gate and a jagged rock, plus one 'forbidden' colour. Each act has one strong object (an egg, a lighthouse, a yellow barrel, a carrier). The carrier on a drained seafloor reads at thumbnail size.

candidates.working_title: The World's Most Remote Island Exploded. They Went Back Anyway.
candidates.premise: In October 1961 a volcano opened right behind the only village on Tristan da Cunha, the most remote inhabited island on Earth. All 264 islanders were shipped to England and housed at an old RAF base among cars, televisions and a cold English winter. About a year later they voted 148 to 5 to go back to a volcanic rock about 2,400 km from the nearest inhabited land, and the film's payoff is why.
candidates.archetype: Rides a search wave happening now: 'tristan da cunha' about 315K monthly searches, +118% (vidIQ). All of these are travel or 'life on' angles; the dramatic 1961-63 story has barely been told.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: October 1961, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. Weeks of tremors, then the ground behind the cottages bulges and splits as a lava dome rises beside the village. PROTAGONISTS: a community of about 264 people with only a handful of surnames, where everyone knows everyone. ESCALATION 1: they flee to Nightingale Island for a night, a passing Dutch liner (Tjisadane) picks them up, and the Stirling Castle takes them on to Southampton. ESCALATION 2: life at RAF Calshot (the road is still called Tristan Close), with buses, money, factory jobs, fog, flu and press cameras. Britain assumes they will settle. ESCALATION 3: a Royal Society expedition checks the island, and in December 1962 a ballot is held. TWIST: 148 to 5 to go home, turning down the modern world. An advance party goes back in April 1963 and about 200 follow in November, including Tristan girls who had married Englishmen in the meantime. PAYOFF: what they went back to (rebuilt fishing, potato patches, a ship every few months) and their own words about why. Today about 240 people live there, still one of the hardest places on Earth to reach.

candidates.working_title: Why Nobody Lives on the American Island Japan Captured
candidates.premise: In June 1942 Japan invaded two US islands in Alaska. On Attu, the 42 villagers and their teacher were taken prisoner and the villagers were shipped to Japan, where more than half died. After a brutal battle won the island back, 34,000 American and Canadian troops stormed Kiska a few weeks later only to find it empty, and still took casualties. The survivors of Attu were never allowed to go home, and the island has been empty ever since.

(Where They Stood, 3.5K subs, 4.4M, 1 month old), which combines WWII, a US story and a forbidden or empty island. candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: June 1942, Attu village, the far western tip of America, past the date line. ESCALATION 1: Foster Jones is killed; Etta is taken away; the villagers are shipped to Otaru, Hokkaido, where more than half die. ESCALATION 2: May 1943, US troops land in fog on frozen tundra; the cold hurts as much as the enemy; the battle ends in a final mass charge and almost the whole Japanese garrison dies. TWIST: August 1943, a huge force storms Kiska and finds no one. PAYOFF: 1945, the Attu survivors come back, but the government resettles them on Atka instead of their home island. candidates.working_title: Hawaii's Forbidden Peninsula (And the People Who Chose to Stay)
candidates.premise: On Molokai, a flat peninsula is walled off by some of the tallest sea cliffs on Earth, a natural prison built by a volcano after half the island slid into the sea. From 1866, Hawaii exiled thousands of people with leprosy (Hansen's disease) there. When the cure came and the law was lifted in 1969, many chose to stay, so outsiders are now the ones kept out: you need a permit or a resident sponsor, and in 2026 public tours may end for good.
candidates.archetype: 'Why can't you visit X' in a US location (Iwo Jima 4.4M on 3.5K subs; IT'S HISTORY forbidden-NY islands 1.2M/942K) and Hawaii's 'forbidden island' demand (Park Vibes 'What's Hidden on Hawaii's Forbidden Island?' 1.3M, 7 months; Caitlin Doughty 'Visiting Hawaii's Tragic & Remote Leprosy Colony' 1.87M). There is also a news hook: May 2026 reporting (Maui Now, Civil Beat) that the last patient-run tour lost its owner and public access may stop after 31 Dec 2026.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: 1866, a ship stops off a strip of land at the foot of a 600-plus-metre cliff. Passengers diagnosed with leprosy are put ashore, some reportedly made to swim. ESCALATION 1: families torn apart by law; around 8,000 people sent over a century; Father Damien arrives in 1873, catches the disease himself and dies in 1889 (now a saint), and Mother Marianne Cope continues the work. ESCALATION 2: in the 1940s sulfone drugs make the disease curable, but the isolation law lasts until 1969. TWIST: free to leave, many stay; the state promises they can live there for life, and to protect their privacy the restrictions turn on visitors (permits, sponsors, no children under 16, time limits). PAYOFF: only a handful of patients remain; in 2026 the woman who ran the last tour company died and no one knows whether the gate will stay open. candidates.working_title: They Fought a Volcano With Seawater. And Won.
candidates.premise: At about 2 a.m. on 23 January 1973 the ground split open beside Heimaey, home to Iceland's most important fishing harbour. 5,000 people escaped in hours because a storm had kept the whole fishing fleet in port. Then a river of lava headed for the harbour mouth, and the islanders fought it for months with roughly 6 million tonnes of pumped seawater. The lava stopped about 100 m short, and the wall of rock it left made the harbour better than before.
candidates.archetype: An island where people stayed: 'Why People Live There' (Geoff 4.7M) and remote-island survival, plus the rising 'disasters explained' keyword (about 239K, +110%) and disaster true stories ('Pinatubo' 703K, 663x). Current news hook: Iceland's Grindavik lava barriers (BuildWitt 'Building Iceland's Lava Barriers' 943K; BBC 'lava sets town on fire' 779K).
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: 1:55 a.m., a 1.6 km curtain of fire opens on the edge of town. LUCK BEAT: a storm the evening before kept almost the entire fleet in harbour, so by daybreak nearly all 5,000-plus people have left by fishing boat. Only one man died in the whole eruption. ESCALATION 1: ash buries houses and volunteers shovel roofs to keep them from collapsing; a new mountain, Eldfell, grows about 200 m. ESCALATION 2: lava starts closing the harbour mouth, and without the harbour the town is finished. Physicist Thorbjorn Sigurgeirsson's idea: cool the lava front with seawater. Fire hoses, then a dredging ship, then high-capacity pumps originally built for the US Navy; men lay pipelines across lava that is still moving. TWIST: the flow stops about 100 m short. The new lava wall becomes a breakwater that gives better shelter than nature did, the island grows from 11.2 to about 13.4 km2, and heat from the cooling lava is later used to warm the town's homes. PAYOFF: 50 years later Iceland is building lava barriers again at Grindavik. End on a fishing boat sailing out past a wall of black lava.
candidates.hero_image: A wall of glowing lava towering over a line of tiny figures spraying a single arc of water at it, with fishing boats in the harbour behind them. Alternative: half a house buried in black ash with a fountain of fire behind it.
candidates.mobile_fit: Fire vs water (orange vs blue), one tiny-human-against-giant-force image, readable at a glance. The plot has one clear goal (save the harbour) and one moving line (the lava front) that the viewer can track.
candidates.engine_fit: Strong. Globe move to the Westman Islands, real 3D terrain, animated lava flow and steam, and a before/after morph of the coastline showing the island grow. Note: SRTM stops at 60N, so use Copernicus GLO-30 or ArcticDEM for Heimaey's terrain (free, attribution required). Public-domain material: USGS 1973 lava-cooling report photos (US gov) and diagrams. CC0 low-poly figures and boats.
