(2) The pump count and origin vary (32 vs 43; the USGS says they were built for the US Navy), the volume varies (6.2M tonnes vs 7.3M m3), and the district-heating claim rests on secondary sources; verify all before use. (3) A happy ending lowers the stakes; the pacing must keep the harbour-closing threat alive until the last act. (4) Terrain data needs a non-SRTM source (see engine_fit).

candidates.working_title: Colorado Isn't a Rectangle (And the Supreme Court Ruled the Mistakes Stay)
candidates.premise: Everyone 'knows' Colorado is a perfect rectangle. It isn't. Its borders zigzag through hundreds of small kinks (one GIS count says 697 sides) because 1860s-70s survey crews with chains and star sightings missed the lines they were sent to mark. When New Mexico sued to fix it, the Supreme Court ruled in 1925 that the wrong line is the legal line. The payoff answers a question every viewer has: why doesn't America just fix its borders? Because a border isn't a line on a map. It's a row of stones in the ground, and once people live by the stones, the mistake becomes the law.
candidates.archetype: Rides 'borders that make no sense' ('7 Borders That Make Absolutely No Sense' got 702K on a 17.7K-sub channel) and 'facts you learned in school that are wrong' (245K-614K on 1.6K-5.7K-sub channels). The demand for this exact premise is already proven in Shorts: 'Colorado is Not a Rectangle' got 7.7M views and 'How Colorado Has 697 Sides?' got 641K. Long-form supply is almost zero: the best long-form result with matching words has 2.4K views. This is the biggest proven-demand, no-long-form gap I found.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: a slow 3D flyover along Colorado's 'ruler-straight' southern border through the San Juan Mountains. Then the line visibly jogs sideways in the mountains. 'Colorado has four sides. Except it doesn't.' PROTAGONIST: surveyor Ehud Darling, 1868, hired to find the 37th parallel with Gunter's chains, a transit and star sightings across mountain country, marking the line with stone and earth mounds. ESCALATION 1: other crews (Reeves on the western line, Chandler Robbins setting the Four Corners point in 1875) each add their own drift, so the 'rectangle' is really a long chain of short segments. ESCALATION 2: a 1902-03 resurvey (Carpenter) finds Darling's line sits well off the true parallel. Land, ranches and taxes are in the 'wrong' state, and New Mexico sues in 1919. TWIST: in New Mexico v. Colorado (1925) the Supreme Court keeps Darling's crooked line, because both sides had lived by it for half a century. TWIST 2: the 2009 headlines saying 'the Four Corners Monument is in the wrong place'. It sits about 1,800 ft from the intended spot, and it is still legally exactly right. PAYOFF / MODERN STAKES: the same rule still bites. Georgia lawmakers keep trying to undo an 1818 survey error so they can reach the Tennessee River's water during droughts. CLOSE: 'The map isn't the border. The stones are.' Hand off to the next video: the one bad map behind America's weirdest borders (see the Mitchell map candidate).
candidates.hero_image: A fat, bright Colorado silhouette that looks like a clean rectangle, with one edge 'zoomed in' to show a jagged red sawtooth. Text: 'NOT A RECTANGLE'.
candidates.mobile_fit: The whole film comes back to one shape everyone already knows: a big rectangle that turns out to be broken. Each reveal is one zoom from a simple outline into a single kink in 3D terrain. No dense labels: one state, one line, one stone marker per shot. People with mountains, chains and survey stones are easy to animate with low-poly characters.
candidates.engine_fit: Ideal. DEM terrain builder flyovers along the real border, a hi-res satellite patch at the Four Corners, line overlays comparing the intended parallel with the surveyed line (a simple two-line morph), Natural Earth state borders, counters for the 'sides', and low-poly survey crews with a chain and transit. Public-domain material: GLO/BLM survey plats, the Supreme Court opinion text (description only), and USGS/LOC photos of boundary markers.
candidates.probes: 'colorado is not a rectangle': Short 7.7M ('Colorado is Not a Rectangle'), Short 83K; best long-form: Kallixa 'I Found the Most UNBALANCED US State' 69K (not this story); matching long-form tops out at 2.4K (a 50-facts list). 'colorado has 697 sides': Short 641K, Short 59K ('Why Colorado's Border Zigs and Zags'); zero matching long-form. 'why state borders are not straight': no matching long-form above 3.2K; Shorts 1-38K. 'four corners monument wrong place': Short 57K, Short 25K; long-form tops out at 2K. 'wyoming is not a rectangle': only Trebbie 'Why are Wyoming and Colorado Squares?' 86K (1:55). 'surveyor mistakes that became borders': no long-form; Short 'Two Lost Survey Teams Left a Kink in Australia's Border' 27K. 'why us state borders are wrong': the big incumbents are 'fix the borders' or 'weird borders' lists (Geography by Geoff 2.2M and 948K, Atlas Pro 3.5M 'The Problem With the USA's Borders'). None of them tells the survey-error-becomes-law story.
candidates.risks: (1) The '697 sides' figure is a GIS count reported by Big Think, Ripley's and others, not an official number. Say 'one count says 697' and lean on the verified facts (Darling 1868; Carpenter 1902-03; New Mexico v. Colorado, 267 U.S. 30 (1925); the Four Corners point about 1,800 ft off its intended spot). Do not use the unverified 'Wyoming has 223 sides'. (2) The exact jog sizes and Georgia's 1818 error distance need a facts ledger before scripting. (3) The topic could feel thin at 15 minutes. The Four Corners twist and the Georgia water stakes are what carry it to about 12-14 minutes, so don't pad. (4) It overlaps in theme with the Mitchell map candidate. Make one of them episode 2 and the other the handoff.

candidates.working_title: America Bought Louisiana From a Country That Owned It for 20 Days
candidates.premise: Every American learns that in 1803 the US 'bought Louisiana from France for $15 million' and doubled in size. The truth is stranger. France had formally held the territory for just 20 days. Napoleon sold land he had promised Spain he would never sell. Nobody, buyer or seller, knew where its borders were. And the US had only bought the right to deal with the Native nations who actually lived there. The question 'what did America actually buy?' turns into a heist-like story of envoys sent to buy one city who came home with half a continent.
candidates.archetype: A 'fact you learned in school is wrong' premise ('Things You Learned in School That Are No Longer True' 245K on 1.6K subs; 'The History Facts You Were Never Supposed to Question' 614K on 5.7K subs) built on a map. Topic demand is huge: the Short 'How America Bought Louisiana - Napoleon's $15M Deal' has 18M views and 'The Louisiana Purchase' Short has 2M. Long-form supply is weak and short: 'The Louisiana Purchase Explained in 5 Minutes' (General Knowledge) 578K, 'How Much Did Napoleon Get for Louisiana?' (SideQuest, 5:33) 565K, Knowledgia 489K. No 10-18 minute long-form tells the myth-busting map angle.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: New Orleans, 30 Nov 1803, in the Cabildo. The Spanish flag comes down and the French flag goes up. Twenty days later, in the same square, the French flag comes down and the US flag goes up. 'America bought Louisiana from France. France had owned it for twenty days.' PROTAGONISTS: Robert Livingston and James Monroe in Paris, authorized to spend up to $10M on New Orleans and the Floridas. ESCALATION 1: Napoleon's army in Saint-Domingue (Haiti) is destroyed by the revolution and yellow fever, and his American empire plan collapses. ESCALATION 2: Talleyrand suddenly asks Livingston what the US would pay for the whole of Louisiana. The envoys have no authority, no instructions and no map with edges. ESCALATION 3: the price ($15M, 'three cents an acre') is financed by British and Dutch bankers (Barings, Hope & Co.) while Britain is about to fight Napoleon again. TWIST 1: when asked where the borders are, Talleyrand answers that the Americans have made a noble bargain and he supposes they will make the most of it. The treaty only says 'the same extent' as under Spain and France. TWIST 2: Napoleon had promised Spain never to hand Louisiana to a third power. TWIST 3: the US didn't buy the land so much as the exclusive right, among Europeans, to acquire it from the Native nations who lived there. PAYOFF: Jefferson sends Lewis and Clark partly to find out what he bought, and the western border with Spain isn't settled until 1819. Final map morph: the 'doubled America' shape everyone knows, redrawn as what was actually known in 1803, a coastline and a river with a fog-of-war interior.
candidates.hero_image: A glowing, enormous Louisiana Purchase shape over a dark US map, with a price tag reading '$15M' and a big red stamp: 'FRANCE OWNED IT 20 DAYS'.
candidates.mobile_fit: The core image is one giant shape on a map that fills the phone screen. The 'fog of war' interior and the two flag swaps in the same square are big, simple, one-idea shots. Characters (Napoleon, two nervous American envoys, Talleyrand) give face-like anchors, and the funny scenes play as low-poly character moments.
candidates.engine_fit: Strong. 3D globe to US map moves, an animated 'fog of war' reveal of the unknown interior, the river network (Natural Earth rivers: Mississippi and Missouri drive the borders), great-circle arcs for the Atlantic diplomacy and the Saint-Domingue expedition, counters for price and acreage, and a border morph for the 1819 Adams-Onis line. Public domain: the treaty pages and period maps (LOC), plus portraits used sparingly (ep01 critique: no static-portrait lingering).
candidates.probes: 'louisiana purchase what did america actually buy': Short 18M, Short 2M; long-form General Knowledge 578K (5:00), Knowledgia 489K, General Knowledge 'What If The U.S. Hadn't Bought Louisiana?' 327K; the 'actually buy' angle tops out at 22K ('How Did America Actually Pay For Louisiana?'). 'napoleon sold louisiana': SideQuest 565K (5:33); Cinematic History Tale 'Why Napoleon Gave America Half a Continent Almost for Free' 39K; matching long-form tops out at 2.6K. 'louisiana purchase myth': TED-Ed 879K (3:39), History Matters 1.5M (3:23, about Creole reaction, a different angle); no myth-busting long-form above 1.3K. 'france owned louisiana for 20 days': only Shorts (6.4K, 4.5K), so the twist is unclaimed in long form. candidates.risks: (1) This is more history than pure geography. Keep it map-driven (the borders, the unknown interior, the 1819 line) so it stays on-brand for Myth Juice. (2) The Native-land framing must be precise and respectful. Use 'right of preemption'/'exclusive right to acquire' wording from historians, and do not quote a dollar figure for later payments to tribes unless it is sourced. (3) The famous Napoleon bathtub anecdote with his brothers Joseph and Lucien comes from Lucien's memoir, which may be self-serving, and my quick web check did not confirm it. Use it only if sourced, and flag it as Lucien's account. (4) The 20-day figure is solid (Spain to France 30 Nov 1803, France to US 20 Dec 1803), but the treaty itself was signed in April, so word it carefully: France 'formally took possession' for 20 days.

candidates.working_title: You Can't See the Great Wall From Space. The Myth Is Older Than Spaceflight.
candidates.premise: Nearly everyone learned that the Great Wall of China is the only man-made thing visible from space, or even from the Moon. It isn't, and the story of how that 'fact' was born is the real mystery: it was printed in 1754, popularized by Ripley's Believe It or Not in 1932, and repeated in an American travel book in 1938, all decades before any human went to space. Then the astronauts went up and looked. The payoff shows what you really can see from orbit and from the Moon, and why the 'only' part was always impossible.
candidates.archetype: A mass 'fact you learned in school is wrong' premise ('Things You Learned in School That Are No Longer True' 245K on 1.6K subs). Demand is proven in Shorts: 'How Really Huge is the Great Wall of China?' 1.1M, 'The Great Wall of China - A Wonder You Can See from Space!' 1M (the Short still repeating the myth shows how alive it is), 'Can we see The Great Wall From Space?' 79K. There is no dedicated long-form. The Wall appears only as one item in lists such as Infographics Show '50 Geography Facts That Are Fake' (211K, 4 days old) and Map Pack's version (2.5M).
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: the view from the Moon. The Earth is a blue marble about the size of a coin at arm's length. Zoom on China: nothing. 'You were told you could see it from here. Nobody ever could.' MYSTERY: so who said it first? DETECTIVE TRAIL: 1754, English antiquarian William Stukeley, in a letter about Hadrian's Wall, writes that the Chinese Wall 'may be discerned at the Moon'. Nobody had been anywhere near the Moon. 1895: Henry Norman repeats it. 1932: Robert Ripley's cartoon makes it 'the only work of man visible from the Moon', in millions of American newspapers. 1938: Richard Halliburton's bestselling kids' book cites 'astronauts', 23 years before Gagarin. ESCALATION: the claim enters textbooks around the world. TWIST: humans finally reach orbit and the Moon. Apollo astronauts say no wall is visible from the Moon, and China's own first astronaut, Yang Liwei (2003), says he couldn't see it, which prompted debate about fixing Chinese textbooks. TWIST 2: the Wall is long but only about as wide as a highway and the color of the hills around it, while airports, cities at night, open-pit mines and highways are far easier to spot from orbit. PAYOFF: a guided 'what you can actually see' tour from 400 km, using night lights and big human-made shapes, ending back at the Moon view where no human-made object is visible at all.
candidates.hero_image: An astronaut silhouette at a spacecraft window looking down at a cloudy, featureless China, with a huge red 'NOPE' over the spot where the Wall should be.
candidates.mobile_fit: Space views are the most phone-readable visuals there are: one planet, one window, one bright line or none. Each beat is a single zoom level (Moon, orbit, plane, ground). The detective trail runs through four big characters (Stukeley, Ripley, Halliburton, an astronaut), each with one simple prop. No maps dense with labels.
candidates.engine_fit: Perfect for the photoreal globe: Moon-distance pull-backs, the atmosphere shader, VIIRS night lights for 'what you CAN see', NASA GIBS hi-res patches of the Wall vs a highway vs an airport at the same scale, and simple angular-size math as on-screen counters (a few big numbers only). Public domain: NASA/ISS astronaut photos, Apollo Earth photos, period newspapers via LOC. Ripley's cartoon art is likely still copyrighted, so recreate it in our style rather than showing the original.
candidates.probes: 'great wall of china visible from space myth': no dedicated long-form; Infographics Show '50 Geography Facts That Are Fake' 211K (4 days old, list item only); SciManDan 70K (1:40); Short 1M (repeating the myth). 'can you see the great wall of china from space': NatGeo 'Secrets of the Great Wall' 12M (a general doc, not the myth); matching long-form is all short clips (Namaste World 219K, 2:34); Shorts 1.1M, 79K, 46K, 41K. 'astronaut great wall of china': only Shorts ('China's First Astronaut Couldn't See the Great Wall' 3.7K; 'the myth is older than spaceflight' 1K), so the origin-trail angle is unclaimed in long form.
candidates.risks: (1) Nuance: from low orbit, under perfect light, some astronauts report glimpses and zoom-lens photos exist. The script must say 'not from the Moon, barely if ever by naked eye from orbit, and never the only thing' to stay true. (2) Verify Yang Liwei's 2003 quote and the textbook-revision reporting before scripting (my quick web check confirmed Stukeley 1754, Norman 1895, Ripley 1932, Halliburton 1938 and Armstrong's denials). (3) The US hook is softer (China setting), but the myth's spreaders, Ripley and Halliburton, were American, and US schools taught it. (4) Keep it non-political about China.

candidates.working_title: Columbus Didn't Prove the Earth Was Round. He Proved He Was Wrong.
candidates.premise: Americans grew up on the story of brave Columbus versus ignorant scholars who thought the Earth was flat. In 1492 every educated European knew the Earth was round. The real argument was about its size, and the experts who rejected Columbus were right: he had shrunk the planet by roughly two-thirds and would have starved at sea if an unknown continent hadn't been in the way. The twist is who invented the flat-earth story: Washington Irving, the American author of 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow', in his 1828 Columbus biography.
candidates.archetype: The 'History facts you were never supposed to question' format (614K on a 5.7K-sub channel; '10 Famous Ancient Events That Never Happened' 1.1M; 'Things You Learned in School That Are No Longer True' 245K on 1.6K subs). The demand is broad (medieval-flat-earth debunks: Kaz Rowe 730K, Metatron 172K), while the dedicated Columbus long-form is thin and unclaimed: History Camp 145K (1 month old), Today I Found Out 96K (7 min), TimeGhost 62K (5 min). Nothing on the Washington Irving origin tops 24K.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: an American classroom poster of Columbus pointing at the horizon while monks gasp at the edge of a flat world, then a hard cut to a real 1492 globe: round. 'Everybody knew. So what was the fight really about?' PROTAGONIST: Columbus, a self-taught salesman of one big idea, with his math: a small Earth plus a huge Asia means Japan is about 2,400 nautical miles west of the Canaries. ANTAGONISTS (who turn out to be right): the royal commission of scholars, who use Eratosthenes-style figures and say the gap is far too big for any ship's water and food. ESCALATION: seven years of rejections, then Isabella's gamble, and 33 days of open sea with the crew near mutiny. TWIST 1: land appears exactly where Columbus's wrong map put Japan, because an unknown continent sits in the gap. Our engine overlays Martin Behaim's 1492 globe on the real Earth: Japan lands on Mexico. TWIST 2: the experts' number is vindicated 29 years later when Magellan's crew crosses the real gap, the Pacific, and nearly starves. TWIST 3 (myth origin): 1828, Washington Irving dramatizes a flat-earth showdown at Salamanca that never happened, and 19th-century American textbooks and authors carry it into every classroom. PAYOFF: the hero of the myth was wrong and lucky, the 'ignorant' scholars were right, and the myth itself is an American invention.
candidates.hero_image: Two globes side by side: a small one labelled 'Columbus's Earth' and a much bigger one labelled 'the real Earth', with a tiny ship in the gap between them.
candidates.mobile_fit: The central visual is a single size comparison of two spheres, one small and one big, readable at any size. The Behaim-globe-on-real-globe overlay is the same trick ep01's critique praised (the 3D antipode overlay), done as one bold move. Characters (Columbus, a stern commission, a terrified crew, Irving at his desk) carry the funny scenes.
candidates.engine_fit: Excellent. Photoreal globe plus a second sphere wrapped in the public-domain Behaim 'Erdapfel' gores (1492) for the overlay. Great-circle arcs for the planned vs real distance, a true-size shrink morph of the Earth, distance counters, and low-poly ships and crew. Public domain: the Behaim globe facsimiles, Toscanelli-style reconstructions, Irving's 1828 text, and 19th-century textbook engravings.

'columbus was wrong about the size of the earth': the max long-form is the same 96K; dozens of tiny Shorts (under 2.4K), so the angle is fragmented and unclaimed. (2) The Salamanca/Talavera commission details are partly reconstructed by historians. State only what is documented (the commission rejected the plan over distance), and attribute the 'flat earth council' scene to Irving. (4) The Magellan beat is widely covered (Map Pack 'Insane True Story of the First Trip Around Earth' 3.5M), so use it as a single payoff beat, not a section.

candidates.working_title: America Was Named by Accident (And the Mapmaker Tried to Take It Back)
candidates.premise: Why is America called America? Because a 29-year-old poet and a mapmaker in a small French town read a sensational travel pamphlet, credited the wrong man, and printed 'America' on a 1507 world map. Within a few years the mapmaker removed the name, but it had already escaped. The only surviving copy of the map sat forgotten in a German castle for centuries until a Jesuit teacher found it in 1901, and the US paid $10 million for it.
candidates.archetype: An origin-of-a-name myth-bust with a mass US hook. Demand is proven: History Matters 'Who Named the United States?' 1.5M (3:27 animated), 'How did America get its Name???' Short 504K, 'How Did Each U.S. State Get Its Name?' 6.3M, RobWords 'The origin of every US state's name' 2M, Map Men 'Where is America?' 3.4M (a different angle: what the word refers to). The specific Waldseemuller story has no English long-form above 31K (Geography Geek 'The map that gave America its name', 11 min). Terra X did it in German (1M), which proves the story works.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: Library of Congress, a dim vault, one enormous old map behind glass. Zoom to a single word in tiny Latin print on a sliver of South America: AMERICA. 'This is the first time anyone ever wrote that word. The man who wrote it later tried to erase it.' PROTAGONISTS: Martin Waldseemuller and the poet Matthias Ringmann in Saint-Die. CATALYST: Vespucci's 'Mundus Novus' pamphlet (a Renaissance bestseller and sensational, including what Europeans read as lurid descriptions), and a letter claiming four voyages, which historians suspect was embellished by publishers. ESCALATION: Ringmann's playful logic: Europe and Asia have women's names, so why not 'Amerige, land of Americus'. 1,000 copies are printed. TWIST 1: Columbus is never credited. Vespucci, a Florentine merchant and navigator whom Emerson would later sneer at as a 'pickle-dealer', gets two continents. TWIST 2: in the 1513 edition the land becomes 'Terra Incognita', and on the 1516 Carta Marina it is 'Terra Nova'. Waldseemuller drops the name. TWIST 3: too late. Copycat mapmakers spread it, and Mercator (1538) stamps 'America' on both continents. TWIST 4: all 1,000 copies vanish except one, found in 1901 at Wolfegg Castle and bought by the US government for $10 million. PAYOFF: the country's name is a copied typo of history, kept alive by other people's maps, which is exactly how map myths work.
candidates.hero_image: The 1507 Waldseemuller map with the single word 'AMERICA' circled in red and a giant red strike-through, reading as 'the mapmaker crossed it out'.
candidates.mobile_fit: One word on one map is the whole idea, and it reads instantly. Keep shots big: a full-screen map fragment, a single word, a single castle, a single vault. Avoid panning over the dense map at full extent (ep01's lesson); use crop-and-zoom on high-contrast details instead.
candidates.engine_fit: Good. The LOC's public-domain high-res scan of the 1507 map (plus the 1513 Ptolemy and 1516 Carta Marina) allows Ken Burns crops and an 'old map morphs onto the real globe' transition (map gores to sphere). Globe arcs for Vespucci's voyages, Natural Earth coastlines for the old-vs-true outline overlay, and low-poly characters for the printing shop and castle-library discovery.

Then Tried to Take It Back' Short with 527 views, so the retraction angle is unclaimed. 'how america got its name': History Matters 1.5M, Atlas Pro 170K (6:21, 8 years old), Name Explain 105K; Short 504K. 'amerigo vespucci': Terra X (German) 1.04M; English docs under 72K. 'the map that named america': Geography Geek 31K; Shorts 1-4K. 'who named america': Atlas Pro 170K, Name Explain 105K.

(2) Retraction nuance: Waldseemuller never wrote 'I regret naming it America'. candidates.working_title: America Sent an Expedition to Find a Continent. It Was a Mirage.
candidates.premise: In 1906 Robert Peary reported snow-capped mountains far out on the Arctic Ocean and named them Crocker Land after a wealthy backer. The American Museum of Natural History sent an expedition in 1913 to claim it. The men walked over a hundred miles across sea ice toward mountains that kept retreating. Their Inuit guide told them it was a mirage, and it was. Then the expedition was trapped for four years, a guide was shot by an American officer, and historians later found that Peary's own diary for the 'sighting' day says no land was visible.
candidates.archetype: Rides 'phantom land on the map' (Map Men 'The Phantom Island of Google Maps' 3.2M; Top5s '5 Islands That Mysteriously Vanished' 1.4M; Geomargin 'Investigating an Unknown Phantom Island' 644K on a small channel) crossed with 'expedition disaster true story' (Scary Interesting 'The Disturbing 1819 Coppermine Expedition' 1.3M; '119-Day Survival Story' 1.5M; Julius Manuel 'That One Wrong Line on the Map! 865 Days of Hell' 231K). Crocker Land itself is barely claimed in long form (The History Guy 72K is the max).
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: April 1914, on the frozen Arctic Ocean. Two Americans and Inuit guides with dog sleds see a white mountain range on the horizon, exactly where the map says Crocker Land should be. They drive toward it. It moves away. PROTAGONISTS: Donald MacMillan (leader) and Ensign Fitzhugh Green, plus the guide Piugaattoq, who knows the Arctic far better than either. BACKSTORY: 1906, Robert Peary, desperate for money for his North Pole push, reports distant snow-clad summits and names them for San Francisco banker George Crocker. ESCALATION: the expedition stakes years and lives on a line on a map. Piugaattoq calls it a mirage (the Fata Morgana effect is explained visually), and MacMillan finally admits he is right. TWIST 1: on the way back, Green shoots Piugaattoq after an argument over the route, and is never prosecuted. TWIST 2: the expedition is stranded for years as relief ships fail to reach them. TWIST 3: historians open Peary's journal for the day he 'saw' Crocker Land and find 'No land visible.' PAYOFF: a map is only as honest as the person who drew it; and the land everyone was promised was literally light bending over ice.
candidates.hero_image: Three tiny dog-sled figures on endless white ice, walking toward a glowing mountain range on the horizon that is visibly flickering or fading. Text: 'IT WAS NEVER THERE'.
candidates.mobile_fit: Huge empty white space, one horizon line, tiny human figures and one phantom mountain range: the strongest possible silhouette composition for a phone. Each beat is a single dramatic image (mirage, shot, ice-locked ship, diary page).
candidates.engine_fit: Strong. DEM terrain and bathymetry for northern Ellesmere and the Arctic Ocean, a Fata Morgana effect as a horizon-stretch shader, the globe pullback to show where the phantom land was drawn, low-poly sled teams and dogs, and an ice-locked ship. Public domain: Crocker Land Expedition photos (AMNH and Bowdoin archives; check rights), Peary-era maps showing Crocker Land, and US government material.

'peary crocker land mirage': no long-form above 762 views; Shorts under 10K, so wide open. 'islands that never existed on maps': Short 'THIS PLACE NEVER EXISTED!' 1.1M; long-form tops out at 153K. 'the land that was on maps but never existed': Short 419K; long-form tops out at 27K. 'fata morgana arctic expedition': Julius Manuel 231K (the Peary Channel and Mikkelsen side of the same 'wrong line on Peary's map' story).
candidates.risks: (1) This is less of an 'everyone believes this' myth. The hook is 'maps tell the truth', so the thumbnail must sell the mirage, not the myth. (2) Peary's fraud is the likely reading (his diary says 'No land visible') but the intent is inferred: say 'historians believe'. (3) The killing of Piugaattoq must be handled soberly and factually, and his name spellings vary in sources. (4) Arctic expedition stories skew to longer formats. Keep it to 12-15 minutes by cutting the four-year stranding into one escalation beat. (5) Dates conflict slightly across sources (departure Feb or March 1914; mirage admitted about 22-27 April). Pin them in the facts ledger.

candidates.working_title: One Bad Map Drew America's Weirdest Borders
candidates.premise: Why is a piece of Minnesota stuck inside Canada? Why did Ohio and Michigan nearly go to war over Toledo? Why did Maine lumberjacks and British troops face off in 1839? Same answer: one 1755 map. John Mitchell's map was on the table when the US and Britain drew the borders of the new country in 1783, and its errors (a Mississippi source in the wrong place, Lake Michigan drawn too far north, a mislabelled river) became fights that lasted decades. One map, three border crises, and the strangest bumps on the US map today.
candidates.archetype: A 'borders that make no sense' listicle with one unifying spine ('7 Borders That Make Absolutely No Sense' 702K on 17.7K subs). Each chapter has proven demand on its own: the Northwest Angle (From Here to There 'Why This Town Is In Both The US & Canada' 6.2M; CBS 'America's small town in Canada' 5.1M; Off the Cuff 4.2M; Half as Interesting 1.4M), the Toledo War (KnowledgeHusk 995K; Mr. Beat 429K; History Guy 324K; Short 'Michigan Won This Land by Losing a War to Ohio' 762K). Nobody has tied them to the single map: 'mitchell map 1755' has no long-form above 1.4K.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: on Minnesota's Northwest Angle, a road crosses into Canada and back into the US, and you phone customs from a booth in a shed. 'This bump exists because of a mistake printed in 1755.' PROTAGONIST: John Mitchell, a Virginia doctor and botanist (not a professional surveyor) who drew the most detailed map of North America of his time, a map meant to sell British claims against France. ESCALATION 1: Paris, 1783. The negotiators use Mitchell's map to write the border in words: 'due west from the most northwestern point of the Lake of the Woods to the Mississippi'. In reality the Mississippi starts far to the south, so the line is impossible, and the patch-up later leaves the Angle stranded. ESCALATION 2: the Northwest Ordinance line 'due east from the southern extreme of Lake Michigan' relies on maps (Mitchell's among them) that put the lake's tip too far north. Ohio and Michigan both claim Toledo, militias march in 1835, and the only casualty is a sheriff stabbed by a man named Two Stickney. TWIST: Michigan 'loses' and gets the Upper Peninsula as a consolation prize, which turns out to hold some of the richest copper and iron deposits in the country. ESCALATION 3: which river is the 'St. Croix'? Maine and New Brunswick lumberjacks and militias face off in the bloodless Aroostook War (1838-39), defused by the 1842 Webster-Ashburton Treaty. PAYOFF: one man's map is still visible in the kinks of the US border, and it was used in boundary arguments long after anyone trusted its geography. Final overlay: Mitchell's map laid over the true continent, sliding until the errors line up with today's border bumps.
candidates.hero_image: An old sepia map with one modern red border line, and a little rectangle of Minnesota visibly floating above the US-Canada line. Text: 'ONE MAP DID THIS'.
candidates.mobile_fit: Every chapter boils down to one bump on a map that viewers can see at thumbnail size: the Angle, the Toledo strip, Maine's crooked top. The comedy (Two Stickney, the 'war' with no deaths, the lumberjacks) runs on big-character animation. Avoid full-map pans; isolate one region per beat.
candidates.engine_fit: Strong. The LOC public-domain high-res Mitchell map, georeferenced and overlaid on the real terrain and coastlines (the old-vs-true slide is a signature shot), Natural Earth borders and lakes, DEM terrain for Lake of the Woods and the St. John valley, great-circle arcs to Paris, low-poly militias and lumberjacks, and counters for the Upper Peninsula's copper and iron.
candidates.probes: 'mitchell map 1755': no matching long-form (max 1.4K, a lecture); Shorts 1.1-1.4K ('A Bad 1755 Map Cut Off This Part of the USA', 'The Map That Accidentally Drew America'), so the unifying angle is unclaimed. 'northwest angle minnesota': CBS 5.1M (5:48), Off the Cuff 4.2M (14:16), Half as Interesting 1.4M (5:04), CBC 439K, From Here to There 434K; Short 756K. 'why is part of minnesota in canada': From Here to There 6.2M (57 min), CBS 5.1M, Off the Cuff 4.2M. 'toledo war': KnowledgeHusk 995K (6:50, 9 years old), History Guy 324K, Studio Alpaca 68K; Short 762K. 'ohio michigan war': Mr. Beat 429K. 'aroostook war': long-form tops out at 5.7K (HelenasDen), wide open.
candidates.risks: (1) The Northwest Angle by itself is well covered (several 1M+ videos). The film only works if the single-map spine leads and the Angle is one act, not the hook alone. (2) Mitchell's direct role in the Toledo dispute needs a careful facts ledger: the Ordinance language plus the period maps' Lake Michigan placement. Say 'maps of the day, like Mitchell's' if the evidence is only general. (3) It overlaps in theme with the Colorado candidate. Pick one for episode 2 and use the other as the end-card handoff. (4) Upper Peninsula wealth claims (comparisons to the California Gold Rush) must be sourced before any number is used.

candidates.working_title: They Fought a Volcano With Firehoses. And Won. (Heimaey, Iceland, 1973)
candidates.premise: At 2 a.m. on 23 January 1973 the ground split open on the edge of Iceland's biggest fishing town. About 5,000 people got off the island that night, mostly because a storm the day before had kept the whole fishing fleet in harbour. Then the lava started heading for the harbour, the one thing the town needed to survive, and a handful of locals decided to stop it by spraying seawater on it. They managed it. In the end the lava left the harbour better than it had been before.
candidates.archetype: Humans against a lava flow, plus a disaster told as a true story. Evidence: 'Building Iceland's Lava Barriers' (BuildWitt) 943K and 'This Giant Bulldozer Saved An Icelandic Town From Lava' 844K show the 'town vs lava' premise pulls nearly 1M for mid-size channels. 'Pinatubo: The Volcano That Claimed 850 Lives' got 703K on a 44.5K-sub channel. Iceland volcano Shorts run at 8M to 96M views. Long-form supply for Heimaey itself is close to zero: the best is 98K (KiKi Swiat, 3y), and VERUM's 27K (4mo) is the most recent.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: 01:55, a farmer's house and a 1.6 km curtain of fire opening a few hundred metres from sleeping streets. Church bells and the fire siren go off, and 5,000 people walk to the docks in their pyjamas. LUCK: a storm the previous day had kept roughly 70 boats in port, so the whole town is at sea within hours. PROTAGONISTS: the few hundred who stay behind (firemen, fishermen, volunteers shovelling ash off roofs), and physicist Thorbjorn Sigurgeirsson, who says seawater can freeze lava in place. ESCALATION: ash buries hundreds of houses and a new mountain (Eldfell) grows out of a cow pasture. The lava front then turns toward the harbour mouth, and if the harbour closes the town is finished. The first try is literally fire hoses. Next comes a dredging ship pumping seawater, then high-capacity pumps shipped in from the United States, with pipes laid across moving, still-hot lava. TICKING CLOCK: the gap at the harbour mouth shrinks week by week. TWIST: the cooled lava walls hold, the eruption stops in July, and the new rock acts as a breakwater that makes the harbour better than before. The island is about 20% bigger. PAYOFF: people come home, dig out their houses (Eldheimar, the 'Pompeii of the North'), and 50 years later Grindavik builds its lava walls on the same idea.
candidates.hero_image: A wall of black, steaming lava with thin white jets of water arcing onto it from tiny figures holding hoses, and a small red-roofed harbour town right behind them.
candidates.mobile_fit: The image works without explanation: hoses against a volcano. Every beat is a single big shape: one island, one glowing crack, one harbour mouth getting narrower, one wall of rock. The harbour-mouth gap can be shown as a single shrinking gauge, which reads well on a 6-inch screen.
candidates.engine_fit: Excellent. The DEM terrain builder can render Heimaey before and after, with the island growing 20% and the harbour mouth narrowing, as a true-shape morph. Lava front advance can be an animated mask on the terrain. Low-poly CC0 people and boats cover the night evacuation (a fleet of tiny lights leaving the harbour) and the hose crews. The globe opener drops from Iceland down to the island. There is room for light humour: the first plan really was the town fire brigade's hoses against a volcano. Public-domain material includes the USGS documentation of the lava-cooling operation (Open-File Report 97-724, plus USGS general-interest material) and NASA Landsat imagery of the island today.
candidates.probes: heimaey eruption 1973: best long-form 98K (KiKi Swiat 35m, 3y), 70K (8m), 36K. 'iceland town fought volcano with seawater': Terran Works 18K (9mo), everything else under 5K. 'eldfell westman islands 1973 eruption': VERUM 27K (4mo). 'volcano erupted in the middle of a town iceland 1973': no matching long-form, only Iceland Shorts at 96M/40M/8M. 'grindavik lava barriers town': BuildWitt 943K (2y), Real Big Machines 844K (1y), Short 'Lava flowed over a giant wall. What stopped it?' 941K. 'town that fought a volcano': max matching 149K. 'heimaey': max long-form 34K. Verdict: high demand for the premise, and the specific story is unclaimed in English long-form. Probed across the lens and dropped as saturated or claimed: Lake Nyos (Nick Crowley 3.75M, RealLifeLore 2.08M, Brew 1.27M), Salton Sea origin (IT'S HISTORY 1.5M, Park Vibes 1.28M), Tromelin (Scary Interesting 5M, Atlas One 3M in 1mo), Clipperton (2.9M/1.4M), Lady Be Good (3.2M), Frank Slide (1.5M), Yungay (Geoclysm 1.1M), Johnstown (1.1M), Galveston 1900 (745K x2, recent), Alaska 1964 (866K/777K, recent), Knox Mine (612K/526K), Mt Pelee (597K plus Shorts 790K), Montserrat/Plymouth (PBS Terra 578K, 862K), Vargas 1999 (623K), Armero (Spanish 4.5M).
candidates.risks: Things to verify: total seawater volume (sources say 6.2 million tonnes or 7.3 million m3, so use 'millions of tonnes'), number and origin of the US pumps (32 vs 43), and whether anyone died. The evacuation itself had no deaths, and a later gas death is reported in some sources. Death toll is close to zero, so the stakes come from losing the town and the harbour, and the script has to make the economic life-or-death clear early. Iceland-sourced photos are mostly copyrighted, so lean on animation, USGS material and terrain. Some people have heard of Grindavik, which helps the hook.

candidates.working_title: The Night 12 Cables Snapped Under the Atlantic, One by One
candidates.premise: On 18 November 1929 an earthquake shook the seafloor south of Newfoundland. Over the next 13 hours the transatlantic telegraph cables broke one after another, in order, further and further out to sea, and nobody could say why. Hours later a tsunami hit Newfoundland's isolated Burin Peninsula in the dark, and the outside world didn't hear about it for days. More than 20 years later, scientists used the exact times the cables broke to prove that a gigantic underwater avalanche had raced down the slope.
candidates.archetype: An underwater spectacle combined with a mystery that finally gets solved, so 'drain the ocean' meets a true disaster. Evidence from the outlier pull: 'We Drained the Chesapeake Bay' 170K in 1 week on 1.4K subs; 'What Antarctica Looks Like Without Ice' 1.8M on 2.9K subs; 'underwater archaeology discoveries' keyword up 185%. Cable-mystery adjacent: Bloomberg 'The Mystery of the Vanishing Undersea Cable' 1.33M. Nat Geo 'Drain the Oceans: Deadly Pacific' 10.8M. Supply for the event itself: the best long-form is 182K, a 9-year-old Canadian TV episode.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: 5:02 p.m., a telegraph operator watches a line from Europe go dead. A minute later a second line dies, then another, and the breaks keep marching south-east all night. MYSTERY: an earthquake ought to break everything at once, so why in sequence, hours apart and hundreds of km away? PARALLEL THREAD: about 2.5 hours after the quake, three waves hit the fishing villages of the Burin Peninsula (Port au Bras, Lord's Cove, Taylor's Bay). Houses float out to sea with lamps still burning. Characters include the Rennie family of Port au Bras: the mother and three children drowned and two-year-old Margaret was pulled alive from the wreckage (verify details). TICKING CLOCK: winter is coming, homes, boats and food stores are gone, and with the lines down nobody knows. Help only arrives after a coastal steamer gets word out by wireless and a relief ship brings doctors and nurses. ESCALATION: 28 dead, the only deadly tsunami in Canadian history. TWIST: in 1952 Bruce Heezen and Maurice Ewing plot the cable-break times on a seafloor map. The breaks trace an invisible avalanche of mud and sand pouring down the continental slope at highway speed (estimates of about 60 to 100 km/h) for hundreds of km. The cables that cut the villages off became the clock that measured the killer. PAYOFF: these 'turbidity currents' carve the great submarine canyons, and today's internet cables still face the same hazard.
candidates.hero_image: A cutaway of the dark Atlantic seafloor slope with five or six glowing cable lines, each snapping with a bright spark in sequence as a brown avalanche cloud sweeps downhill.
candidates.mobile_fit: There is one simple, mesmerising visual idea: lines breaking one by one, like dominoes. The thumbnail reads instantly as 'something under the sea broke them'. Village scenes are single houses and single waves, with very few labels. Timestamps can be shown as one big ticking clock instead of tables.
candidates.engine_fit: This is the engine's best case. The DEM/bathymetry terrain builder can drain the water off the Grand Banks and the Laurentian Fan to show the real slope and canyons, which is the same format as the Chesapeake/Great Lakes outliers. Great-circle cable routes go on the globe, with an avalanche particle flow moving down the real terrain and break markers firing at the historical times. Low-poly houses, boats and characters cover the Burin night. Historic 1929 photos of the Burin damage are probably public domain (Canadian, pre-1949, verify per image), and NOAA bathymetry is public domain.
candidates.probes: '1929 grand banks earthquake tsunami': max 182K (Serial Chill Zone reupload of 'Disasters of the Century', 9y), 127K (NL govt, 10y), nothing recent above 13K. 'underwater avalanche snapped transatlantic cables': no long-form at all, only Shorts at 1.3K to 4K (so someone is testing it on Shorts). 'grand banks cable breaks 1929 turbidity current': no matching long-form. '1929 newfoundland tsunami': max 182K and 127K, both 9-10 years old. 'transatlantic cables broke mystery': adjacent cable content 1.74M (RealLifeLore2), 1.33M (Bloomberg), 1.29M (CNBC), but none on 1929. 'underwater landslide documentary': Nat Geo Drain the Oceans 10.8M, Nat Geo X-Ray Earth East Coast tsunami 1.69M. Verdict: unclaimed, with clear adjacent demand.
candidates.risks: The scientific details are debated: Heezen and Drake (1964) and later work argue the first, near-instant breaks came from a slump, and only the later ones from the turbidity current. Speed estimates vary (about 60 to 100 km/h), and the magnitude is 7.2 in most sources. Script it as 'up to highway speed' and avoid false precision. The Burin character details (the Rennie family, the nurse on the relief ship, how the news got out) need a careful fact pass. Most of the stakes are in Newfoundland, which is less US-centric, but the US/Europe cable angle and the East Coast tsunami question give US viewers a hook.

candidates.working_title: The Year California Became a 300-Mile Lake
candidates.premise: In the winter of 1861-62 it rained on California for about 43 days. The Central Valley filled up like a bathtub into a brown inland sea, roughly 250 to 300 miles long. The new governor reportedly went to his own inauguration by rowboat, and the state capital had to move to San Francisco. Geologists say it was not a freak event, it will happen again, and in 2023 a vanished lake came back to prove the point.
candidates.archetype: A 'what's hidden or what if' spectacle backed by a true historical disaster, the same format as 'What If All the Ice Melted' (961K on 1.5K subs) and 'We Drained the Great Lakes' (165K on 1.4K subs), but reversed: we fill the valley. Demand evidence: Tulare Lake Shorts at 22M ('How California's Largest Lake Disappeared') and 15M. Map Pack 'Why One of USA's Biggest Lakes Is Reappearing' 1.6M. Joe Scott 'Forget Earthquakes. THIS Is What Could Doom California' 1.21M (an ARkStorm future scenario, not the 1862 story). Paul McAllister on Tulare/Boswell 223K (1mo). Rising keywords: 'disasters explained' +110% and 'what would happen if' +134%.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: January 1862, Sacramento. A man rows a boat down the main street past second-floor windows. The new governor, Leland Stanford, is sworn in, and the story goes he travels there by rowboat and climbs back into his own house through a window. PROTAGONIST AND WITNESS: geologist William Brewer of the California Geological Survey, whose letters describe a sheet of brown water from the Coast Range to the Sierra. These letters are public domain and very quotable. ESCALATION: storm after storm, hydraulic-mining debris clogging rivers, towns swept away, hundreds of thousands of cattle drowned, the legislature fleeing to San Francisco, and Los Angeles and Oregon flooding too. TICKING CLOCK: the rain won't stop and the valley's only drain is a narrow gap at the Golden Gate. TWIST 1: Sacramento's answer was to physically raise its downtown streets by about 10+ feet, and the buried first floors are still under the city. TWIST 2: sediment cores show megafloods like this, and bigger ones, hit California every century or two. TWIST 3: in 2023 the ghost Tulare Lake reappeared on farmland. PAYOFF: USGS's ARkStorm scenario puts the price of a repeat near the trillion-dollar range, and 'California's real Big One isn't an earthquake.'
candidates.hero_image: A satellite-style map of California with the whole Central Valley filled by one long brown inland sea, with a tiny rowboat in front of the state capitol dome.
candidates.mobile_fit: One shape does the work: California with a giant lake inside it. The 'before/after' fill reads in a second, even at thumbnail size. The scenes stay simple: one city underwater, one boat, one rising-water gauge on a building.
candidates.engine_fit: This is a signature shot for us. The DEM terrain builder can flood the real Central Valley topography to the documented water level (the same technique as the 'drained' outliers, run in reverse), with true-scale comparisons such as a lake the size of Lake Erie or Lake Michigan appearing. GIBS satellite patches can show the Tulare Lake return in April 2023, and NASA/USGS imagery is public domain. 1862 lithographs and photos of flooded Sacramento (Library of Congress, California State Library, public domain by age) suit Ken Burns treatment. Low-poly characters cover the rowboat governor and the raising of Sacramento, which also allows light humour (a city jacking itself up).
candidates.probes: 'great flood of 1862 california': max matching long-form only about 7K. Waterwake 'Why California's Real Big One Isn't an Earthquake' 211K (42m, 2mo), Earth in Hindsight 60K (77m, 3w), Geoclysm 'California's Inland Sea' 14K (6mo). 'california 1862 megaflood central valley lake': Shorts 22M and 15M (Tulare), 'Uncovering' 295K (4m). 'arkstorm': Joe Scott 1.21M (3y), FOX 11 153K. 'the year california turned into a lake': max 288K, but off-topic. 'tulare lake returns 2023': Map Pack 1.6M (3y), Wolficorn 468K, Park Vibes 197K (2mo), Paul McAllister 223K (1mo). 'california megaflood 1862 documentary': MEMORIA 11K (2mo). Verdict: there is a lot of demand around the topic and nobody has a big hit on the 1862 narrative itself. Two small channels started on it in the last 2-3 months, so the window is open but closing.
candidates.risks: Fact discipline matters. The rowboat inauguration is widely reported but should be framed as 'by most accounts'. Brewer's wording is '250 to 300 miles', so title it '300-Mile' only if the script says 'up to'. The 'state went bankrupt' claim is not supported, so don't use it. Death toll estimates (often quoted as about 4,000) are weak, so avoid a precise number. ARkStorm dollar figures depend on which study you cite (2010 USGS vs the 2022 update). The 'what if it happens again' angle must not become fearmongering. A probed alternate in the same US flood family is the 1928 Okeechobee hurricane ('the lake that walked out of its bed', about 2,500 dead). It is unclaimed (best 138K, 13y, and Unfilmed 74K, 1mo), but demand is weaker and the subject is heavier.

candidates.working_title: The Loneliest Island on Earth Fled a Volcano to England. Then Voted to Go Back.
candidates.premise: In October 1961 the ground cracked open right beside the only village on Tristan da Cunha, the most remote inhabited island on Earth. All 264 islanders were taken out and shipped to England, a country most of them had never seen. They were housed at an old RAF camp, studied by doctors and chased by reporters. Then, offered modern Britain for good, they voted 148 to 5 to go back to the volcano.
candidates.archetype: A remote place combined with a disaster and survival story, riding a live wave. 'Tristan da Cunha' is a rising keyword (+118%, about 315K/mo). Ruhi Cenet's 'Exploring the Most Remote Island on Earth' got 27.7M views in 11 days. Yes Theory got 11.2M, Redfern 11.7M, Geography By Geoff 4.75M, Impossible Travel 945K (3mo). The forbidden/remote-island premise is proven for small channels: 'Why Can't You Visit Iwo Jima?' 4.4M on 3.5K subs, 'Every Forbidden Island' 878K on 1.5K subs. The 1961 eruption itself is barely covered: best is 57K (Royal Society, 9y).
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: an island 2,400 km from anywhere. Earthquakes for weeks, rocks splitting, and then a hill of steaming rock bulging up a few hundred metres from the cottages. PROTAGONISTS: the islanders, descendants of a few shipwrecked sailors and settlers with their own 19th-century English, led by Chief Islander Willie Repetto. EVACUATION: they spend a night on a nearby island with the penguins (Nightingale Island) and are picked up by a passing Dutch liner. Then Cape Town, then a ship to Southampton. CULTURE SHOCK, with room for gentle humour: traffic, money, television, newspapers, queues and strangers. The serious beat is that with no immunity to common viruses many fell ill, and some of the elderly died (verify numbers). ESCALATION: Britain assumes they'll settle, and jobs and council houses are offered. Meanwhile a Royal Society expedition returns to Tristan in 1962 and finds the lava stopped short of the village, though the landing beach and the crayfish factory were destroyed. TWIST: in a secret ballot at Calshot, adults vote 148 to 5 to go home to the volcano. PAYOFF: they return in 1963 and rename the new harbour 'Calshot Harbour', and today's island, the one with the 27M-view videos, exists because they chose it.
candidates.hero_image: A tiny green volcanic island in an enormous empty blue ocean, with a red eruption glowing right beside a cluster of white cottages and a thin arrow arcing north to England.
candidates.mobile_fit: The image is one dot of land, one red glow, one long arrow, which reads at any size. Emotional beats are single characters: the chief, a family on a ship deck, an islander staring at a London bus. No dense maps are needed, because the globe shows only 'here' and 'there'.
candidates.engine_fit: Strong. The photoreal globe can show the true isolation (zoom out from the island until no other land is visible, then a great-circle arc to Southampton, 10,000+ km). The DEM terrain builder can render Tristan's single huge cone, with the 1961 dome added beside the village. Low-poly CC0 people, ships and a 1960s England street can carry the culture-shock comedy. The night-lights layer can contrast the island's darkness with England's glow. Public-domain photos from 1961 are scarce, since the British press photos are copyrighted, so this is mostly animated reconstruction, with NASA/Landsat imagery of the island.
candidates.probes: 'tristan da cunha volcano 1961 evacuation': max 57K (Royal Society film, 9y), History Chap 227K (general history, 1y), and everything recent is under 5K. 'tristan da cunha': Ruhi Cenet 27.7M (11 days), Redfern 11.7M, Yes Theory 11.2M, Geoff 4.75M, Ramilla 2.0M, Josh Cahill 1.57M, Shorts 14M/4.1M/3.4M. 'tristan da cunha islanders england': Impossible Travel 945K (3mo), History Guy 504K (3y), britishdocs 1989 doc 409K. 'most remote island volcano eruption evacuated' and 'islanders went back to their volcano island': no matching long-form. 'tristan da cunha eruption': nothing on the eruption beyond 57K. Verdict: the 'what is life like there' angle is saturated, while the 1961 eruption and exile story is unclaimed and sits next to a 27M-view video that is driving suggested traffic right now.
candidates.risks: The geography is the setting and the trigger, but the volcano kills no one directly. The drama is exile and choice, so the script must keep a ticking clock in the England act (illness, pressure to stay, the vote). Facts to verify: the exact population (260 to 264), the 148-to-5 tally (Time magazine, find a second source), how many died in England, and the ship names and timeline. Archival imagery is limited and copyrighted, so expect heavy animation. Timing matters, because the Tristan surge from the 27M video may fade within weeks, so it is worth fast-tracking if chosen.

candidates.working_title: The Wave That Erased a Lighthouse, Then Raced 3,700 km to Hawaii
candidates.premise: At 2 a.m. on 1 April 1946 an earthquake off Alaska sent a wave over the brand-new concrete lighthouse at Scotch Cap and killed all five keepers. The same wave then crossed the Pacific at jet-airliner speed with nobody able to warn anyone ahead of it. About five hours later it hit Hawaii on a school morning, and because it was April Fools' Day, some people thought the warnings were a joke.
candidates.archetype: A true disaster with a ticking clock across a whole ocean, plus a lighthouse-keeper hook. The rising keyword 'how lighthouse keepers survived winter on a rock in the middle of the ocean' is up 147% (about 173K/mo), and that exact-title video got 624K in 1mo. Maritime Horrors' 'The Scotch Cap Lighthouse Tragedy' got 1.44M, a 1M Short covers the same lighthouse, and Wild Weather's 'Deadliest Tsunamis' got 13.2M. The cross-Pacific race and the Hawaii side are unclaimed: the best Hawaii-1946 long-form is 179K (10y) and FAULT LINES has 29K (1mo).
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: Scotch Cap, Unimak Island. Five Coast Guardsmen in a reinforced-concrete lighthouse built on a bluff. A quake at 01:29, then a wall of water. The radio station up the hill sees the light go dark, and in the morning there is only a foundation. TICKING CLOCK: a giant onscreen clock starts. The wave crosses open ocean at around 700-800 km/h, a few feet high, so ships don't even feel it. There is no Pacific warning system, and the one post that saw it has been wiped out. INTERCUT: Hawaii waking up. Teachers and children at Laupahoehoe school on its low point by the sea, and Hilo's waterfront. ESCALATION: the sea pulls back and people walk out to look at stranded fish. Then come the surges. Characters: young teachers at Laupahoehoe, including Marsue McGinnis, who survived hours in the water (verify). TWIST: the earthquake was only moderate, yet the wave was enormous, a 'tsunami earthquake' that puzzled scientists for decades. PAYOFF: the disaster led to the Seismic Sea Wave Warning System (forerunner of the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center), so the next time, people got the hours the 1946 victims never had.
candidates.hero_image: A lone white lighthouse on a dark cliff with a towering black wave about to swallow it, plus a small Pacific inset with a red ring racing from Alaska to Hawaii.
candidates.mobile_fit: A lighthouse against a giant wave reads instantly. The rest of the film rests on two visual devices that work on phones: a huge countdown clock, and a single expanding ring crossing a nearly empty ocean on the globe. The Hawaii scenes use a few large characters on a beach.
candidates.engine_fit: Excellent fit for the globe. The tsunami can propagate across real Pacific bathymetry (the wave speeds up over deep water, which ties to the depth layer), with great-circle travel-time rings and Hawaii's arrival marked. The DEM renders Unimak's cliff and Hilo Bay. NOAA/NGDC and US-government photos of 1946 Hilo damage are largely public domain, and the US Coast Guard has before/after photos of Scotch Cap (US government, public domain). Low-poly lighthouse, keepers, schoolchildren and fishing boats complete it.
candidates.probes: '1946 april fools tsunami hilo': Wild Weather compilation 13.2M (all tsunamis), Astraway 938K (90m compilation), no dedicated long-form above 3K.
