candidates.working_title: The First Steamboat on the Mississippi Sailed Straight Into an Earthquake
candidates.premise: In 1811 a crazy-looking new machine, America's first steamboat in the West, set off down the Ohio and Mississippi to prove steam could beat the river. Aboard were the builder, his pregnant wife and their dog, with a great comet in the sky. Halfway there, the strongest earthquakes in the eastern US's recorded history tore the river apart around them. Banks collapsed, islands vanished, and weeks after they passed, the Mississippi briefly ran backwards.
candidates.archetype: A true survival voyage where geography is the villain, set in America's heartland (high-value US market). Evidence: The History Guy 'The Hard Shock: The New Madrid Earthquakes' 1.52M; MapReels 'The Mississippi River Isn't Really a River. It's a Wound.' 1.14M in 2 months; Hidden on Earth 'The Mississippi River Is Hiding Something' 424K (4mo). The US-region 'is hiding something' format pulls 300-470K on small channels (context pull). The 119-day survival story got 1.5M, which shows the pull of journey-under-threat stories. The steamboat angle has essentially no long-form (max 11K, 13y).
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: December 1811, night on the Mississippi. A paddle steamer tied to a tree as the ground roars, the trees thrash and the riverbank falls into the water. PROTAGONISTS: Nicholas Roosevelt, partner of Robert Fulton, and his wife Lydia, who refused to stay home while heavily pregnant. People bet they would die. SET-UP, with humour: crowds along the Ohio have never seen a steamboat. In Louisville people reportedly thought the comet had fallen into the river. Lydia gives birth on the way. They have to wait weeks for the Falls of the Ohio to rise high enough to pass. ESCALATION: 16 December, the first great shock. The river fills with uprooted trees, and channels and sandbars move overnight, so the pilot's knowledge is useless. They reach New Madrid to find the town wrecked and sunk, with people begging to come aboard. TICKING CLOCK: the boat can't go back upstream, so the only way is down through a river that keeps changing. TWIST: they make it to New Orleans in January 1812, and the steam age of the Mississippi begins in the middle of a natural catastrophe. Weeks later the February shock makes the river run backward for a while, creates waterfalls, and forms Reelfoot Lake. PAYOFF: the fault is still there. Myth-buster beat: the famous 'church bells rang in Boston' claim is probably not true.
candidates.hero_image: A tiny paddle steamer with a smoking chimney on a dark river where the bank is collapsing and a waterfall has appeared, and a long-tailed comet overhead.
candidates.mobile_fit: Boat, crack, comet: three big shapes. The whole film is one journey line on one river, which is the simplest possible map. The characters (couple, baby, dog, pilot) can be shown in big, close shots.
candidates.engine_fit: Good. Natural Earth rivers and the DEM show the Ohio and Mississippi route, with the boat's progress drawn as a single glowing line. The terrain builder can show Reelfoot Lake forming and the Kentucky Bend. LiDAR and DEM can reveal sand blows (USGS public-domain imagery). There are CC0 low-poly boats and people, and the comet can be done as a sky effect. 1811-12 engravings, the 1871 Latrobe account, and USGS New Madrid material are all public domain. There is genuine room for comedy (riverbank crowds, the comet panic, the steam 'monster').
candidates.probes: 'new madrid earthquake 1811 mississippi river ran backwards': History Guy 1.52M (4y), Vanished Worlds 103K (4mo), ankerssm 81K. 'new madrid earthquake steamboat new orleans 1811': USGS 327K (7m), TheGeoModels LiDAR 307K, no steamboat-led video. 'first steamboat on the mississippi earthquake 1811': max matching long-form 18 views (IDSTER 11K, 13y, 9m). 'steamboat new orleans maiden voyage 1811 nicholas roosevelt': zero relevant. 'mississippi river flowed backwards': MapReels 1.14M (2mo), Hidden on Earth 424K. 'when the mississippi ran backwards': max 103K. 'the earthquake that rang church bells in boston new madrid': no myth-bust exists. Verdict: New Madrid as a topic has one 1.5M video, but the steamboat-voyage story angle is completely unclaimed.
candidates.risks: Sourcing is the main danger. Much of the voyage colour comes from the 1871 account by Lydia's brother J.H.B. Latrobe, written 60 years later, so attribute vivid details ('according to the family's account'). The dog's name (Tiger), the passenger list (Lydia plus a child vs only Lydia) and where exactly the boat was during each shock all need checking against historians (e.g. Jay Feldman's 'When the Mississippi Ran Backwards'). The 'river ran backwards' happened in February 1812, after the boat had passed, so don't imply they saw it. Avoid Tecumseh prophecy claims and the 'New Madrid is about to split America' fearmongering common in this search space.

candidates.working_title: The Lake Hanging Over a City
candidates.premise: High above the Peruvian city of Huaraz sits a glacial lake held back by a pile of rubble. In 1941 it burst and wiped out a third of the city. Today it holds more than 30 times as much water. So a local farmer and mountain guide took a German energy giant 10,000 km away to court over it, German judges went to look at the lake, and in 2025 the verdict came in.
candidates.archetype: A killer-lake premise plus a true underdog story with a live ticking clock. Proven 'lake that kills' demand: Lake Nyos videos at 3.75M (Nick Crowley), 2.08M (RealLifeLore 'The Most Dangerous Lake on Earth') and 1.27M (Brew), with Shorts at 14M. The Lake Peigneur Short got 19M. Huaraz 1941 specifically is breaking out for small dubbed channels right now: 'HUARAZ 1941: The lagoon that BURIED a third of the city' 570K (2mo), 'Furia de la Tierra' 270K (2mo), Camadas do Tempo 168K (1mo). There is no English-native long-form telling the 1941 story together with the court case.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN: 13 December 1941, early morning. A block of ice drops into Lake Palcacocha, the moraine wall gives way, and a wall of mud, water and boulders runs down the valley into Huaraz while the city is waking up. Thousands die, with estimates from about 1,800 to 5,000+. GEOGRAPHY AS VILLAIN: a city built directly in the line of fire of a lake that sits about 20 km up and 1,500+ m above it (verify). Peru learns the hard way and starts draining and damming glacial lakes. ESCALATION: as the glacier retreats, Palcacocha grows again, to more than 30 times its old volume, with makeshift siphon pipes and a city of about 120,000 below. PROTAGONIST: Saul Luciano Lliuya, a farmer and mountain guide whose family house is in the flood path. In 2015 he sues RWE in Germany for 0.5% of the cost of protecting Huaraz, matching the company's estimated share of historical global emissions. Everyone expects him to be laughed out of court. TWISTS: in 2017 the court agrees to hear evidence, a first, and court experts later travel to Peru to survey the lake. On 28 May 2025 the Hamm court dismisses the claim because it judges the risk of a burst at about 1% in 30 years. But it also rules that big emitters can, in principle, be liable for damage on the other side of the world. PAYOFF: he lost the case but won the principle, and the lake is still up there.
candidates.hero_image: A turquoise glacial lake on a mountainside directly above a sprawling city, with a single dashed red arrow running down the valley into the rooftops.
candidates.mobile_fit: Lake above city with an arrow: the danger is understood in under a second without a single word. The court drama comes down to two faces (the farmer and the judge) and one number (0.5%), with no legal clutter.
candidates.engine_fit: Strong. The DEM terrain builder renders the Cordillera Blanca, Palcacocha and the Quebrada Cojup valley down to Huaraz in true 3D, with the 1941 flood path animated down the real topography and the glacier retreat shown with Landsat/GIBS imagery over time (NASA/USGS, public domain). A globe arc from Huaraz to the Ruhr shows the 10,000 km lawsuit distance. Low-poly characters cover the farmer, siphon crews and a courtroom. 1941 archival photos are uncertain for copyright, so animate instead.
candidates.probes: 'lake palcacocha huaraz glacial lake': Scientific American GLOF explainer 1.41M (4m), 'HUARAZ 1941' 570K (2mo), Camadas do Tempo 168K (1mo), Short 1.1M (GLOF). 'peruvian farmer sues rwe glacier': news clips only (DW 9.5K, Reuters 5K, Folha 11K) and no long-form story. 'huaraz 1941 flood': 570K (2mo), 270K (2mo), 168K (1mo), Short 'In 1941 This Lake Destroyed a City in 15 Minutes, Now They're Draining It' 31K. 'glacier lake above city could burst peru': only Pure Earth Nepal 2.56M (adjacent 'unstable Himalaya' premise, 2mo). 'farmer sued rwe over melting glacier documentary': nothing. 'lake nyos disaster' (premise check): 3.75M, 2.08M, 1.27M plus 14M Short. Verdict: demand is proven and growing, the English long-form is unclaimed, and the 2025 verdict gives a fresh ending.
candidates.risks: Climate litigation can polarise US comments, so keep it a human, geographic story and let the court's own words carry the ending, with no advocacy. The 1941 death toll is very uncertain (1,800 to 5,000+), so give a range. Lake height, distance and volume figures and the details of the court's site visit need verification. The story is less US-centric than the others, and the hook has to be 'a lake aimed at a city' rather than 'climate case'. Archival imagery is thin, so heavy animation is needed. Peru disaster stories are currently trending through dubbed Spanish/Portuguese channels, which shows demand and also means competition may arrive quickly.

candidates.working_title: The Island That Moved to England, Then Voted to Go Back to the Volcano
candidates.premise: In October 1961 the ground split open about 500 m behind the only village on Tristan da Cunha, the most remote inhabited island on Earth. All 264 islanders were shipped to England: cars, TV, wages, the Swinging Sixties. Fourteen months later they voted 148 to 5 to go back to the volcano, and most of them did. Why would anyone choose that?
candidates.archetype: Remote/forbidden-island premise, which is exploding right now. Context outliers: 'Why Can't You Visit Iwo Jima?' (Where They Stood, 3.5K subs) 4.4M; 'Every Forbidden Island You're Not Allowed to Visit' (1.5K subs) 878K; 'The Most Impossible to Reach Islands on Google Earth' 2.6M. Tristan itself: Ruhi Cenet 'Exploring the Most Remote Island on Earth' 27.7M in 11 days, Joe HaTTab 32M, Geography By Geoff 4.7M. That wave is why 'tristan da cunha' is +118% (~315K/mo). Suggested traffic was 93% of ep01's impressions, so sitting next to a 27M video that is still climbing is the best placement we can get. Myth-bust angle: 'everyone wants to escape the remote island'. They ran back.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN (May 2026, true): British paratroopers jump from an RAF A400M onto an island with no airstrip to reach one sick man. 'That is how hard it is to reach Tristan. Now imagine getting everyone off.' MYSTERY: Aug-Oct 1961, earthquakes rattle the village, rocks roll down the slopes, then a hill starts to swell at the edge of town. 10 Oct 1961 it cracks open. PROTAGONISTS: the islanders, led by Chief Islander Willie Repetto, with Administrator Peter Wheeler. ESCALATION: a night camped among seabirds on Nightingale Island; a passing Dutch liner (Tjisadane) picks them up; Cape Town; the Stirling Castle to Southampton and a press frenzy. ENGLAND: housed at the old RAF Calshot base; first escalators, traffic, pay packets, jobs at Fawley refinery; winter colds and flu they had no immunity to, and some older islanders die; reporters and scientists treat them as curiosities. MIDPOINT TWIST: a 1962 Royal Society expedition finds the village mostly intact. Lava buried the crayfish factory and both landing beaches but stopped short of the houses. CLIMAX: Dec 1962 ballot, 148 to 5 to go home; the government is reluctant; an advance party goes in April 1963, the main group in Nov 1963. PAYOFF: what they actually wanted (no boss, no rent, no crime, a community where everyone decides together). They name their new harbour 'Calshot Harbour' after the English camp. Today 221 people live there, the volcano is still active, and the 2026 airdrop shows what that choice costs. End on the last line, then hand off to the next video.
candidates.hero_image: A tiny row of white cottages at the foot of a huge dark volcanic cone in an empty ocean, a fresh orange lava glow right behind the houses, and a small line of people with suitcases walking TOWARD it. Text: 'THEY CHOSE THIS'.
candidates.mobile_fit: One cone, one village, one glow: three big shapes that read at thumbnail size. The story is a simple A to B to A journey (island, England, island) that works as a big globe arc on a phone: a single 6,000-mile line, not a dense map. The people are low-poly characters at medium-close framing, so no small labels are needed. Emotional stakes (home or comfort) carry without visuals that need a big screen.
candidates.engine_fit: Strong. Photoreal globe zoom from the empty South Atlantic down onto the island (SRTM/GEBCO terrain of the 2,062 m cone plus the seafloor around it); a 'drain the ocean' shot showing Tristan as the tip of a 3.5 km-tall mountain on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge; a great-circle arc for the evacuation route Tristan, Nightingale, Cape Town, Southampton; a 3D terrain shot of the 1961 vent next to the village; contrast scene of a grey Hampshire street with low-poly islanders. Archival: 1962 Royal Society expedition material, and UK government photos from 1961-63, whose Crown copyright (50 years for published works) has expired. Check each item.
candidates.probes: ytsearch 'tristan da cunha': 11 long-form videos with 100K+ views; Joe HaTTab 32.1M (7mo), Ruhi Cenet 27.7M (11 days), Redfern 11.7M (10y), Discovery Destination 5.0M (6mo), Geography By Geoff 4.7M (1y): all 'life on the remote island' travel angles, none about the evacuation. 'tristan da cunha volcano evacuation 1961': 0 long-form at 100K+; the best is The History Chap 227K (1y, mostly the garrison story), then Royal Society archive 57K; every evacuation-angle long-form is under 2K views (Folkvoya 1.6K, Coordenada Incognita 594, 'Who Lives There' paratrooper video 579). 'island that voted to go back to the volcano': max long-form 1,156 views. 'most remote island evacuated to england': same picture. So the angle is untaken by any video with real views. Facts checked: 1961 eruption, Calshot, and the 148-5 vote (historytoday.com/archive/evacuation-tristan-da-cunha; Time 'Paradise Enow'; Hansard 24 Jul 1962); May 2026 paratrooper drop (gov.uk 'Military conducts daring parachute drop...', MercoPress 2026-05-10).
candidates.risks: Several mass-produced channels have started on the same 'they went back' angle; all are stuck under 2K views, but our title and thumbnail must clearly beat theirs, and we should publish soon while Ruhi Cenet's video is still feeding suggestions. Population figures vary (260-264), so use one sourced number. Details still to verify: who died in England and how many, the exact dates of each return party, and the exact 'Calshot Harbour' naming. The 2026 hantavirus case involves real deaths and private people, so keep it to a short, factual cold open with no medical speculation. Archive film (British Pathé) is not public domain, so use animation and Crown-copyright-expired stills. Do not show real islanders in a way that mocks them; the humour should come from culture shock (escalators, buses), never from the people.

candidates.working_title: We Drained Lake Powell. Here's the Canyon It Drowned.
candidates.premise: America's second-largest reservoir hit its lowest level ever on 15 Aug 2026, then October storms sent it up about 12 feet in two weeks. We remove the rest of the water using the USGS 1-meter terrain model (lake floor plus 1947 pre-dam surveys) to show what's down there: a drowned red-rock canyon system, a grotto called the Cathedral in the Desert, stranded marinas, and a mud delta creeping toward the dam. We also cover the summer of 1983, when the same dam nearly tore itself apart from too much water.
candidates.archetype: The 'drain it / what's hidden at the bottom' format, our most proven outlier type: 'We Drained the Chesapeake Bay...' (Contour Atlas, 1.4K subs) 170K in 1 week; '...Great Lakes' 165K; 'What Antarctica Looks Like Without Ice' (2.9K subs) 1.8M. It meets a hot US topic: 'lake powell' is +150% (~163K/mo, US). Probe: Desert Rat Exploration 'I Have NEVER Seen Flooding Like This at Lake Powell' 3.4M in 2 weeks, and Eric Hanson's Glen Canyon essays at 1.9M and 1.2M, so US viewers are watching this lake right now. No drain-format video of Lake Powell exists.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN (June 1983): the spillway of Glen Canyon Dam starts coughing out red sandstone and chunks of concrete 60-80 ft into the air; engineers bolt plywood boards onto the top of the dam to hold back the rising lake. 'In 1983 this lake nearly destroyed the dam. In 2026 it nearly ran dry.' REWIND: Glen Canyon before 1963, 'the place no one knew'. David Brower of the Sierra Club traded it away to save Echo Park and regretted it for the rest of his life; Floyd Dominy built the dam. THE DRAIN (spine of the film): we lower the water in steps. 3,700 ft full pool and the 1983 peak (8 ft of steel boards added on top). At 3,519.91 ft, the Aug 2026 record low, stranded Hite Marina, canyons and waterfalls reappear, and the Cathedral in the Desert comes up again. At 3,490 ft the turbines stop (2026 was about 30 ft away). At 3,370 ft, dead pool, the river can no longer pass the dam. TWIST: the lake is filling from the bottom. Mud deltas up to 100+ ft thick have taken roughly 7% of its capacity since 1963 (USGS SIR 2022-5017), and the October 2026 flood brought in more mud. PAYOFF: where the water left, the canyon is coming back to life; the federal 2-year operating plan (Aug 2026) means the fight starts again every two years. Final image: the dam standing in front of a canyon it can no longer fill.
candidates.hero_image: The 710-ft concrete wall of Glen Canyon Dam with all the water removed: it holds back nothing but a deep, empty red canyon, with one tiny houseboat sitting on the dry canyon floor. Text: 'WE DRAINED IT'.
candidates.mobile_fit: The drain shot is one huge shape change (blue disappears, red canyon appears) that reads on a 6-inch screen. Use few labels: one water-level gauge on screen as a big counter dropping. The 1983 cold open is a single dramatic image (a jet of rock and water). Show each beat as one landmark at a time, never a dense map.
candidates.engine_fit: Our best possible fit. The DEM terrain builder plus the USGS 'One Meter Topobathymetric DEM for Lake Powell, 1947-2018' (DOI 10.5066/P9XX0J1Y, which combines 2017 multibeam bathymetry, 2018 lidar and historic pre-dam topography) gives a real drained canyon in 3D. Animated water plane at exact elevations (3,708 / 3,700 / 3,519.91 / 3,490 / 3,370). NASA Earth Observatory before/after Landsat images of the 2026 record low; GIBS regional patches; low-poly engineers on the dam for 1983; public-domain Bureau of Reclamation and USGS photos from construction and from 1983.
candidates.probes: 'lake powell': 11 long-form videos with 100K+ views, all 'rising/dying/flood' news angles (thePOVchannel 540K, US Weather Alert 498K in 3 days, Explorer Vault 'New Footage Beneath Lake Powell...' 314K). 'lake powell dead pool': Eric Hanson 'It's Already Dead...' 1.95M (4mo), 'They Knew It Was Wrong...' 1.24M (1y), OverBuilt 543K. 'what's hidden at the bottom of lake powell': max long-form 314K, all mass-produced 'new footage' videos. 'we drained lake powell': no drain-format video at all (Desert Rat flood vlog 3.4M, Eric Hanson). 'glen canyon dam 1983 almost failed' / 'the dam that almost broke 1983' / 'glen canyon dam spillway cavitation': The Hydraulic Record 171K (3mo), Jeffe Aronson 238K (10y), a 1.5M short; nothing combines the 1983 crisis with the drain visual. News checked: record low 3,519.91 ft on 15 Aug 2026 (PBS NewsHour/AP; NASA Earth Observatory 'Lake Powell drops to record low levels'); October 2026 surge of about 12-14 ft, second-highest October inflow since 1963 (sltrib.com 2026/10/26; KSL; KJZZ 2026-11-04); federal 2027-28 guidelines on 21 Aug 2026 (western-water.com 2026/08/21); 1983 plywood and steel flashboards (damfailures.org case study; watereducation.org).
candidates.risks: Crowded with clickbait 'Lake Powell is RISING/DYING' channels, so our packaging must be clearly different (drain visual, real terrain) or we get lumped in with them. Eric Hanson owns the 'the dam was a mistake' essay angle, so we stay on story and place, not advocacy. Water policy is political: stay factual and avoid doom claims. Lake levels will have moved by publish date, so treat 2026 numbers as fixed historical points. Check that the 1947-era DEM coverage includes the side canyons we show. The 1983 '3,708 ft' figure is the gate top plus steel boards, not a confirmed peak, so source the exact peak (about 3,708.3 ft, July 1983) before using it.

candidates.working_title: He Didn't Walk Around the World. He Did Something Harder.
candidates.premise: On 2 Nov 2026 ex-paratrooper Karl Bushby walked into Hull, 28 years after setting off from the tip of South America. He had two rules: no transport, and no going home until he got there on foot. Headlines say 'around the world'. He never crossed the Atlantic, yet he covered about 31,000 miles, more than the distance around the Earth. The map shows why it took 28 years: a jungle with no road, a frozen sea, a country that banned him, and an inland sea he had to swim.
candidates.archetype: Real-time demand at peak: 'karl bushby' is +148% (~281K/mo). Shorts: 61M, 35M and 13M views; news clips: CBS 5.2M, Sky 1.49M, Global News 1.46M, BBC 1.24M (5 days). Real long-form story videos are few and recent: Brett Cooper 'He Left His Son Behind...' 234K in 1 day (personal/family angle), Casos Reais 247K, Chizomiz 128K. Same premise type: route and border stories pull big. RealLifeLore 'Why the Americas Still Aren't Connected by a Road' 4.9M, Cogito 'Journey Through the Darien Gap' 3.2M. The myth-bust ('he didn't walk around the world') fits the Myth Juice brand.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN (5 Oct 2026): a 57-year-old in a wetsuit crawls onto Shakespeare Beach, Dover. Eurotunnel refused to let him walk through the tunnel, so he swam the Channel. He last stood in England 28 years ago. SETUP (1 Nov 1998): Punta Arenas, Chile; a birthday card from his father, an army idea and the two rules. ACT 1, the Americas: the Darien Gap with no road and guerrilla country, then 18 days in a Panamanian jail for entering without a visa; his handcart stolen in Montana. ACT 2, March 2006, the Bering Strait: 58 miles across, but 14 days and about 150 miles on the ice with Dimitri Kieffer; arrested by Russian border troops for not using an official port. ACT 3, stuck: visas refused, a 5-year Russian ban (2013), so he walks about 3,000 miles across the US to protest at the Russian embassy in Washington; the ban is overturned; Siberia, Mongolia, China under police escort; COVID and an Iran visa wall in Turkmenistan. ACT 4 (Aug 2024): with Russia and Iran closed, he swims the Caspian Sea, 288 km in 31 days. ACT 5: Europe, repeated trips back to Mexico while visas reset (the rules let him pause but he had to restart from the exact spot), the Channel. TWIST: the map. He covered about 80% of the planet's longitudes but walked more than its full circumference. PAYOFF: Hull, his mother asks 'Where have you been?', and he meets his granddaughter for the first time.
candidates.hero_image: A photoreal globe with one glowing red line snaking from Cape Horn up the Americas, over the frozen Bering Strait, across Asia and into England, with a tiny walking figure on it. Text: '28 YEARS. NO WHEELS.'
candidates.mobile_fit: One line on one globe is the clearest image possible on a phone, and the line grows as the film goes, so the viewer always knows where we are. Each act is a single landscape with one figure (jungle, ice, steppe, sea): big shapes, no dense labels. A step counter or year counter is the only on-screen text.
candidates.engine_fit: Ideal. The film is a globe route: great-circle and path animation over 31,000 miles, true-size moves, NASA GIBS patches for the Darien Gap and the Bering Strait ice in March 2006, a DEM terrain flyover of Chukotka, the Caspian as a 'drain the sea' moment (it is shallow in the north), and night-lights for his arrival in Hull. Low-poly walker character throughout gives one consistent visual language. No real footage of him is needed (all photos of him are copyrighted).
candidates.probes: 'karl bushby': long-form with 100K+ views = 5, all news clips except A Mug Of Life interview 183K, Casos Reais 247K, Brett Cooper 234K (1 day), Chizomiz 128K. 'man who walked around the world 28 years': only 1 long-form match with 100K+ (Casos Reais 247K). 'walking around the world without transport': 0 long-form with 100K+ matching. 'karl bushby route map every step': no map or route long-form at all (1 match, 240 views). News checked: arrival in Hull 2 Nov 2026 (ITV Calendar 2026-11-02; Irish News; Yorkshire Post 'Where have you been?'); Channel swim landing 5 Oct 2026 and Eurotunnel refusal (Yorkshire Post; explorersweb.com; euroweeklynews 2026/08/07); route details (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Bushby: Darien 2001, Bering 17-31 Mar 2006, 2013 ban and Washington walk, Caspian Aug 2024, 288 km in 31 days).
candidates.risks: News decays fast: we must publish within roughly 2-3 weeks to catch the peak, though the evergreen search ('karl bushby' plus the legend) will last. Werner Herzog was filmed on the Dover beach, so a feature documentary may come later; that keeps interest alive but could claim the long-form space. Brett Cooper (large channel) already owns the 'left his son' family angle, so we stay on the map and borders. He is a living private-ish person: no invented dialogue or inner thoughts, keep family details to what he has said publicly, and use an animated stand-in rather than his likeness. Sources conflict on some dates and distances (ban year, Bering mileage, 29 vs 30 countries), so build a facts ledger. The 'not the first' claim (e.g. Dave Kunst's 1970-74 walk) must be checked before we say it.

candidates.working_title: The Iceberg That Stole a Soviet Base (and Lived 40 Years)
candidates.premise: In 1986 a slab of ice bigger than Rhode Island broke off Antarctica, carrying a Soviet research station with it. It then sat stuck on the seabed for 34 years, broke free, spent months spinning in an invisible ocean whirlpool, aimed itself at a penguin island, and in 2026 finally died, turning bright blue as it went. Satellites watched almost all of it.
candidates.archetype: Antarctica / big-earth-object spectacle, plus a non-human 'biography' in which the iceberg is the hero. Context outliers: 'What Antarctica Looks Like Without Ice' (2.9K subs) 1.8M, 773x. Probe demand: the short 'Earth's Biggest Iceberg A-23A' 23M; BBC 'World's largest iceberg heading for British territory' 2.5M; Inside Edition 3.9M; 'CHASING ICE' calving 65M. Long-form supply is weak and out of date: Bright Side 258K (9 min, 1y, written before the berg died). The death in 2026 (tracking stopped in March, gone by about July) is the news peg that no long-form has covered.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN (8 Jan 2026): a NASA image of a giant iceberg glowing electric blue with meltwater. 'This is what an iceberg's death looks like. This one took 40 years.' BIRTH (Aug 1986): the Filchner Ice Shelf calves; the Soviet station Druzhnaya I is on the ice that drifts away; in 1987 a rescue mission relocates the base (Druzhnaya III). SLEEP: the berg runs aground in the Weddell Sea and sits on the seabed for about 34 years, an ice island. ESCAPE (2020): it thins enough to lift off and starts to drift. ENCOUNTER (1 Dec 2023): the RRS Sir David Attenborough intercepts it and scientists sample the water around it. TRAP (Apr-Dec 2024): it gets caught in a Taylor column over the Pirie Bank seamount and spins about 15 degrees a day for months. candidates.working_title: The Rock That Destroyed Three Lighthouses
candidates.premise: Fourteen miles off Plymouth, a reef that barely breaks the surface kept sinking ships, so from 1696 people tried to put a light on it. The first builder was kidnapped by the French mid-build, then said he wished to be inside his tower during the greatest storm ever, and he got his wish. The second tower burned, and its 94-year-old keeper swallowed molten lead. The third was so strong the rock under it gave way first. The fourth still stands.

The four-tower Eddystone story has no recent strong telling.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN (1755): a 94-year-old keeper throws water up at a burning lantern roof, looks up, and molten lead pours into his mouth. He says he swallowed it. His doctor doesn't believe him until the autopsy. 'This was the second lighthouse this rock destroyed.' REWIND: the Eddystone reef and the wrecks; Henry Winstanley, a showman who ran a London water-theatre full of mechanical tricks (comic material). 1697: a French privateer kidnaps him mid-build; Louis XIV sends him back ('France is at war with England, not with humanity'). 1698: his wooden tower is lit; waves bury it, so he makes it taller and boasts he'd like to be inside during the greatest storm there ever was. 26-27 Nov 1703: the Great Storm, and he is there; by morning only iron stumps remain; days later a ship wrecks on the now-dark rock. ACT 2: Rudyerd, a silk merchant, builds with shipwrights; it stands 46 years, then the 1755 fire and Henry Hall; Dr Spry recovers a 7-oz lump of lead; the learned world scoffs, so he experiments to prove it. ACT 3: John Smeaton models a tower on an oak tree, dovetails granite blocks, and rediscovers hydraulic lime (the birth of modern concrete and of civil engineering). It is lit in 1759 and stands about 120 years. TWIST: the tower doesn't fail; the rock beneath it cracks. 1882: they take Smeaton's tower apart and rebuild it on Plymouth Hoe, where you can climb it today. PAYOFF: out at sea the stump of Smeaton's tower still stands next to the fourth (Douglass) lighthouse, automated in 1982.

candidates.working_title: No Map. No Compass. 2,500 Miles: The Voyage That Proved the Experts Wrong
candidates.premise: For decades experts argued that Polynesians settled the Pacific by accident, blown off course and drifting. In 1976 a double-hulled canoe sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti with no compass, chart or clock, guided by one of the last traditional navigators reading stars, swells and birds. They had to hit a target the size of a city in the largest ocean on Earth. They made it. Then the second voyage ended in tragedy.
candidates.archetype: Myth-busting plus a real voyage, riding the rising keyword 'ancient polynesian star navigation methods' (~205K/mo) and the Hōkūleʻa 50th anniversary (2026). The premise pulls: TED-Ed 'How did Polynesian wayfinders navigate the Pacific Ocean?' 2.2M (5 min explainer, 9y); Stefan Milo 'Did Polynesians Reach America? DNA evidence' 1.26M; RealLifeLore 'Why You Can't Travel Between Hawaii's Islands by Boat' 7.1M (Hawaii plus map); Atlas Pro 'How To Navigate Using the Stars' 1.07M. Strong US appeal (Hawaii). Context outlier 'The History Facts You Were Never Supposed to Question' (5.7K subs, 614K) shows the 'experts were wrong' hook works on small channels.
candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN (dusk, day 31, June 1976): a white tern flies past the canoe; the navigator says land is close. Next morning, an atoll (Mataiva) on the horizon. THE MYTH: Cook marvels that one people spread across the whole Pacific; in 1956 Andrew Sharp argues it was accidental drift; Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki (1947) says the settlers came from South America. PROTAGONISTS: anthropologist Ben Finney, artist Herb Kāne and surfer Tommy Holmes found the Polynesian Voyaging Society and build Hōkūleʻa (launched 1975). There is no Hawaiian navigator left, so they bring Mau Piailug from tiny Satawal in Micronesia. ESCALATION: Honolua Bay, 1 May 1976; the star compass (stars rising and setting in 'houses'), reading swells, crossing the doldrums; crew tensions and a fight on board. TWIST 1: landfall, and thousands greet them in Papeete (4 June). Mau, fed up with the crew, flies home. TWIST 2: 1978, the second voyage capsizes in a storm; big-wave surfer Eddie Aikau paddles off on a surfboard for help and is never seen again ('Eddie Would Go'). PAYOFF: Nainoa Thompson learns from Mau and navigates to Tahiti in 1980; a 2020 DNA study finds Polynesians and Native Americans met around 1200 AD, so contact happened, just not the way Heyerdahl said. Hōkūleʻa is still sailing today (Moananuiākea voyage, 2026).

candidates.working_title: The English Town the Sea Built, Then Ate
candidates.premise: Around 1235 the North Sea piled up a sandbank at the mouth of the Humber, and a man moved into a stranded shipwreck there to sell drinks to sailors. Within about 60 years it was a booming port called Ravenser Odd, with a royal charter, two MPs and a reputation for piracy. By 1362 the sea had taken it back so completely that nobody knows exactly where it was. In 2026, University of Hull scientists are still scanning the seabed for it.

candidates.story_spine: COLD OPEN (5 Dec 2013): a storm surge cuts Spurn Point in two and turns it into a tidal island. 'This has happened before. Last time, a whole town went with it.' BIRTH: the Meaux Abbey chronicle describes the sea throwing up sand and stones and a ship wrecked there, whose hulk becomes the first house and a place selling food and drink to sailors. BOOM: a market, a royal charter (1299), its own court and jail, two MPs, ships for the king's Scottish wars. Grimsby, Hull, German merchants and even the King of Norway accuse it of piracy (it allegedly forced passing ships to sell there). Possible beat (to verify): Edward Balliol sails from Ravenser to invade Scotland in 1332. FALL: from the 1340s storms eat the town; the graveyard opens and the sea exposes the dead; looters strip the chapel; St Marcellus's flood (1362) finishes it. TWIST: the same 250-year spit cycle that built Ravenser Odd destroyed it, Spurn today is following the same pattern, and this coast (Holderness) is among the fastest-eroding in Europe, with dozens of villages lost. Brief echo: it happened again at Dunwich, once one of England's great ports, whose last church fell off the cliff in the early 1900s (and the 'bells ringing under the sea' legend is a myth). PAYOFF: 2021-2026 multibeam surveys by Steve Simmons and Phil Mathison; a stone under examination (Aug 2026). The town is still down there somewhere.

shortlist.working_title: We Drained Lake Powell Down to Dead Pool
shortlist.premise: Lake Powell, America's second-largest reservoir, hit a record low in August 2026, then jumped about 12-16 ft in October storms. We remove the rest of the water using the USGS topobathymetric model (2017 multibeam, 2018 lidar and pre-dam surveys), and the drowned Glen Canyon comes back: side canyons, the Cathedral in the Desert, stranded marinas, the power-pool and dead-pool lines, and a mud delta over 100 ft thick creeping toward the dam. The dam itself is the human story: in 1983 it nearly tore itself apart from too much water, and in 2026 it came within about 30 ft of losing power from too little.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, June 1983: the dam's spillway tunnel coughs red sandstone and concrete into the river, and crews bolt plywood, then steel boards, onto the gates to hold the lake back. 'In 1983 this lake nearly broke the dam. In 2026 it nearly ran dry.' HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the water plane drops 100 ft in one move and canyon walls appear. CH2: the canyon nobody knew before 1963 (at most 2 names: Brower, who traded it away and regretted it, and Dominy, who built the dam). CH3, drain step 1: full pool, and the 1983 cavitation crisis shown as a cut-away of the tunnel. CH4: the record low of 3,519.91 ft strands Hite Marina, and the Cathedral in the Desert re-emerges. CH5: 3,490 ft, the turbines stop; 3,370 ft, dead pool, and the river can no longer pass the dam. TWIST (about 85% in): the lake is filling from the bottom, with sediment deltas taking roughly 7% of capacity since 1963, and the October flood brought more. PAYOFF: the full drain down to the mud and bedrock, the dam standing in front of a canyon it can no longer fill. One-sentence answer: under Lake Powell is a drowned canyon, and the lake is slowly turning into mud. Hand-off: Lake Peigneur.

shortlist.working_title: The Year California Became a 300-Mile Lake
shortlist.premise: In the winter of 1861-62 storms hit California for about 43 days, and the Central Valley filled into a brown inland sea about 250-300 miles long, roughly the length of Lake Michigan. Sacramento drowned. By most accounts the new governor went to his inauguration by rowboat, and the legislature fled to San Francisco. The city later jacked its downtown streets up a full storey. Sediment cores show floods like this recur every century or two, and in 2023 the vanished Tulare Lake came back on farmland to prove it.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, January 1862: a rowboat glides down a Sacramento street past second-floor windows. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the real Central Valley DEM floods from the south and north until one long lake fills California. CH2: the witness, geologist William Brewer, whose letters describe water from the Coast Range to the Sierra (named people: Brewer and Stanford, 2 in all). CH3: why the valley is a bathtub, with one narrow drain at Carquinez Strait and the Golden Gate (cut-away). CH4: Sacramento raises itself. A cut-away shows the buried first floors that are still under the city, with a low-poly in-world gag of a city jacking itself up. CH5: the ghost lake. Tulare Lake, once the largest lake west of the Mississippi, was drained for farms, and a GIBS before/after shows it returning in spring 2023. TWIST (about 85% in): the cores show that 1862 was not the biggest; such floods recur. PAYOFF: refill the valley over today's night lights (the USGS ARkStorm scenario), stated without fear-mongering. Final line: California's real Big One has already happened once, and it was water.
shortlist.hero_image: Orbital view of California with the whole Central Valley filled by one long, bright, muddy-brown lake, the Sierra snow-white beside it, and a tiny rowboat in front of a half-submerged capitol dome in the foreground corner.

shortlist.working_title: Tristan da Cunha Chose the Volcano Over England
shortlist.premise: In October 1961 a volcano opened a few hundred metres behind the only village on Tristan da Cunha, the most remote inhabited island on Earth. All 264 islanders were shipped about 6,000 miles to England and housed at an old RAF camp at Calshot, among buses, escalators, wages and winter flu. In a 1962 ballot they voted 148 to 5 to go back to the volcano, and most did in 1963. The film answers the question every viewer has: why would anyone choose that?
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN (verify): May 2026, RAF paratroopers jump onto an island with no airstrip to reach one sick man. 'That's how hard it is to reach Tristan. Now imagine getting everyone off.' Alternative cold open: 10 Oct 1961, the hill behind the cottages swells and splits. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: pull back from the island until no other land is in frame, then drain the ocean to show Tristan as the tip of a giant seamount. CH2: the eruption, a night among seabirds on Nightingale Island, and a passing Dutch liner picks everyone up. CH3: the arc to Southampton and life at Calshot. The culture shock (escalators, traffic, money) runs as gentle in-world gags; the serious beat is the colds, the flu and the deaths of some elderly islanders. CH4: the 1962 Royal Society expedition finds the village standing. A before/after terrain shot shows the lava stopping short but burying the crayfish factory and both landing beaches. CH5: the ballot, 148 to 5. The return in 1963, and the new harbour named 'Calshot Harbour'. PAYOFF: what they went back for, in their own reported words, and the island today. Named people: Chief Islander Willie Repetto and at most one more. Comment prompt: would you have gone back?

shortlist.working_title: What Hawaii Looks Like Without the Ocean
shortlist.premise: Drain the Pacific around Hawaii step by step, and paradise becomes the tallest mountain on Earth measured from its base (Mauna Kea, about 10,000 m), with city-sized landslide blocks and a chain of older, sinking islands running all the way to Midway. That atoll is an old Hawaiian volcano that has sunk, and the 1942 battle was fought over it, with the carriers from that battle lying in the deep water nearby. Below the Big Island, the next Hawaiian island is already growing underwater.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, 1 April 1946, Laupahoehoe: the sea suddenly drains off the reef, children run out to look, and it comes back. 'For a few minutes the sea drained away. We're going to finish the job.' HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the first 120 m drop joins Maui, Molokai, Lanai and Kahoolawe into one Ice Age island. The DRAIN LADDER gives one reveal per chapter. At -1,000 m: the Nuuanu slide, where half of an Oahu volcano lies on the seafloor in city-sized blocks. At -5,000 m: the Big Island stands up as one mountain, with an Everest silhouette beside it for scale and its weight bending the seafloor into a moat. Then follow the chain northwest as the islands get older and lower, out to Midway's ring of reef. The Kaga, Akagi and Yorktown wrecks lie in the deep water off it (found 1998 and 2019). TWIST (about 85% in): every island you know is on the same conveyor and will become a Midway. PAYOFF: swing back southeast to Kama'ehuakanaloa growing below the Big Island, then refill the ocean. 'Everything you've seen of Hawaii is the very tip.' Named people: 0-2.
shortlist.hero_image: The Big Island half-drained: the water line dropped partway down, so the dark mountain's exposed flank is many times bigger than the familiar green island on top, with a small white Everest silhouette beside it for scale. Bright blue water below, warm sunlight on the rock.
shortlist.archetype: A direct sibling of the biggest live outlier, 'What Antarctica Looks Like Without Ice' (1.8M on 2.9K subs, 3 weeks), and of the drained-Pacific wave (a Korean channel at 1.12M in 2 months; Unseen Works 115K in 4 days). Keep to the USGS view of landslide hazard (no mega-tsunami hype). The carriers lie in deep water near Midway, so do not say they are 'on its flank' without checking.

shortlist.working_title: The Dutch Drained a Sea and Found 400 Ships
shortlist.premise: Every other channel pretends to drain a lake. The Netherlands really did it. They dammed and pumped dry most of the Zuiderzee, and farmers ploughing the new seabed kept hitting shipwrecks (more than 400 recorded) and wartime bombers with their crews. A city of over 200,000 people (Almere) now stands on what was open sea within living memory, and in 1945 the sea briefly took one polder back.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN: a plough in a flat green polder, 5 m below sea level and far from any coast, hits black oak. It is the hull of an 18th-century merchant ship. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the sea lifts off the map in one move, and hulls lie scattered across fields. CH2: the sea as killer. The January 1916 storm flood drowns Marken, and engineer Cornelis Lely's old plan is finally approved (1 named person). CH3: 28 May 1932, the last gap in the 32 km Afsluitdijk closes (CC0 Anefo photos, Ken Burns, 4 s or less). CH4: the pumps start, the seabed appears, and ploughs race archaeologists. Schokland becomes an island in a sea of grass, and Urk wakes up landlocked (in-world gag). CH5: bombers that fell into the lake are still being dug out with their crews (the Lancaster ED603 recovery). TWIST: on 17 April 1945 German troops blow the Wieringermeer dike and the sea takes the whole polder back within days, and the Dutch drain it again. PAYOFF (about 85% in): Almere on the 1960s seabed, and the never-drained Markerwaard where ships still lie. Final line: in one lifetime a sea became a city.
shortlist.hero_image: Top-down view of a 300-year-old wooden ship skeleton lying in a bright green Dutch field with a tiny red tractor beside it, and a thin blue line floating high above to mark the old sea surface.
shortlist.archetype: The drain-reveal premise done for real (Contour Atlas drains at 165-170K on 1.4K subs; 'Antarctica Without Ice' 1.8M). Every one takes the engineering or lifestyle angle; per the ideator's probes, none asks what was on the seabed.

shortlist.working_title: San Francisco Is Built on Top of Its Ships
shortlist.premise: In 1849 so many crews deserted their ships to chase gold that hundreds of vessels were left in San Francisco's Yerba Buena Cove. The city turned them into a hotel, a jail and warehouses, then filled in the cove around them, moving the shoreline blocks inland. Construction crews still dig them up under the Financial District (the Niantic, the General Harrison in 2001). Drain the Bay, and the twist is that the 1849 shoreline still decides which streets shake hardest in an earthquake.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, 2001: an excavator near the Embarcadero lifts Gold Rush ship timbers out of a foundation pit under downtown. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the 1849 shoreline is overlaid on the modern skyline and the old cove fills in under the towers. CH2, 1849: gold news, crews desert, and a forest of masts fills the cove. CH3: a city with no buildings uses ships as buildings, a hotel, a jail and a saloon (in-world gags on the real terrain). CH4: land is worth more than ships, so sand hills are shovelled into the cove, the 1851 fires burn hulls to the waterline, and streets are laid over them. CH5: drain the Bay. Most of it is only a few metres deep, the Golden Gate is a deep canyon, and the City of Rio de Janeiro wreck (1901, fog, 128 dead) lies on its floor. Optional beat: the atomic-test carrier USS Independence on the shelf off the Farallones. TWIST (about 85% in): filled ground amplifies shaking, and in 1989 the worst damage followed old fill (USGS framing). PAYOFF: a cut-away descending from a glass tower through rubble and sand to a ship's ribs. Named people: 0-2 (the ships are the characters).
shortlist.hero_image: Cut-away of a downtown glass skyscraper whose foundations rest directly on a buried wooden sailing ship, its broken masts poking up through layers of sand and rubble. Warm sandy browns against blue glass.

shortlist.working_title: Iceland Fought a Volcano With Seawater. And Won.
shortlist.premise: At about 2 a.m. on 23 January 1973 a 1.6 km fissure opened at the edge of Heimaey, home to Iceland's most important fishing harbour. Nearly all 5,000 people got off the island within hours, because a storm had kept the fishing fleet in port. Then lava headed for the harbour mouth, the one thing the town could not live without. The islanders sprayed millions of tonnes of seawater on it for months, using pumps built in the US, and the flow stopped short. The new rock left the harbour better sheltered than before, and the island was about 20% bigger.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, 01:55: a curtain of fire opens a few hundred metres from sleeping streets, and a night fleet of tiny boat lights leaves the harbour. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the lava front, an animated mask on the real terrain, creeps toward the harbour mouth, with a big shrinking-gap gauge. CH2: ash buries houses, volunteers shovel roofs, and a new mountain (Eldfell) grows out of a pasture (terrain grows). CH3: physicist Thorbjorn Sigurgeirsson proposes cooling the lava with seawater. First come the town's fire hoses (an in-world gag), then a dredger. CH4: high-capacity pumps arrive from the US, and men lay pipes across lava that is still moving; the ticking clock is the gap narrowing week by week. CH5: the flow stalls, and the eruption ends in July. TWIST (about 85% in): the lava wall becomes a breakwater better than nature's. PAYOFF: a before/after coastline morph of the island, about 20% bigger, then a fishing boat sails out past the black wall. 50 years later Grindavik builds lava walls on the same idea. Named people: 1-2.
shortlist.hero_image: A towering wall of glowing orange lava with thin white jets of water arcing onto it from tiny figures holding hoses, a small red-roofed harbour town right behind them. Orange against blue, maximum contrast.

shortlist.working_title: Why Nobody Lives on Attu Island Anymore
shortlist.premise: In June 1942 Japan invaded two American islands in Alaska. On Attu, the Unangax (Aleut) villagers were captured and shipped to Japan, where nearly half died. A brutal battle in fog took the island back. Weeks later more than 34,000 American and Canadian troops stormed Kiska and found it empty, yet still lost men to friendly fire and a mine. The Attu survivors were never allowed home, and America's westernmost island has been empty ever since.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, June 1942, Attu village at the far western tip of America: soldiers come over the hills while the radio operator is at his set. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: a 3-second arc from Japan along the Aleutian chain across the date line to one fog-bound island, then a regional terrain view. CH2: the captives. Foster Jones is killed, teacher Etta Jones is taken, and the villagers are shipped to Otaru, where nearly half die (no gore). CH3: May 1943, US troops land in fog on frozen tundra, with the cold as deadly as the enemy (kept short and symbolic). CH4, TWIST: Kiska. A huge armada storms an empty island; the garrison had slipped away in fog weeks earlier, and the invasion still costs lives (dry irony, no jokes about deaths). CH5: the survivors return to Alaska in 1945 but are resettled on Atka. The Coast Guard station closes in 2010, and (per the ideator, verify) the last Attu-born survivor died in 2023. PAYOFF (about 85% in): the empty village site on America's westernmost island, now a wildlife refuge. Comment prompt: should they have been allowed to go home? Named people: Etta and Foster Jones.
shortlist.hero_image: A lonely green-grey island in thick fog with a tiny abandoned village site and a faded US flag on a pole, and one red invasion arrow crossing the date line toward it. Alternative: thousands of landing craft racing toward a completely empty beach.
shortlist.archetype: The closest analogue to the biggest live outlier, 'Why Can't You Visit Iwo Jima?' (Where They Stood, 3.5K subs, 4.4M in 1 month): WWII, US soil, an empty island. shortlist.working_title: The Steamboat That Sailed Into the New Madrid Quake
shortlist.premise: In 1811 America's first steamboat on the western rivers, the New Orleans, set off down the Ohio and Mississippi to prove that steam could beat the current. Aboard were the builder Nicholas Roosevelt, his pregnant wife Lydia and their dog, with a great comet in the sky. Partway down, the strongest earthquakes in the recorded history of the eastern US tore the river apart around them. Banks collapsed, channels moved overnight and towns were wrecked, and weeks after they passed, the Mississippi briefly ran backward.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, night of 16 December 1811: the steamboat is tied to a tree, the ground roars and the riverbank slides into the water. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: an overhead DEM view of the river as a bank slumps and new sandbars appear. CH2: the set-up, with humour. Crowds on the banks have never seen a steamboat, the 1811 comet makes people nervous, Lydia gives birth on the way, and they wait weeks for the Falls of the Ohio to rise. CH3: the first great shock. The river fills with uprooted trees and channels move, so the pilot's knowledge is useless. CH4: New Madrid is wrecked and sinking, people beg to come aboard, and the boat cannot go back upstream. CH5: they reach New Orleans, and the steam age on the Mississippi begins in the middle of a catastrophe. TWIST (about 85% in): after they had passed, the February 1812 shock made the river run backward, threw up waterfalls and formed Reelfoot Lake (shown forming on terrain). PAYOFF: LiDAR sand blows across the Bootheel show that the fault is still there (no doom), plus a quick myth-bust of the 'church bells in Boston' claim. Named people: Nicholas and Lydia Roosevelt.
shortlist.hero_image: A tiny paddle steamer with a smoking chimney on a dark river at dusk, the riverbank beside it caving in and trees toppling, and a long bright comet overhead. Warm lantern light on the boat against the dusk sky.
shortlist.archetype: A survival journey where the geography is the villain, set in the US heartland. Active same-river host: MapReels 'The Mississippi River Isn't Really a River. It's a Wound.' 1.14M in 2 months. Also The History Guy 'The Hard Shock: The New Madrid Earthquakes' 1.52M and Hidden on Earth 'The Mississippi River Is Hiding Something' 424K (4 months). The steamboat-voyage angle has no long-form (max about 11K, 13 years old).

shortlist.working_title: Ironbottom Sound Drained: A Seafloor of Warships
shortlist.premise: Off Guadalcanal lies water so full of sunken warships that sailors named it Ironbottom Sound. Dozens of warships from both navies went down there in the 1942-43 night battles that turned the Pacific war. Drain it and you walk from wreck to wreck. In 2025 the Nautilus finally mapped the floor and filmed 13 wrecks, four for the first time, including the bow that USS New Orleans lost in battle and survived without.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, night of 8-9 August 1942 off Savo Island: Allied cruisers on picket, crews exhausted, and in about half an hour four heavy cruisers are sinking. HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the Sound drains between Guadalcanal, Savo and the Florida Islands, and the first hulls appear. CH2: the Tokyo Express, night supply runs drawn as bright arcs on black. CH3: the 13 November 1942 close-range brawl in the dark, and afterwards USS Juneau is torpedoed and the five Sullivan brothers are lost (state honestly that Juneau sank outside the Sound). CH4: the radar-guided battleship duel that sinks Kirishima. CH5: Tassafaronga, where New Orleans loses its bow and limps home. TWIST (about 85% in): the bow lay alone for 83 years until Nautilus found it in 2025. PAYOFF: refill the Sound; islanders fish above a floor of steel from both navies. Named people: at most 3 (the Sullivans count as one family beat).
shortlist.hero_image: A half-drained tropical basin under a bright sky, a lone grey cruiser bow standing upright on the exposed seafloor in the foreground, other hulks scattered behind, and the green peak of Guadalcanal behind them.

shortlist.working_title: Colorado Isn't a Rectangle, and It's the Law
shortlist.premise: Everyone 'knows' Colorado is a perfect rectangle. It isn't. Its borders zigzag through hundreds of small kinks because 1860s-70s survey crews with chains and star sightings missed the lines they were sent to mark. When New Mexico sued to fix the error, the Supreme Court ruled in 1925 that the wrong line is the legal line. Why doesn't America just fix its borders? Because a border isn't a line on a map. It's a row of stones in the ground, and once people live by the stones, the mistake becomes the law.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN: a 3D flyover along Colorado's 'ruler-straight' southern border, until the line visibly jogs sideways in the San Juan Mountains. 'Colorado has four sides. Except it doesn't.' HERO SHOT BY 0:30: the intended 37th parallel and the surveyed line overlaid on real terrain, with the first kink filling the frame. CH2: surveyor Ehud Darling, 1868, with chains, a transit, star sightings and stone mounds in mountain country (comic hardship on the terrain). CH3: errors pile up as crews add their own drift, with one kink zoom per beat. CH4: a 1902-03 resurvey finds the line off the parallel, ranches and taxes sit in the 'wrong' state, and New Mexico sues. CH5, TWIST: in 1925 the Supreme Court keeps Darling's crooked line. Second twist: the Four Corners Monument sits about 1,800 ft from the intended spot and is still legally correct. PAYOFF (about 85% in): the rule still bites, as Georgia keeps trying to undo an 1818 survey error to reach Tennessee River water. Final line: 'The map isn't the border. The stones are.' Named people: Darling and at most one more. Hand-off: the 1755 Mitchell map behind America's weirdest borders.
shortlist.hero_image: A fat, bright Colorado silhouette that looks like a clean rectangle, with one edge magnified to reveal a jagged red sawtooth line. Text: 'NOT A RECTANGLE'.
shortlist.archetype: 'Borders that make no sense' ('7 Borders That Make Absolutely No Sense' 702K on 17.7K subs) crossed with 'facts you learned in school are wrong' (245K-614K on 1.6K-5.7K subs). Demand is proven in Shorts: 'Colorado is Not a Rectangle' 7.7M, 'How Colorado Has 697 Sides?' 641K. Matching long-form tops out at about 2.4K. The big US-border incumbents (Atlas Pro 3.5M, Geography by Geoff 2.2M) never tell the survey-error-becomes-law story.

shortlist.working_title: The Coldest Place on Earth Lost Its Power
shortlist.premise: In April 1982, just as the months-long polar night began, a fire destroyed the power plant at the Soviet Vostok Station, about 3,500 m up on the East Antarctic ice. One man died, and twenty were left with no power or heat as the cold headed toward -80 C. No aircraft could reach them until the next summer, so they improvised and survived the winter. The following winter the same station recorded -89.2 C (-128.6 F), the coldest temperature ever measured on Earth's surface, and about 4 km under their floor lay a liquid lake sealed beneath the ice.
shortlist.story_spine: COLD OPEN, before dawn on 12 April 1982 (verify the date): fire in the diesel plant, the generators gone in minutes, and mechanic Alexei Karpenko dies (handled with respect). HERO SHOT BY 0:30: pull back from the one burning hut to the vast ice dome and the 1,400 km to the coast, with a large temperature counter falling. CH2: the stakes. Twenty men, polar night, and no plane able to land until summer because fuel and hydraulics freeze. CH3: improvisation. Drip stoves are made from gas cylinders, everyone lives in soot, and an old generator is dug out of the snow (light, respectful humour). CH4: a coded radio message to Moscow, the weather observations kept going, and a second fire at the drilling rig. CH5: relief arrives with the first flights of the summer season. TWIST 1 (about 85% in): 21 July 1983, the thermometer reads -89.2 C. TWIST 2: a cut-away through about 4 km of ice to Lake Vostok directly below. PAYOFF: one lit window on endless white. Named people: Karpenko and the station chief. Comment prompt: would you have survived?
shortlist.hero_image: One tiny hut with a single warm orange window on an endless blue-white ice plain under stars, with a huge '-128F' in the corner. Alternative: a vertical cut-away showing the hut on top, a thick band of ice, and the dark lake at the bottom.
shortlist.archetype: A remote-station survival story with a deadline (the '119-Day Survival Story' 1.5M), next to the hottest live host cluster: 'What Antarctica Looks Like Without Ice' 1.8M in 3 weeks on 2.9K subs, Outlier Atlas 'Living at the South Pole' 1.0M in 3 weeks, and 'coldest place on Earth' videos at 13.7M-120M. An exact, elevation-by-elevation 3D drain of Lake Powell built on the USGS 1-m topobathymetric model, where every drop of the water plane lands on a real, dated waterline:

- 3,370 ft: dead pool.
- The 2017-18 lakebed and the old river channel.

- On-site channels show only what is exposed today.

result.facts_status:
The core story is true and well documented. Several premise details need correcting or softer wording.

TRUE:
1. Lake Powell is the second-largest US reservoir. The AP record-low story says so: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/lake-powell-hits-record-low-threatening-key-water-and-electricity-supply-for-millions

2. Record low: CORRECT THE NUMBER.
   - 3,519.91 ft was only the provisional mid-August 2026 reading, 0.01 ft under the April 2023 record.
   - The lake kept falling. NASA Earth Observatory gives 3,517.24 ft on Sept 10, 2026: https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/lake-powell-drops-to-record-low-levels/
   - The low was 3,516.62 ft in mid-September 2026: https://earthsky.org/earth/lake-powell-is-shrinking-dead-pool-2026/ and https://www.worldatlas.com/lakes/lake-mead-lost-192-feet-lake-powell-lost-179.html
   - Confirm with Reclamation daily data before scripting.

3. 'Within about 30 ft of losing power': true. 3,516.6 minus 3,490 is about 27 ft.

4. Minimum power pool 3,490 ft and dead pool 3,370 ft:
   - https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/how-glen-canyon-dam-works
   - Reclamation's 2024 memo treats about 3,394 ft as a practical outlet floor, and flags cavitation and scour risk if water has to leave only through the four bypass tubes: https://www.usbr.gov/uc/DocLibrary/Memos/20240326-EstablishmentInterimOperatingGuidanceGlenCanyonDamLowReservoirLevels-TechnicalDecisionMemo-508-TSC.pdf

5. The October 2026 jump: true, but figures vary.
   - KSL: more than 10 ft in the month, about 3,532 ft: https://www.ksl.com/article/51641721/lake-powell-gained-more-than-10-feet-this-month-will-its-run-continue
   - KJZZ: about 14 ft; about 850K acre-feet of rain-driven inflow; it would take about 5 straight good winters to reach half full: https://www.kjzz.org/science/2026-11-04/recent-rains-were-a-drop-in-the-bucket-for-colorado-river-reservoir-water
   - Fox 10 reports a 16-ft surge.
   - Inflow of 65,000 cfs was the second-highest October daily inflow since 1963.
   - Say 'about 15 feet' and date-stamp it.

6. 1983: well documented.
   - The left spillway opened June 2. On June 6 there was rumbling and material was thrown out of the tunnel exit.
   - The water was tinted red by eroded Navajo sandstone (PopSci: https://www.popsci.com/scitech/article/2003-03/water-vapor-almost-busts-dam).
   - The crater in the tunnel was 32 ft deep, 40 ft wide and 150-180 ft long (sources differ).
   - Flashboards were 4-ft plywood, then 8-ft steel boards in early July.
   - The peak was 3,708.34 ft in mid-July 1983, 6.6 ft below the dam crest:
     - https://damfailures.org/case-study/glen-canyon-dam-arizona-1983
     - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risks_to_the_Glen_Canyon_Dam
     - https://coyotegulch.blog/2019/07/19/for-a-while-in-1983-sheets-of-plywood-were-all-that-kept-the-mighty-glen-canyon-dam-from-overflowing-arizona-central/
   - SOFTEN the wording. It was the spillway tunnels that were tearing apart. Engineers feared losing control and damage reaching the rock, but the concrete dam itself was not observed failing. Use 'the spillways were tearing themselves apart' and 'within 7 ft of the top', not 'the lake nearly broke the dam'.

7. Brower traded Glen Canyon to stop Echo Park Dam and later called it his great regret ('we never should have lost Glen Canyon'): true and well sourced, e.g. https://www.intermountainhistories.org/items/show/56. I could not verify the exact quote 'Glen Canyon died in 1963'; do not use it. Dominy was Reclamation Commissioner from 1959 to 1969 and championed the dam. A strong true scene: Brower and Dominy rafted the Grand Canyon together in John McPhee's 'Encounters with the Archdruid'.

8. Sediment:
   - USGS SIR 2022-5017: storage capacity fell 6.79% (1.833M acre-feet) from 1963 to 2018, about 33,270 acre-feet per year: https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/sir20225017
   - Delta thickness: about 180 ft for the Colorado and about 120 ft for the San Juan per KNAU 2013 (https://www.knau.org/earth-notes/2013-05-08/earth-notes-glen-canyon-dam-what-flows-in-and-not-out), and about 150 ft at Hite per NPS (https://www.nps.gov/glca/learn/nature/sedimentation.htm). 'Over 100 ft' is safe.
   - SENSATIONAL RISK: 'creeping toward the dam'. The Colorado delta is more than 125 miles from the dam, and the San Juan delta is about 27 miles from the confluence (SLTrib 2022). Time to reach the dam is disputed: 80-100 years (advocates) versus 500-700 years (agencies). USGS's first-order estimate is about 750 years to fill the remaining volume. The twist is true only on a centuries timescale and must say so.

9. Hite Marina: WRONG CAUSATION in the story spine. Hite has been closed for about two decades (low water plus sediment). The 2026 low did not strand it. For 2026, use Bullfrog Marina being moved toward the main channel and the Bullfrog-Halls Crossing ferry not running: https://www.kunc.org/news/2026-05-17/its-a-different-lake-now-as-lake-powell-drops-an-iconic-marina-chases-deeper-water

10. Cathedral in the Desert re-emerged again in 2026, now with graffiti (SLTrib spring 2026). True.

11. The USGS model exists and is public domain: 1-m 'Topobathymetric DEM of Lake Powell, 1947-2018' (Danielson, Tyler, Poppenga 2020, DOI 10.5066/P9XX0J1Y; https://www.usgs.gov/data/one-meter-topobathymetric-digital-elevation-model-lake-powell-arizona-utah-1947-2018), plus a modified version by Jones and Root, 2021 (DOI 10.5066/P9H60YCF).

DO NOT SAY:
- 'nearly broke the dam'
- 'mud is about to reach the dam'
- 'biggest rise since 1964'. That is an AI-channel claim; the documented fact is the second-highest October daily inflow since 1963.

Present-tense numbers change daily, so date-stamp them.

result.story_strength:
6.5/10. It is very strong as visual spectacle and only moderate as a human story.

STRENGTHS:
- The drain ladder gives 5-7 true, escalating, phone-readable reveals: full pool, the 1983 peak, the record low, the turbines stopping, dead pool, the riverbed.
- 'Too much water in 1983, too little in 2026' is a clean, true bookend.
- The one-sentence answer works.
- There is a real ticking clock (the dropping water line toward 3,490 and 3,370; the rising one toward the crest in 1983).
- There is a vivid, true scene: plywood nailed onto a 710-ft dam, and red sandstone-tinted water.
- Brower vs Dominy is a genuine pair of rivals. Their rafting trip in McPhee's book is a usable true scene.

WEAKNESSES:
- The protagonist is a dam. The 1983 operators are mostly unnamed.
- The 2026 near-miss is an anticlimax: it never reached power pool, and then storms raised it.
- The 1983 crisis is already well told (The Hydraulic Record 171K, a 1.5M Short).
- The sediment twist is true but slow. It is centuries away and the deltas are more than 125 miles from the dam, so it lands as a reflective 'huh', not a shock.
- The payoff (a canyon under the lake) is already familiar to this audience from hundreds of drone and before/after Shorts (5.5M, 4.9M, 4.7M).

The ending ('a dam in front of a canyon it can no longer fill') is good but quiet. It would need a sharper closing image or a data hook, such as 'the lake has lost about 7% of its space to mud', to land.

result.facts_status:
The core story is true and well documented, with a primary source. Several premise details need fixing.

VERIFIED:
- Primary source, Brewer's letters ("Up and Down California", Book 3 ch. 1; text at http://www.yosemite.ca.us/library/up_and_down_california/3-1.html). Jan 19, 1862: the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys were under water, "a region 250 to 300 miles long and an average of at least twenty miles wide, a district of five thousand or six thousand square miles". Jan 31: "The legislature has left the capital and has come here, that city being under water." Feb 9: the "Lake" was "sixty miles wide, from the mountains on one side to the hills on the other". Brewer reports this secondhand, from a ranch hand, at one point in the Sacramento Valley. March 7: Brewer rows through Sacramento himself: "Most of the city is still under water, and has been for three months." Lake Michigan is about 307 miles long, so the comparison holds.
- B. Lynn Ingram, Scientific American, Jan 2013 (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/atmospheric-rivers-california-megaflood-lessons-from-forgotten-catastrophe/): "at least 300 miles long and 20 miles wide"; the legislature moved to San Francisco on Jan 22, 1862.
- USGS (https://www.usgs.gov/programs/science-application-for-risk-reduction/science/arkstorm-scenario): ARkStorm is "analogous to" 1861-62; "The geologic record shows 6 megastorms more severe than 1861-1862 in California in the last 1800 years"; about $725B in losses; up to 1.5M evacuations. USGS PCMSC (https://www.usgs.gov/centers/pcmsc/news/arkstorm-californias-other-big-one): Lucy Jones says "once every 100 or 200 years"; storms lasted "45 days". So the twist is supported, as long as it is attributed to USGS.
- Tulare Lake: NASA Earth Observatory (https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/return-of-tulare-lake-151174/) says it was "the largest freshwater lake west of the Mississippi"; its feeder rivers were dammed and diverted by 1920; Landsat 8 image of March 29, 2023, Landsat 9 of 2022, and a MODIS series from Mar 2 to Apr 1, 2023.
- Sacramento's street raising: about 10 ft on average, up to about 15 ft (What Cheer House), over roughly 13 years in the 1860s-70s (https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=136276, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_Cheer_House_(Sacramento,_California), https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/the-original-street-level-of-sacramento-sacramento-california). It was mostly fill behind retaining walls, with some buildings raised and some ground floors becoming basements. "A full storey" is fair as a maximum.

FIX OR SOFTEN:
1. "About 43 days": Wikipedia says 43, USGS says 45. Say "about six weeks".
2. The Stanford rowboat story is uncited secondary lore. Wikipedia: "was said to"; SF Museum account at https://sfmuseum.org/hist5/callib.html. Ingram adds that he came home through a second-storey window. Use "the story goes", and lead instead with Brewer's documented rowboat trip.
3. Death toll: Wikipedia's ">4,000" rests on an ABC7 Chicago article, and Ingram says "thousands". Both are unknowable; avoid.
4. "State went bankrupt" (Ingram) and "one-third of property destroyed": avoid. Brewer's "It is supposed that over one-fourth of all the taxable property of the state has been destroyed" can be quoted as a rumor of the time.
5. "Water from the Coast Range to the Sierra" is true only at one point (Brewer's secondhand 60-mile report). The water averaged about 20 miles wide in a valley up to about 60 miles wide, and covered roughly 300 of the Central Valley's roughly 450 miles. "The whole Central Valley as one lake" overstates it.
6. Specific Santa Barbara Basin flood-layer claims (1605 "50% more powerful") are Wikipedia-only. Stick to the USGS line.
7. Never imply El Niño causes megafloods. The 1861-62 ENSO state is not established, and Cal OES has publicly pushed back on viral ARkStorm misinformation.
8. Say "freshwater" lake, because the Great Salt Lake is larger.

Other sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Flood_of_1862, https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/journals/quaternary-research/article/large-california-flood-and-correlative-global-climatic-events-400-years-ago/2BDC9161BF99A290926777D4746BBA77, El Niño outlook coverage at https://watchers.news/2026/10/16/very-strong-el-nino-favors-wetter-south-and-warmer-north-in-noaas-2026-27-winter-outlook-u-s/ and https://gvwire.com/2026/10/30/will-el-nino-bring-a-wetter-winter-to-california-noaa-says-the-odds-are-rising/

7/10.

Strengths:
- A real, quotable primary witness. Brewer's letters are vivid and datable: "still raining!", telegraph pole tops under water, "the winds made high waves which beat the farm homes in pieces", and his own rowboat tour of Sacramento in March.
- The stakes are concrete: a state capital under water for about three months, and the legislature fleeing.
- A built-in ticking clock: storm after storm for about six weeks, with the water coming back after it had dropped ("they are again up").
- A satisfying physical "why": a bathtub with a drain less than a mile wide.
- A great human-scale consequence: a city lifting itself out of the mud.
- A modern proof: Tulare in 2023.
- A real twist backed by USGS: 1862 was not the biggest, with six bigger storms in about 1,800 years.
- Only two named people. Funny beats come naturally: Brewer going to a drowned capital to ask for his salary, and the sofa count.

Weaknesses:
- Brewer is mostly safe in San Francisco and reports the January peak secondhand, so there is no personal jeopardy.
- The famous Stanford rowboat moment is uncited lore.
- There is no single climactic event after the January 9-10 levee break.
- The planned ending (a "what if" refill / "the real Big One is water") is the exact ending of the top incumbent and of three or more recent uploads, so it will feel familiar to viewers who have seen them.
- The Sacramento-raising and Tulare chapters were each covered by 3+ videos at 80-220K in the last 1-3 months.

result.facts_status:
The core story is TRUE and well documented. Several details in the pitch need correcting.

CONFIRMED:
- Tremors began in August 1961. On 10 October 1961 a new cone and lava dome rose a few hundred feet EAST of Edinburgh of the Seven Seas.
- All 264 people left by open boat on the lobster boats Tristania and Frances Repetto and spent the night on uninhabited Nightingale Island. The next day the diverted Dutch liner Tjisadane took them to Cape Town. They then sailed on the Stirling Castle and docked at Southampton on 3 November 1961.
- First housing was Pendell Army Camp, Merstham, Surrey. They moved to the former RAF Calshot married quarters in Hampshire on 23 January 1962.
- Royal Society expedition: 12 members led by Ian Gass, January to March 1962. It found most of the village undamaged. Lava destroyed the crawfish canning factory, "the most disastrous effect," and covered the main beach.
- Ballot: 148 to 5, a secret ballot at Calshot in December 1962. Teenagers and children had no vote. Two independent sources: Time magazine (14 December 1962) and Margaret Mackay's 1964 book "Angry Island".
- Return in stages:
  - 12 men sailed in August 1962 (arrived 9 September 1962), led by Johnny Repetto.
  - An advance party of about 50-52 left in March 1963 (Hansard, 12 February 1963).
  - About 200 followed in November 1963.
- A harbour built in the mid-1960s was named Calshot Harbour (Christchurch Press, 1967).
- Willie Repetto was Headman (Chief Islander) at the time and presented a longboat to the Queen. His documented quotes: "We can't get used to the English climate" and "We's got enough to last a lifetime." Johnny Repetto: "Tell them we'll never leave again."
- 2026 airdrop, 9-10 May 2026: six British Army paratroopers from 16 Air Assault Brigade, plus an ICU doctor and nurse jumping in tandem, from an RAF A400M. It was for a suspected hantavirus case in a British passenger off the MV Hondius cruise ship. Oxygen on the island was critically low. The UK Ministry of Defence called it the first time the UK military had parachuted in medical personnel for humanitarian support.
- Population today: 221 (2026 census figure on Wikipedia).

CORRECTIONS AND FLAGS:
(1) The elderly deaths happened in SURREY (Pendell Camp), not at Calshot. Hansard, 18 December 1961: "three elderly islanders have died" and "nearly all the islanders have colds" (influenza, bronchitis; isolation from viruses). Mackay: "no deaths in the Hampshire camp." Do not put the death beat at Calshot.
(2) Lava did not bury "both landing beaches". Sources say the main beach, or "the only safe landing beach". HMS Puma blasted a new landing near Little Beach Point.
(3) Time's 1962 claim that the volcano "ruined most houses, killed all the sheep" is contradicted by the Royal Society: farm animals largely survived, about 200 cattle were counted. Do not use it.
(4) Do not say "RAF paratroopers". They were British Army paratroopers jumping from an RAF plane. The patient was a cruise passenger, not an islander.
(5) "Never used money" is false. The islanders had cannery wages from the 1950s and £2,000 in savings. "Escalators" is unverified.
Documented culture-shock gags you can use: first horse and real trees, learning to walk on ice, calling a taxi driver "sir", "all strange faces and nobody saying hello", the TV and noise complaint. One darker beat is documented: two teddy boys attacked 62-year-old, one-armed Gordon Glass and smashed his watch.
(6) Quote-attribution trap: Time puts the TV/cars complaint in the mouth of Basil Lavarello, but Mackay names him as the most publicized islander who wanted to STAY. Use him carefully.
(7) "Most remote inhabited island" is the common label (National Geographic, Wikipedia), but it is a superlative; Pitcairn is sometimes argued. "Often called" is safer.
(8) The vent was a small parasitic cone on the coastal plain beside the village, not the 2,062 m summit erupting "behind the roofs".
