result.facts_status:
The core story is true and well documented. Several details in the pitch need fixing.

TRUE:
- 1 April 1946 tsunami. It was generated by an Aleutian-trench earthquake (Earth Magazine gives M8.1; other sources give about 8.6), arrived about 5 hours later, and killed 159 people in Hawaii (96 in Hilo). At Laupahoehoe the sea drew back and children went to look at fish flopping on the sand. Earth Magazine says it swept away '16 children and five teachers'; other sources give 24 dead in total, with breakdowns of 20+4 or 21+3. The disaster led to the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center (1948). Sources: https://www.earthmagazine.org/article/benchmarks-april-1-1946-hawaii-tsunami-ushers-pacific-wide-warning-system/ , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laup%C4%81hoehoe,_Hawaii , https://www.hawaiitribune-herald.com/2021/04/01/hawaii-news/a-wall-of-water-survivors-reflect-on-devastating-tsunami-that-struck-hilo-75-years-ago/
- Nuuanu slide. About half of Ko'olau volcano collapsed, roughly 1 to 1.5 million years ago. The debris runs about 200 km and is called one of the largest landslides on Earth. USGS says the largest block is 'about the size of Manhattan'; the Tuscaloosa block is about 30x20x1.5 km. Moore et al. (USGS 1994) count 68 slides longer than 20 km along the ridge, some over 5,000 km3. So 'city-sized blocks' is accurate and conservative. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nu%CA%BBuanu_Slide , https://www.usgs.gov/publications/giant-hawaiian-landslides , https://www.usgs.gov/publications/prodigious-submarine-landslides-hawaiian-ridge , https://usgs.gov/news/volcano-watch-oahu-niihau-and-kauai
- Mauna Kea is 4,205 m above sea level and about 6,000 m below, roughly 10,200 m from base to peak. The base definition is debated, so say 'more than 10 km'. Mauna Loa's true relief is about 17 km because the Moho is pushed down as much as 8 km. Sources: https://www.usgs.gov/faqs/how-big-are-hawaiian-volcanoes , https://usgs.gov/center-news/volcano-watch-how-high-mauna-loa
- The moat is real: the Hawaiian Deep is a flexural trough about 5.5 km deep, with an arch beyond it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_Trough
- Midway is a shield volcano about 28 million years old that sank while its reef grew upward. Drilling in 1965 (USGS) hit basalt at 157 m on Sand Island and 384 m under the reef. One 1972 K-Ar date gave 18 million years; that is an outlier, so use about 28 million years. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway_Atoll , https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70010514
- Kama'ehuakanaloa (renamed from Lo'ihi in July 2021). Summit about 975 m below sea level, last eruption probably 1996, emergence 'thousands of generations' away. Source: https://www.usgs.gov/observatories/hvo/news/volcano-watch-kamaehuakanaloa-volcano-formerly-known-loihi-seamount
- Kaga found 16-18 Oct 2019 by RV Petrel at about 5.4 km. Akagi identified 20 Oct 2019 at a similar depth. Yorktown found 19 May 1998 by Ballard at 16,650 ft (about 5 km). Nautilus filmed all three in Sept 2023. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_aircraft_carrier_Kaga , https://news.mit.edu/1998/mindell-0610 , https://nautiluslive.org/blog/2023/09/14/exploring-iconic-shipwrecks-battle-midway-provide-never-seen-details , https://www.papahanaumokuakea.gov/new-news/2019/10/21/kaga/

MUST FIX:
(1) The hero shot is wrong for Kaho'olawe. At the Last Glacial Maximum (about -120 m, 18,000 years ago) only Maui, Lana'i and Moloka'i were joined. The Kaho'olawe link was 'permanently broken between 200,000 and 150,000 years ago' by subsidence (Wikipedia, Maui Nui; Star-Bulletin). Say the -120 m drop joins three islands, and let Kaho'olawe join at a deeper level that we read off the bathymetry. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maui_Nui
(2) The carriers are not 'off Midway' or on its flank. From the sinking coordinates, Kaga (30°23'N 179°17'W) is about 165 nmi (about 300 km) northwest of Midway and Yorktown (30°36'N 176°34'W) about 150 nmi north; the press said 'about 200 miles north'. All three lie on the abyssal plain about 5 km down, inside Papahanaumokuakea. Soryu and Hiryu remain unfound in every report I saw.
(3) Laupahoehoe death counts vary, so say 'more than twenty people, most of them children'.
(4) Avoid the disputed Lana'i mega-tsunami deposits and any mega-tsunami hype. USGS treats giant collapses as very rare.
(5) The 1946 wave came from Alaska and is not part of Hawaiian geology. It is a metaphor for the open, not part of the science.
(6) 'Every island becomes a Midway' needs one nuance: the island will sink and erode, and past the Darwin Point near Kure it drowns into a seamount rather than staying an atoll.

result.facts_status:
The core story is TRUE and well documented, but several of the pitch's specifics need correcting.

CONFIRMED:
- Crews deserted and ships piled up in Yerba Buena Cove. The NPS says "by 1851, over 800 ships" filled the cove (many were not abandoned permanently). https://www.nps.gov/safr/learn/historyculture/buried-ships-of-san-francisco.htm
- Ships were used as warehouses, a saloon and housing, and the shoreline was filled with "sand, dirt and debris" (same NPS page).
- Niantic: arrived 5 July 1849; the captain discharged the last five crew on 11 July; it became a storeship and then the site of the Niantic Hotel (1851-72). It was rediscovered in 1872, 1907 and 1978, and its stern is at the Maritime Museum. https://home.nps.gov/safr/learn/historyculture/niantic.htm
- General Harrison: uncovered at Battery and Clay in 2001, reburied, and marked by an outline on the sidewalk (NPS; National Geographic 2017, https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/map-ships-buried-san-francisco).
- Apollo was a saloon and coffee house, destroyed on 4 May 1851, and lies under the Federal Reserve site. https://www.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_(storeship)
- Euphemia was a floating county jail (about $8,000, 1849-51). https://www.cdcr.ca.gov/insidecdcr/2018/06/06/ships-served-as-first-prisons-for-fledgling-state/
- Rome: hit by Muni Metro tunnel crews on 2 Dec 1994, and trains still run through it. https://www.sfmta.com/node/13600
- Candace (1818 whaler): exposed at 30 Spear St in 2005; the identification is "most probably". https://jamesdelgado.com/about-jim/archaeologist/candace/
- The May 1851 fire burned the cove's ships to the waterline (NPS).
- SS City of Rio de Janeiro: hit rocks in fog on 22 Feb 1901, killing 128 of 210 (mostly Chinese and Japanese immigrants). NOAA located it in 2014 in 287 ft of water, buried in mud. https://sanctuaries.noaa.gov/news/press/2014/pr121014.html
- USS Independence: a Crossroads target ship, scuttled in Jan 1951, lying upright at about 2,600 ft off the Farallones. It was surveyed with an autonomous vehicle in 2015, and Pacific Wrecks says it was first located in 2009. https://news.usni.org/2015/04/17/noaa-boeing-survey-wwii-era-carrier-uss-independence-sunk-near-san-francisco-in-1951
- 1906: the USGS says "damage was greatest on artificially filled ground, marshy ground and areas of incoherent sands", and that the Marina and South of Market "sustained heavy damage during the Loma Prieta earthquake of 1989". https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/events/1906calif/18april/soil.php
- 1989: USGS Professional Paper 1551 says soft soils amplified shaking and sandy artificial fill liquefied in the Marina. https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/pp1551
- The USGS gives a 72% chance of an M6.7+ Bay Area quake in 2014-2043 (Fact Sheet 2016-3020). https://www.usgs.gov/publications/earthquake-outlook-san-francisco-bay-region-2014-2043

FIXES NEEDED:
(a) Buried-ship count. Use "dozens", or "roughly 40 to 60, maybe 70", never "hundreds buried". The NPS says about 40-60, and Filion's 2023 map says 70+.
(b) Shoreline wording. The shoreline moved OUT into the bay; the 1849 shoreline (around Montgomery Street) now sits blocks inland.
(c) Euphemia was not the first jail (the Calaboose was).
(d) Quake twist. The worst San Francisco damage in 1989 was the Marina, on 1910s hydraulic fill, plus South of Market. It was NOT the 1849 buried-ship cove, so "the 1849 shoreline decides which streets shake hardest" overreaches. A search snippet attributes a passage to an archived USGS page (UNT web archive, returned HTTP 503): "the business district, which was built on ground made by filling in the cove of Yerba Buena", where pavements "were buckled, arched, and fissured". If it can be fetched, it would support a cove-specific 1906 beat, but I could not open the page, so this is unverified. Stay with "old shoreline / filled ground" (USGS framing) and do not claim the ships themselves cause shaking. No source says that.
(e) Fire date. The NPS Niantic page says 2 May 1851, while the standard date for the Great Fire is 3-4 May 1851. Use "May 1851".
(f) Independence lies at about 2,600 ft, which is the continental slope, not the "shelf".
(g) Bay depth. Figures vary by source: average 12-15 ft (Wikipedia), median about 12 ft (USGS tables), and 351 vs 372 ft for the deepest point. Use "most of the Bay is shallower than a two-storey house".
(h) City of Rio de Janeiro deaths: 128 per NOAA (some secondary sources differ).

Yes, an angle is clearly unclaimed: "Drain the Oceans, but real." Nat Geo's Drain the Oceans franchise (2-32M views per episode) and Contour Atlas only simulate drains. Here a real sea was really pumped dry, and the film works as a dig down through the seabed's layers. No incumbent asks what was on the bottom.

Proposed structure (reverse-chronology dig):
1. Cold open on the US-anchored find. A US government source says that while the Dutch were pumping one of the polders, "a plane with a U.S. star insignia gradually came into view". It was B-24H 42-7638 "Big Banner" of the 44th Bomb Group, shot down on 22 Dec 1943 with one survivor. The bodies of five crew were found in it during the 1970s recovery, and parts are now in the USAF museum in Dayton.
2. The ships: more than 400 wrecks. The anchor is the English "Queen Anne" merchantman, ca. 1700-1720, near Rutten, with still-filled wine bottles, jars of olives and peaches, and two Queen Anne spoons.
3. The drowned medieval villages: Marcnesse, Nagele and Fenehuysen I and II, found in 2020.
4. The 1945 re-flood as the midpoint twist.
5. A modern ticking clock that nobody uses: the dry land that revealed the ships is now destroying them. Drying, soil settling and ploughing are turning wrecks into "ghost ships", and the Queen Anne's wood was pulverised in a heatwave. Meanwhile the never-drained Markerwaard still holds ships preserved in the mud.
6. Payoff: Almere, 230K people on a 1968 seabed.

This is a sharper spine than the ideator's chronological 1916-1968 order, which repeats the incumbents' beats (Lely, the Afsluitdijk, the polders). Packaging should sell the bomber and the ships, never "Dutch engineering". "Ship found in a farm field" is itself a proven US premise (the Steamboat Arabia/Kansas cornfield videos get 0.3-1M views).

result.facts_status:
The core story is TRUE and well documented, but several lines in the premise and spine are wrong or overstated and must be fixed.

Verified:
- Zuiderzee Works: Zuiderzee Act of 14 June 1918, based on Lely's 1891 plan. The 32 km Afsluitdijk closed on 28 May 1932 (Wikipedia's table also lists 23 May). Polders drained: Wieringermeer 1930, Noordoostpolder 1942, Eastern Flevoland 1957, Southern Flevoland 1968. Markerwaard abandoned in 1986. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuiderzee_Works
- Shipwrecks: RCE says "over 400 shipwrecks" were studied, the "world's largest 'dry' naval graveyard" (https://mass.cultureelerfgoed.nl/themes/flevoland). Van Popta's database has 450 (NOS 2021, https://nos.nl/nieuwsuur/artikel/2366226-database-van-450-scheepswrakken-het-hele-verhaal-van-de-scheepsramp), with an estimated 3,000-4,000 wrecking disasters over about 700 years. Batavialand counts about 480 sites. Only a handful are identified. "Largest" is the heritage agencies' own claim, not a formal ranking.
- Ploughing and drainage work did expose and damage wrecks: the first ploughing and drain-laying are named in an RUG paper, and NOS says early Noordoostpolder finds came almost weekly. One plough find was reported (search summary of UKrant, page returned 403): farmer Dijkstra, potato field, a three-master carrying wine barrels.
- Queen Anne: https://www.visitflevoland.nl/en/locaties/974838362/shipwreck-of-the-queen-anne and RUG 2018 https://www.rug.nl/about-ug/latest-news/news/archief2018/nieuwsberichten/opgraving-vroeg-18e-eeuws-koopvaardijschip-in-de-noordoostpolder-begonnen?lang=en
- Four drowned villages: https://nltimes.nl/2020/10/26/four-submerged-villages-found-noordoostpolder
- B-24H 42-7638 "Big Banner": USAF museum fact sheet "WWII Relics from the Polders" (https://www.nationalmuseum.af.mil/Visit/Museum-Exhibits/Fact-Sheets/Display/Article/196177/wwii-relics-from-the-polders), Flevoland heritage (https://flevolandsgeheugen.nl/id/10890), https://mass.cultureelerfgoed.nl/b-24-liberator-big-banner. The salvage year conflicts: 1975 (Dutch sources) vs a project begun in 1976 (USAF). The sources say the wreck was "seen 1968" (Dutch) or "early 1970s" (USAF), so say "the 1970s". The co-pilot is called Charlie or Charles Taylor.
- ED603: raised from the open IJsselmeer near Kornwerderzand/Workum in Sept 2023 inside a pumped cofferdam. Remains of 3 missing crew were identified and buried in Workum on 9 Oct 2025. Raid: Bochum, night of 12/13 June 1943. https://raf.mod.uk/news/articles/ww2-lancaster-recovered-from-the-sea-bed-after-80-years/ and https://www.gov.uk/government/news/three-members-of-raf-lancaster-crew-buried-in-the-netherlands
- Wieringermeer: dike blown at 00:15 on 17 April 1945 with two charges of about 1,000 kg. The polder was full within 48 hours, about 3.75 m deep. It was declared dry again by the end of 1945 (11 Dec is common; TracesOfWar says July). No flood deaths, though resistance member A.C. de Graaf was shot. The motive is unclear and must not be asserted. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inundation_of_the_Wieringermeer
- 1916 flood, 13-14 Jan: 16 drowned on Marken (HHNK, https://en.hhnk.nl/podcast-stormvloed-1916-110-jaar-geleden). The total is vague: 19 in North Holland plus 32 at sea per Wikipedia, about 51 per Scientias.
- Almere: 229,574 people (CBS, 1 Jan 2025). Its polder was drained in 1968 and the first residents came in 1976. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almere

Errors to fix:
1. "Pumped dry most of the Zuiderzee" is false. The Zuiderzee was about 5,000 km² and the polders are about 1,650 km² (roughly a third, or about half of the water behind the dam). For US viewers: an area bigger than the city of Los Angeles.
2. "In 1945 the sea took the polder back" is wrong: by 1945 it was the freshwater IJsselmeer. Say "the water/the lake".
3. "Urk wakes up landlocked" is FALSE. Urk stopped being an island in 1939-42 but is still a harbour on the IJsselmeer. Schokland is the one that ended up in fields.
4. Wieringermeer was drained in 1930, before the Afsluitdijk closed, so the spine's order "dam closes, then pumps start" is wrong for the first polder.

result.facts_status:
The core story is TRUE and unusually well documented by US government primary sources. Several of the candidate's details need fixing.
PRIMARY SOURCES: USGS Open-File Report 97-724 (Sigurgeirsson; Jonsson & Matthiasson), https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/1997/of97-724/lavaoperations.html, /methods.html, /capacity.html, /water.html, /effect.html, /manpower.html, /lavacommentary.html. USGS booklet "Man Against Volcano" (Williams & Moore, 1976), https://pubs.usgs.gov/gip/70039211/report.pdf. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldfell and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heimaey.
CONFIRMED:
- The eruption began at about 01:55 on 23 Jan 1973. The fissure was about 1.6 km (1 mile) at first and grew to about 3 km, opening about 1 km from the town centre.
- There were 5,300 residents (not "5,000"). Nearly all were on the mainland within about 6 hours. The fishing fleet was in port, which sped up the evacuation; Wikipedia says storms had kept it there. A 2013 Iceland Review piece says US military helicopters from Keflavik flew out hospital patients (secondary source).
- Cooling started on 7 Feb with firemen, pumps and fire hoses flown in from the Keflavik airport fire station. So the fire-hose beat is real.
- The dredger Sandey arrived on 1 Mar and pumped about 400 l/s (about 0.4 Mt in total).
- On 11 Mar a report signed by six men (Sigurgeirsson, Sveinn Eiriksson and four others) asked for big pumps "within one week". The first US pumps landed on 26 Mar, a real ticking clock. In all, 32 fully equipped pumps (800-1,000 l/s) arrived at Keflavik on 26-30 Mar aboard three USAF C-141s and one C-5. 43 pumps were used in total. Some were pre-1953 US Navy "invasion pumps" built for fuel, and about half their impeller shafts broke and were rebuilt in Reykjavik.
- More than 19 miles of pipe were used. About 75 men worked at the peak. Pumping ran until 10 July.
- About 6.2 million tonnes of seawater were pumped in all (USGS OF 97-724). The cost was about $1.45-1.5M.
- A chunk of crater wall, "Flakkarinn" ("The Wanderer"), rode the lava toward the harbour mouth.
- The lava stopped about 100 m short of blocking the harbour. The narrowed mouth now works as a breakwater; USGS says "temporarily at least", with a long-term risk of shoaling.
- The island grew from 11.2 to about 13.4 km² (about 2.2-2.5 km², about 20%).
- The lava's heat later heated homes (first house connected in 1974; plants up to 40 MW).
CORRECTIONS / DISPUTED:
(1) Deaths: ONE man died of CO2 poisoning inside a building. Do not say "no one died".
(2) Losses: the town did not escape. A late-March surge, before the US pumps were working, overran about a fifth of the town. About 300 buildings were engulfed or burned and 60-70 more buried by tephra; Wikipedia's lead says about 400 homes. "Won" means the harbour and most of the town were saved.
(3) Water volume: sources disagree. USGS OF says 6.2 Mt; Wikipedia says 7.3 million m³; the booklet says 7.8 million cubic yards (about 6.0 million m³). Say "about 6 million tonnes". The viral "billions of tons" is false.
(4) Did the water work? The USGS booklet says the cooling "definitely had a marked effect" and that sprayed lava cooled 50-100x faster. But Sigurgeirsson himself wrote that "the true value of the lava-cooling operations on Heimaey will probably never be known", and the method was "strongly debated" at the time. Bulldozed tephra ramparts also helped. The narration must say this honestly.
(5) The idea did not come only from Sigurgeirsson: Keflavik fire chief Sveinn Eiriksson and engineer Valdimar K. Jonsson were central too.
(6) Grindavik 2023-25 used earth diversion walls, not seawater. These descend from Heimaey's ramparts, so "the same idea" overstates it. Reports of water spraying near Svartsengi in 2024 are UNVERIFIED.

result.facts_status:
The core story is true and well documented by NPS, USFWS, AP and Alaska public media. The specific numbers conflict, so a ledger is required.

CONFIRMED:
- Japan landed on Kiska on June 6 and on Attu on June 7, 1942, unopposed. About 1,140-1,200 troops landed at Chichagof Harbor. It was a Sunday, and villagers were walking home from church (Nick Golodoff's account).
- Foster Jones had just sent his weather report, radioed that the Japanese had landed, and destroyed the radio. He was the only civilian the Japanese army killed in North America.
- Etta Jones was taken to Japan separately (Yokohama, then Totsuka), survived, and died in Florida in 1965 at 86.
- The 42 Attuans were held in their village for about 3 months, then shipped in Sept 1942 (one source dates the departure Sept 14) by way of Kiska to Otaru on Hokkaido. They were held there until 1945. Deaths came from starvation, tuberculosis, beriberi and eating garbage; Chief Mike Hodikoff and his son died this way.
- After the war the survivors were not allowed home. The government said rebuilding was too costly or inconvenient. 16 went to Atka and 9 stayed in Seattle.
- Battle of Attu: May 11-30, 1943. US losses: 549 killed, 1,148 wounded, about 1,200 severe cold injuries plus 614 disease. Cold injured more men than enemy fire. Japanese: 2,351 dead and only 28 (24-29) captured, ending in a banzai charge.
- Kiska: the Japanese evacuated about 5,183 men under fog in under an hour on July 28-29, 1943. The Allies landed on Aug 15. Casualties: 92 killed and 221 wounded, including 28 Americans and 4 Canadians killed by friendly fire. 71 Navy men died when USS Abner Read struck a mine.
- The Coast Guard LORAN station closed on Aug 27, 2010 (or the 26th). The 2020 census counted 0 residents.
- Gregory Golodoff, the last survivor, died Nov 17, 2023 at 84. The ideator's "2023" is correct.
- In Aug 2017, 11 descendants first visited the site on the USFWS ship Tiglax.
- In Dec 2024, Helena Pagano demanded reparations from Japan. In 1951 Japan paid about $4,000 a year for three years, and Japan says the claim was settled by the San Francisco treaty.

DISPUTED (put in the ledger; use ranges or "nearly half"):
- How many Attuans: 42 (NPS) vs 41 (AP) vs 45 (Pacific Wrecks).
- How many died in Japan: 16 (Wikipedia) vs 21 (survivor Alex Prossof, quoted by NPS) vs 22 (AP) vs "almost half" (NPS). "Nearly half" is safe.
- Kiska troop count: "34,426" is commonly cited as the US+Canadian total, but the Wikipedia infobox says 34,000 US plus 5,300 Canadian. Casualties: 313 (infobox) vs "over 500" (Wikipedia lead) vs "over 100 from friendly fire" (NPS).
- Japanese prisoners at Attu: 24, 28 or 29.
- How Foster Jones died: Japan said suicide (slashed wrists); Etta's letters and his biographer Mary Breu, plus skull damage found later, point to execution by gunshot after he refused to fix the radio. Say "killed by the Japanese" and skip the decapitation claim.
- Attu to Atka distance: AP says 200 miles, which is wrong. KNBA says 500. Great-circle calculation gives about 530 miles (852 km).
- One web summary says the Attuans were taken "June 21 to Yokohama". That is wrong; that was Etta's route.
- Golodoff's account of "experimental injections" is single-witness. Attribute it or skip it.
- Wikipedia's claim of a "formal US apology in June 2017" is unverified. The 1988 Aleut restitution law is the documented act. Do not assert the 2017 apology.

SENSATIONAL OR UNSAFE:
- The "forbidden / can't visit" framing. Attu is in the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge and is reachable with permits. The village site belongs to the Aleut Corporation, and the Coast Guard manages the old LORAN site. "Nobody lives there" is accurate; "you can't go" is not.
- "Empty ever since" is only true if the narration acknowledges the Coast Guard and Navy presence from 1943 to 2010.

(b) The real twist, under-used: they survive Japan, cross the Pacific, and their own government won't let them go home. They end up 530 miles away and the village is never rebuilt.

Yes, there is an unclaimed angle. Tell the earthquakes as one continuous journey down the river, from on board the New Orleans, and show the geography breaking the boat's navigation tools one by one. No incumbent does this.

result.facts_status:
The core story is TRUE and well documented, but several pitched beats need correcting.

CONFIRMED:
- The New Orleans was built at Pittsburgh by Nicholas Roosevelt for Fulton and Livingston. Trial run 15 Oct 1811; departed Sunday 20 Oct 1811; passed Cincinnati 27 Oct; reached Louisville late on 28 Oct (contemporary newspapers, via Hanover College).
- Lydia gave birth to Henry Latrobe Roosevelt at Louisville, 30 Oct 1811. Their toddler Rosetta was also aboard.
- They waited for the Falls of the Ohio to rise and ran them in the last week of November with "five inches" to spare (Latrobe 1871).
- Crew: engineer Nicholas Baker, pilot Andrew Jack, six hands, two female servants, a waiter, a cook, and "an immense Newfoundland dog, named Tiger."
- Reached Natchez 30 Dec 1811 and New Orleans 10 Jan 1812. Sank on a snag near Baton Rouge, 14 Jul 1814.
- Nicholas was the great-granduncle of Theodore Roosevelt (per Heinz History Center).
- The Great Comet of 1811 was real and fed omen talk.

Earthquakes (USGS preferred magnitudes):
- M7.5 on 16 Dec 1811 at about 2:15am, plus an M7.0 "dawn" aftershock.
- M7.3 on 23 Jan 1812.
- M7.5 on 7 Feb 1812 on the Reelfoot fault.
- USGS: "The town of New Madrid was destroyed." Waves "overwhelmed many boats." Reelfoot Lake formed by subsidence of 1.5-6 m in the 7 Feb shock.
- Magnitudes are genuinely disputed (Hough about 7.0-7.5 versus Johnston about 8). Use "the strongest recorded in the eastern US" or "about 7.5", not 8+.

Voyage-in-the-quake episodes come from two family recollections:
- C.J. Latrobe, "The Rambler in North America" (1835, "directly from the lips of the parties themselves").
- J.H.B. Latrobe, "The First Steamboat Voyage on the Western Waters" (1871; Lydia's brother, written with her).

What they describe:
- Squatters near the Yellow Banks reporting shaking.
- Banks "tearing away from the land and falling into the river."
- The pilot "affirmed that he was lost."
- A mid-channel island gone.
- The night moored to an island: by morning the island had disappeared and the hawser had to be cut.
- At New Madrid, people begged to come aboard and were refused for lack of provisions.
- Tiger putting his head on Lydia's lap before shocks.
- A Chickasaw canoe race.
- A cabin fire.
- Lydia "lived in a constant fright, unable to sleep or sew, or read."
These are plausible but are retrospective, from 23 and 60 years later. The 1871 text has demonstrable errors: it puts the Louisville arrival on "the first of October" against newspapers' 28 Oct, and the Natchez dates conflict. Attribute these on screen ("as Lydia later told it").

MUST FIX:
(1) The cold open is wrong. On the night of 16 Dec the boat was NOT at the epicentre with a bank sliding beside it. It lay at anchor on the Ohio below the Falls, near the Yellow Banks (Owensboro area), about 200 miles away. They felt it as if the boat had "suddenly grounded", and some felt sea-sick. Re-open on the vanishing-island night instead: it is documented, undated, a few days later, near the Ohio mouth.
(2) The hero image puts the comet overhead during the collapse. Both Latrobes say "the comet had disappeared about this time." Keep the comet for the October departure.
(3) "Cannot go back upstream" overstates it. Latrobe says there was "no possibility of turning back" and "no place to stop," but the boat later ran Natchez to New Orleans against the current.
(4) The "river ran backward" twist needs care. USGS calls it an "illusion" produced by uplift and waves. Eyewitnesses describe a retrograde current both on 16 Dec (Eliza Bryan: "retrograde for a few minutes", at New Madrid, before the boat arrived) and on 7 Feb ("a retrograde current, rapid as a torrent"). So say the most violent reversal and the waterfalls came on 7 Feb after they had passed, not that it never happened before. Never say "for hours", "the whole river", or that they saw it.
(5) Waterfalls are documented: Matthias Speed, Lexington Reporter, 21 Mar 1812, "a dreadful rapid or falls... about equal to the rapids of the Ohio", tied by Johnston & Schweig (1996) to Reelfoot-fault uplift at Kentucky Bend.

(7) Boston church bells: no evidence. USGS does not claim it; Hough found no Boston newspaper mention and suggests a Charleston SC / Charlestown mix-up. Bells did ring in Charleston, and in Cahokia per John Reynolds. Present it as "no evidence", not "debunked".
(8) The death toll is unknown. Do not invent a number.

result.facts_status:
The core story is TRUE and very well documented: US Navy history office (NHHC), the Ocean Exploration Trust (OET) press release, National Geographic, the National WWII Museum. Several numbers in the pitch need care.

VERIFIED:
- Ironbottom Sound is the Allied sailors' name for Savo Sound, between Guadalcanal, Savo and Nggela (Florida). Five major naval battles, Aug-Dec 1942.
- Savo Island, 8-9 Aug 1942: 4 Allied heavy cruisers lost (Quincy, Vincennes, Astoria, HMAS Canberra) and 1,077 Allied killed. Crews were fatigued after two days of alert, in Condition II (half on watch).
- USS Juneau was torpedoed by the submarine I-26 on 13 Nov 1942 while withdrawing. 687 lost, including the five Sullivans. The wreck was found 17 Mar 2018 by RV Petrel at about 4,200 m, between Guadalcanal and San Cristobal, OUTSIDE the Sound (the pitch correctly says so).
- Kirishima was wrecked by USS Washington's 16-inch fire (Washington had detected the enemy by radar). She capsized and sank about 03:25 on 15 Nov 1942. The wreck lies upside down: Ballard found it in 1992 and Petrel imaged it in 2019.
- Tassafaronga, 30 Nov 1942: a Long Lance torpedo set off New Orleans' forward magazine and severed the bow between No. 1 and No. 2 turrets. The loose bow scraped down her port side. 182 killed (some sources say "over 180"). Lt Cdr Hayter and two others received posthumous Navy Crosses. She reached Tulagi, got coconut-log shoring, sailed stern-first toward Australia (Sydney), got a stub bow, then a new bow at Bremerton. She returned to fight and earned 17 battle stars. Sold for scrap Sept 1959.
- 2025 Nautilus expedition NA173 (OET with NOAA, UNH's DriX survey drone, US Navy history office): 13 wrecks, four imaged for the first time, two newly discovered (the New Orleans bow and IJN Teruzuki). Mapped over 1,000 km². ROV dives below 1,000 m. The bow lies at about 675 m (about 2,200 ft), paint still visible, anchor stamped "Navy Yard". It was identified by eliminating Minneapolis, whose bow lies in shallow water at Tulagi.

DISPUTED / CAREFUL:
1. Ship count varies widely. Wikipedia: "over 50 vessels". Nat Geo: "more than 100 warships". OET: "111 naval vessels, 1,450 planes, 20,000+ lives", which appears to cover campaign-wide losses including transports and small craft. Keep "dozens of warships" or attribute any figure.
2. Savo timing. About 40 minutes from first torpedoes (~01:38) to withdrawal (02:20). Quincy sank 02:38 and Vincennes 02:50, but Astoria sank at 12:15 and Canberra was scuttled that morning. Say "in under an hour four cruisers were wrecked; by noon all four were gone", not "sinking in half an hour".
3. "83 years". The bow was found July 2025, 82 years 7 months after the battle. Media use 83; "more than 80 years" is safest.
4. OET's own release is inconsistent: the subhead says "three brand-new shipwrecks", the body says "four imaged for the first time, two discovered".
5. Bow length. Navsource says about 150 ft; the WWII Museum says "about one-third of the ship". The 588-ft ship lost roughly a quarter, so use "everything forward of the second gun turret".
6. Teruzuki's loss is attributed to PT-boat torpedoes on 12 Dec 1942. Fine.
7. Forgy and "Praise the Lord...": early press credited Chaplain Maguire, and Forgy himself was modest about it. Say "credited to".
8. "Walk from wreck to wreck" is poetic. The wrecks are spread over roughly 1,000 km² at about 600 m average depth.
Nothing in the core story is sensational or unknowable.

- The 2025 discovery is now 16 months old, so it is no longer news.
- We cannot show the real discovery imagery.

- Cold-open on Pearl Harbor or Tassafaronga with New Orleans, not on Savo.

result.unclaimed_angle:
Tell it as one story, "the mistake that became the law", with a war of stones as the spine. All four steps below are confirmed in the Supreme Court record (267 U.S. 30 and the 268 U.S. 108 decree).
1. In 1868 Darling sets stones along the 37th parallel.
2. By 1902 an inspector finds that few of the corners still exist and calls the line "evidently erroneously established".
3. The government sends Howard Carpenter to resurvey and specifically tells him to "obliterate" Darling's monuments. Congress accepts Carpenter's line in 1908, and the President vetoes it.
4. In 1925 the Supreme Court says the old line wins, orders Carpenter's corners destroyed and Darling's destroyed corners put back, and appoints a commissioner (Arthur D. Kidder) to re-mark the line. One secondary source says the confusion lasted until 1960.

Nothing on YouTube tells this. Two more beats nobody uses:
- Even a perfectly surveyed Colorado would not be a rectangle. On a globe the north edge is about 21 miles shorter than the south edge (about 365 vs 387 mi). Use this as a 20-second "pedant beat" so the comments do not do it for us.
- Darling himself: born in Vermont in 1832, a Civil War lieutenant in the 18th U.S. Colored Infantry, died in June 1912 (the year New Mexico became a state) leaving an estate worth $23, "a few items of furniture and his compass". He is buried at Arlington. This comes from one secondary source.

The Four Corners "2.5 miles off" media myth of 2009 gives a myth inside the myth: NGS corrected it to about 1,800 ft or less, and said the monument is legally where it should be. That suits the mapmyth lens.

result.facts_status:
The core story is true and documented in the primary record. Several pitch details need tightening.

Confirmed:
(1) Darling surveyed the 37th parallel in 1868 from the Macomb monument west to the 109th meridian: over 331 miles, 11 astronomical monuments, notes approved in 1869. The extension east was by Major (1874) and Preston (1900). Sources: https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/267/30 and https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/US/267/267.US.30.12.html
(2) A 1902 examiner found that few of Darling's corners remained and that the line was "evidently erroneously established". Carpenter's resurvey of 1902-03 was told to "obliterate" Darling's marks. Carpenter's line would have moved "a large strip" to New Mexico, with "the greater portions of one town and two villages, and five post offices". Congress's 1908 joint resolution accepting it was "vetoed by the President". The opinion does not name him; it was presumably T. Roosevelt, but that is not verified.
(3) New Mexico v. Colorado, 267 U.S. 30 (1925): New Mexico's bill was dismissed and the Darling line held to be the boundary. Key reasoning: "governments are bound by the practical line that has been established as their boundary, although not precisely a true one." The Court did not say which line was correct: "It may well be that neither is entirely correct."
(4) The decree (268 U.S. 108, https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/268/108) appointed Arthur D. Kidder, ordered Darling corners that Carpenter destroyed to be restored and Carpenter's new corners destroyed, and kept the 1917 Perkins restoration.
(5) The New Mexico Bar Bulletin (2007, https://www.sbnm.org/Portals/NMBAR/AboutUs/committees/Historical/NMConstitutionMeetsFacts.pdf) says the Darling line runs south of the parallel from about SR 551 in Union County to about 5 miles west of US 84. New Mexico's constitution still describes 37°N.
(6) NGS (https://www.ngs.noaa.gov/INFO/fourcorners.shtml): Chandler Robbins set Four Corners in 1875. The offset is "only about 1800 feet, or less", with the intended spot to the west. "The location of the physical monument is the ultimate authority." The 2009 "2.5 miles" figure was a media error caused by mixing up the Washington and Greenwich meridians.

Needs care:
- "697 sides" is murky. The Gazette/OutThere Colorado count is a QGIS count, while Wikipedia says "697 boundary markers". Always say "one count says".
- The Edith, CO jog (about 3,400 ft southeast, then about 2,820 ft south) and the swerve of up to about 1,770 ft near Oklahoma come from secondary sources (Big Think was blocked from fetching, so they are cited via search summaries). Edith is in the foothills by the Navajo River, so "in the San Juan Mountains" is loose.
- Per the Lidar magazine profile (https://lidarmag.com/2009/03/21/ehud-n-darling/), Professor John Weissner did most of the star observations, not Darling. That profile also says Macomb's 1859 start monument was about 2 miles too far west, Darling's line had a 24-mile gap in rough country, and Darling's end monument was 1.5 miles west of where Four Corners was set. All of this is single-source.
- "Ranches and taxes in the wrong state" is an embellishment. Use town, villages and post offices.
- The claim that the dispute dragged on until 1960 comes from a secondary source only (https://lidarmag.com/2009/04/05/the-boundary-of-all-these-kingdoms/).
- Georgia: the 1818 survey put the 35th parallel about 1 mile south (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee%E2%80%93Georgia_water_dispute; Camak, Nickajack). Georgia has tried at least 8-10 times: 2008 resolution, 2013 HR 4, and a 2019 resolution vetoed by Gov. Kemp. The latest action I could verify is 2019. My web-search budget ran out before I could check 2020-2026, so "keeps trying" needs a fresh check. The Short from 5 days ago suggests the topic is being talked about again.
- Pedantry: even an error-free Colorado is a spherical quadrilateral, about 21 miles shorter on top.
Other sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Corners_Monument, https://history.denverlibrary.org/node/22389, https://www.ripleys.com/stories/colorado-shape

Public-domain material is strong for maps and archives, and weak for the people.

Public-domain sources:
- U.S. Census TIGER/Line full-resolution state boundaries and the USGS National Boundary Dataset. These carry the real kinks, so every kink zoom can be rendered from true geometry.
- USGS 3DEP 10 m / 1 m DEM along the line, for real 3D terrain at the Edith jog and the Raton/Mesa de Maya stretch.
- USDA NAIP 0.6 m aerial imagery, for the ground under the kinks (fences and roads sometimes follow the line).
- USGS Historical Topographic Map Collection scans, which label the "Colorado-New Mexico State Line" and monuments.
- BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov): plats and field notes of the 1868 Darling, 1874 Major and 1902-03 Carpenter surveys.
- Library of Congress Geography & Map Division: 1861-1880s Colorado Territory maps.
- Hayden Survey (1873-76, in Colorado) and Wheeler Survey photographs by W. H. Jackson and T. O'Sullivan (LOC, USGS, NARA): real 1870s survey crews with transits, chains and mules in Colorado mountains, the ideal period B-roll.
- U.S. Reports pages for the 1925 opinion and decree.
- NGS datasheets for boundary monuments.
- Georgia: LOC maps of 1818-1826, TVA/USGS Nickajack Lake imagery, Landsat.

Not reliably public domain: a portrait of Darling (none found), photos of the Four Corners and Camak Stone on Wikimedia (check each license; some are CC-BY), and anything from the Navajo Nation park (photography there requires a fee).

What our engine would render:
- A globe dive to a glowing "rectangle", then a 3D DEM flyover along the "straight" line that jogs.
- An overlay of the intended parallel against the legal line, with a counter as the "697" ticks up.
- A spherical-quadrilateral morph showing the 21-mile shorter north edge.
- Low-poly CC0 crew scenes. Quaternius/Kenney have no transit or chain props, so stone cairns, a transit and a chain must be modeled.
- A comic stone-war sequence: Carpenter's crew knocks Darling's stones over, then a gavel, then Carpenter's stones knocked over and Darling's put back.
- A Four Corners pin moving 1,800 ft and a "2.5 miles" headline crossed out.
- The Georgia line sliding 1 mile north to touch the Tennessee River.

Caveat: the kinks are 0.3-0.7 mile on a state about 380 miles wide. Every reveal needs an extreme zoom and a thick line, or it will die on mobile, the same failure as ep01.
result.story_strength:
6/10. It rises to about 6.5 if the war of stones becomes the spine.

Characters: Darling is a good find (Civil War officer in a Black regiment, died the year New Mexico became a state with $23 and his compass), but there is no portrait and little first-person material. Carpenter is a natural foil, though only a name in the record.

Stakes: modest and bloodless. The prize is one town, two villages and five post offices. Nobody was hurt, there are no famous property fights on record, and the climax is a court opinion.

Ticking clock: none. The time span runs 1868-1925, or 1960, which is slow.

Twists: good and real. The wrong line wins. The government destroyed the old stones and the Court ordered them put back. Four Corners sits about 1,800 ft off yet is legally correct, and even the 2009 "it's wrong" headline was itself wrong.

Ending: thematically strong ("the map isn't the border, the stones are"). The Georgia water payoff gives present-day stakes but needs a current hook.

Risks: the opening myth is already widely known among geography viewers (a 7.7M Short and list items in 2.5M-view videos), so the reveal may land as "I knew that". Reaching 13 minutes will probably force a drift toward a list of other survey errors. As a 9-11 minute film it is tight and defensible. As a 1M-view swing it looks weaker than spectacle or forbidden-place premises: no visual transformation, low emotional stakes, and a near-zero search floor.
result.red_flags:
1) Mobile legibility. The hero reveal is fine line geometry, exactly the dense-map style that cost ep01 its phone viewers (14% average view duration). It needs giant zooms, thick lines and 3D terrain at every beat.
2) The hook fact is already spent for the target audience (7.7M Short, dozens of copies, likely items in Map Pack's 2.5M and 447K list videos). Lead with the legal twist and the war of stones, not with "it's not a rectangle".
3) Near-zero search: vidIQ shows a volume score of 0 and under 750 searches a month. This depends entirely on Suggested CTR, which was ep01's weakest metric at 1.97%.
4) "697" is unofficial, and sources disagree on whether it counts sides or markers. Say "one count".
5) The pitch overstates details. "In the San Juan Mountains" should be the Edith/Navajo River foothills. "Ranches and taxes" should be "one town, two villages, five post offices". "Darling's star sightings" were mostly made by John Weissner. The President who vetoed in 1908 is not named in the opinion. The 1960 end date is secondary-only.
6) The Georgia payoff currency is unverified after the 2019 Kemp veto (search budget ran out). Recheck before scripting "still".
7) Pedant risk: even without survey errors Colorado is not a rectangle (north edge about 21 miles shorter). Address it on screen or the comments will.
8) Bad timing: catastrophic floods in Archuleta County CO, San Juan County NM and on the Georgia-Tennessee border are in the news this week (Nov 2026). Avoid flippant water or "wrong state" jokes about these communities.
9) Four Corners belongs to a Navajo Nation tribal park and many Wikimedia photos are CC, not public domain. Check licenses.
10) Length risk: the material for a single story runs about 9-11 minutes, and padding to 13+ turns it into a list video that competes directly with Map Pack and Geoff.

result.facts_status:
The core story is TRUE and documented, but it rests mostly on two or three Russian accounts that disagree in the details.

Confirmed by at least two sources:
- In the night of 12 April 1982 (one source says 13 April), the diesel power plant at Vostok burned out in about 15 minutes. Both main generators and both backups were lost, during the 27th Soviet Antarctic Expedition winter.
- Mechanic Alexei (Алексей) Karpenko died of smoke after going in to shut the diesels down.
- The station chief was Pyotr (Пётр) Astakhov, aged 50.
- Without power, the electric snow-melter for drinking water was useless. Aircraft cannot operate below about -60°C.
- The crew moved into small huts and lived on drip stoves burning diesel (proposed by Boris Moiseev), then five stoves welded from gas cylinders. It was +25-30°C next to a stove and about 0°C two metres away. They made candles from paraffin and asbestos rope.
- An old roughly 2 kW diesel from the drilling rig was revived to power the radio. Contact was restored on the evening of 13 April, and later a 1950s diesel was salvaged from the scrapyard.
- A barrel bathhouse was rigged near the end of winter.
- The crew told Moscow not to attempt a rescue and said they would hold out until spring.

Sources:
- Nauka i Zhizn, G. Lyatiev, "Погорельцы шестого континента" (2001): https://www.nkj.ru/archive/articles/5790/
- RT 2022 interview with crew doctor Arkady Maksimov, whose 2022 memoir «Восток на самом дальнем юге» is based on his diary. RT is Russian state media, so use it only for attributed Maksimov material: https://russian.rt.com/russia/article/1002593-pozhar-stanciya-vostok-antarktida
- Michael Ashley, UNSW, in The Conversation (2013): https://theconversation.com/building-a-telescope-in-the-coldest-place-on-earth-21482
- gw2ru: https://www.gw2ru.com/travel/55620-russians-survive-polar-conditions
- Meduza (cause given as a short circuit): https://meduza.io/en/feature/2020/12/22/trouble-at-the-vostok-station

Disputed or needing a ledger:
(a) Head count. Nauka i Zhizn has 21 arriving and 20 after the fire. RT has 20 in total including Karpenko, plus a sick man evacuated in March. The Conversation has 20 present and 19 survivors. Say "about twenty men" or settle it with Maksimov's book.
(b) Relief. Nauka i Zhizn says an Il-14 landed in early November 1982, with a tractor train from Mirny about two weeks later. The Conversation says "after 227 days" a tractor came, which is about 25 Nov. RT says the first plane was in early January 1983, bringing the new chief Budretsky. That is probably a later flight; the early-November plane is best supported.
(c) Second fire. Maksimov says the drilling rig burned in DECEMBER 1982, after relief had arrived, so the spine's Chapter 4 placement is chronologically wrong.
(d) The "coded radio message" comes only from Maksimov via RT.
(e) The Conversation says "Moscow sent mechanics" during the winter, which is implausible and likely garbled. Do not use it.
(f) "Refused rescue" is true as a stance, but a winter rescue was practically impossible anyway. Word it as "they told Moscow not to try", never as a heroic refusal of an available flight.

Temperature: NOAA GHCN-Daily for Vostok (AYM00089606) holds 113 daily means for Apr–Nov 1982. The coldest is -79.2°C on 27 Aug 1982, with August and September means of -69 to -70°C. "Cold heading toward -80" is accurate if phrased that way, and the data proves the observations continued: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/pub/data/ghcn/daily/by_station/AYM00089606.csv.gz

Record and lake:
- -89.2°C (-128.6°F) was measured at Vostok on 21 July 1983 at 05:45 Moscow time, by the NEXT crew (28th expedition). It is the lowest temperature recorded by a weather station. Previous record: -88.3°C in 1960. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_Station. The analysis paper is Turner et al. 2009, JGR, doi:10.1029/2009JD012104 (cited from memory, not fetched).
- Satellites have sensed colder snow-surface (skin) temperatures, about -93 to -98°C between Dome A and Dome F. Phrase the record as "the lowest temperature ever measured by a weather station."
- An unconfirmed -91°C reading at Vostok in 1997 exists.
- Lake Vostok lies about 4 km below the surface, about 250 x 50 km. Russian drillers reached it on 5 Feb 2012 at about 3,768 m. "Sealed for about 15 million years" is an estimate; there is also a kerosene/Freon contamination dispute. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Vostok
- Elevation 3,488 m. Vostok was founded 16 Dec 1957.
- "1,400 km to the coast": the tractor route to Mirny is roughly that long, but this needs a precise source.

Note: the shared web-search budget ran out mid-check, so Maksimov's book and Turner 2009 were not fetched directly. Everything else above was read from the URLs given.
